both components non-decreasing, giving
$\texttt{gibbsExpectationBC\_plus\_monotone\_beta\_singleton}$ (the single spin is
monotone, $\texttt{spinProduct\_singleton\_monotone}$).  Reference: Friedli--Velenik
(Cambridge, 2017), \S3.6; Glimm--Jaffe Prop.~4.2.1.

\subsection{$\beta$-monotonicity of the infinite-volume magnetization
(\texttt{Concrete/LatticeGraphCorrelation/MagnetizationBetaMonotone.lean})}

The order parameter grows with the inverse temperature: $m^+(\beta,h)$ and $m^*(\beta)$
are monotone increasing in $\beta$.  The finite-volume single-spin box expectation
equals a $+$ boundary spin correlation $\langle\sigma_{\langle x\rangle}\rangle$ on the
cubic ambient ($\texttt{plusBoxObsExpectation\_singleSpin\_eq}$, via
$\texttt{Spin.sign} = \texttt{spinProduct}\,\{x\}$ and $\texttt{restrictConfig}$), so it
inherits the boundary $\beta$-monotonicity
($\texttt{plusBoxObsExpectation\_singleSpin\_mono\_beta}$).  Passing to the limit,
$m^+(\beta,h)$ is nondecreasing in $\beta$
($\texttt{plusMagnetization\_mono\_beta}$, for $J,h\ge 0$ and $0<\beta_1\le\beta_2$, by
$\texttt{le\_of\_tendsto\_of\_tendsto'}$), and hence so is the spontaneous magnetization
$m^*(\beta)$ ($\texttt{plusStateSpontaneousMagnetization\_mono\_beta}$).  This completes
the $\beta$/$J$-monotonicity programme (Issue~\#3605: boundary GKS-I/II $\to$ $J$- $\to$
$\beta$-monotonicity $\to$ $m^+$/$m^*$).  Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017),
\S3.6; Glimm--Jaffe Prop.~4.2.1.

\subsection{Box-independence of the $\pm$-state functional
(\texttt{Concrete/LatticeGraphCorrelation/PlusStateCongrN.lean})}

The $\pm$-state functional does not depend on the witnessing box $N$ of the support
hypothesis (well-definedness).  Equal box radii give equal box expectations
($\texttt{plusBoxObsExpectation\_index\_congr}$, proof-irrelevant supports), and any two
witnesses $hS_1 : O.S \subseteq \texttt{cubicBox}\,d\,N_1$,
$hS_2 : O.S \subseteq \texttt{cubicBox}\,d\,N_2$ give the same value
($\texttt{plusStateExpectation\_congr\_N}$): both equal the limit of the screened box
expectations, which are shifts of the same sequence
($\texttt{tendsto\_plusStateExpectation}$, $\texttt{tendsto\_add\_atTop\_nat}$,
$\texttt{tendsto\_nhds\_unique}$).  The $-$ state inherits this
($\texttt{minusStateExpectation\_congr\_N}$, the $(-h,\texttt{flipObs})$
specialisation).  Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.4 Theorem~3.17.

\subsection{Site-independence of the $+$ magnetization
(\texttt{Concrete/LatticeGraphCorrelation/MagnetizationSiteIndependence.lean})}

The order parameter is translation-invariant: $m^+(a +_v x) = m^+(x)$
($\texttt{plusMagnetization\_vadd}$).  The translated single-spin observable equals the
single-spin observable at the translated site
($\texttt{singleSpinObs\_vadd\_eq}$: support $\texttt{vaddFinset}\,a\,\{x\} = \{a +_v
x\}$ and the pulled-back spin value matches, via
$\texttt{configVaddEquiv\_symm\_apply}$ and $\texttt{vaddSubtypeEquiv\_apply\_coe}$,
using the dependent-support extensionality $\texttt{LocalObservable.ext\_of\_support\_eq}$).
Applying the translation invariance of the $+$-state functional
($\texttt{plusStateExpectation\_vadd}$) and bridging the observable/witnessing-box
mismatch with $\texttt{plusStateExpectation\_congr\_obs}$ (built on
$\texttt{plusStateExpectation\_congr\_N}$) gives the site-independence.  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.6.

\subsection{Two-point clustering bounds for the $+$ boundary state
(\texttt{Inequalities/GKSBoundaryConditionTwoPoint.lean})}

Finite-volume GKS consequences for two-point functions, towards the high-temperature
vanishing of the spontaneous magnetization.  With $\{i\} \mathbin{\triangle} \{j\} =
\{i,j\}$ for $i \ne j$ ($\texttt{symmDiff\_pair}$), GKS-I gives non-negativity of the
pair correlation $\langle\sigma_i\sigma_j\rangle^+_\Lambda \ge 0$
($\texttt{gibbsExpectationBC\_plus\_spinProduct\_pair\_nonneg}$) and GKS-II gives the
clustering bound $\langle\sigma_i\rangle^+_\Lambda\,\langle\sigma_j\rangle^+_\Lambda \le
\langle\sigma_i\sigma_j\rangle^+_\Lambda$
($\texttt{gibbsExpectationBC\_plus\_two\_point\_ge\_product}$).  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7; Theorem~3.49 (GKS).

\subsection{Infinite-volume $+$ two-point function
(\texttt{Concrete/LatticeGraphCorrelation/PlusTwoPoint.lean})}

The cubic-exhaustion $+$-state two-point function $\mu^+(\sigma_i\sigma_j)$ is the
$\texttt{plusStateExpectation}$ of the two-spin product observable $\texttt{twoSpinObs}$
(support $\{i,j\}$, $\varphi = s(\sigma_i)s(\sigma_j)$).  The finite-volume bridge
$\texttt{plusBoxObsExpectation\_twoSpin\_eq}$ identifies its $+$ box expectation with the
$+$ boundary spin-product correlation $\langle\sigma_{\langle i\rangle}\sigma_{\langle
j\rangle}\rangle$ on the cubic ambient (via $\texttt{Spin.sign} = {\uparrow}\texttt{toSign}$,
$\texttt{Finset.prod\_pair}$ for $i\ne j$, and $\texttt{restrictConfig}$), and the
screened box expectations converge to $\mu^+(\sigma_i\sigma_j)$
($\texttt{tendsto\_plusTwoPoint}$).  This is the foundation for the clustering bound
$m^{*2} \le \mu^+(\sigma_0\sigma_x)$ towards the high-temperature $m^*=0$.  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.

\subsection{The clustering bound $m^{*2} \le \mu^+(\sigma_0\sigma_x)$
(\texttt{SpontaneousMagnetizationTwoPoint.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Bounds the squared $+$-state spontaneous magnetization by
the infinite-volume $+$ two-point function: $m^*(\beta)^2 \le \mu^+(\sigma_0\sigma_x)$ for
$x \ne 0$, $0<\beta$, $0\le J$
($\texttt{plusStateSpontaneousMagnetization\_sq\_le\_plusTwoPoint}$).  This is the
GKS-II clustering bound taken to the infinite-volume limit, a key step towards the
high-temperature $m^*=0$.

\textbf{Argument:} The finite-box clustering
$\langle\sigma_i\rangle^+_{\mathrm{box}}\,\langle\sigma_j\rangle^+_{\mathrm{box}} \le
\langle\sigma_i\sigma_j\rangle^+_{\mathrm{box}}$ for $i\ne j$
($\texttt{plusBoxObsExpectation\_two\_point\_clustering}$) follows from the single- and
two-spin finite-volume bridges plus the boundary-condition GKS-II inequality
$\texttt{gibbsExpectationBC\_plus\_two\_point\_ge\_product}$.  To pass to the limit, all
three box sequences are aligned at the common radius $M := \texttt{latticeRadius}\,0 +
\texttt{latticeRadius}\,x$, with $\texttt{tendsto\_plusMagnetization\_atRadius}$ providing
the single-spin convergence $\langle\sigma_x\rangle^+_{\mathrm{box}(M)} \to m^+(x)$ at the
shifted radius (box-independence of the limit, via
$\texttt{plusStateExpectation\_congr\_N}$).  Then $\texttt{le\_of\_tendsto\_of\_tendsto'}$
gives $m^+(0)\,m^+(x) \le \mu^+(\sigma_0\sigma_x)$, and site-independence $m^+(x) = m^+(0)
= m^*$ ($\texttt{plusMagnetization\_vadd}$) turns the left side into $m^{*2}$.  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.

\subsection{The $+$-boundary high-temperature representation of $Z^+_\Lambda$
(\texttt{PlusHighTempRepresentation.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Establishes the boundary-condition analogue of the
free-state high-temperature (random-graph) representation, towards the high-temperature
vanishing $m^*(\beta) = 0$.  The headline is FV (3.45) for the $+$ state:
\[
  Z^+_\Lambda \;=\; 2^{|\Lambda|}\,(\cosh\beta J)^{|E|}
    \sum_{\substack{X \subseteq E \\ I(v,X)\ \mathrm{even}\ \forall v \in \Lambda}}
      (\tanh\beta J)^{|X|}
\]
($\texttt{partitionFunctionBC\_plus\_h\_zero\_closed}$), the sum running over subgraphs
$X$ with even degree at every \emph{interior} vertex $v \in \Lambda$.

\textbf{Ingredients:} The per-configuration product form
$e^{-\beta H} = (\cosh\beta J)^{|E|}\prod_e(1 + \tanh(\beta J)\sigma_i\sigma_j)$ (FV (3.42),
$\texttt{boltzmannWeight\_h\_zero\_prod}$) and the observation that the $+$-boundary weight
is the agreement-indicator of the ordinary Boltzmann weight
($\texttt{boltzmannWeightBC\_plus\_eq\_indicator}$).  The new ingredient relative to the
free state is the \textbf{pinned-boundary parity collapse} (FV (3.44)):
\[
  \sum_{\sigma\,:\,\mathrm{agreesOff}\,\Lambda\,(+)}
    \prod_{v} (\sigma_v)^{k_v}
  \;=\; \begin{cases} 2^{|\Lambda|} & \text{if } k_v \text{ even } \forall v \in \Lambda,\\
    0 & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
\]
($\texttt{sum\_indicator\_agreesOff\_plus\_prod\_pow}$).  Since the $+$ state sums only over
configurations agreeing with the all-$+$ boundary off $\Lambda$, the per-vertex parity
argument runs over the interior vertices only (the exterior factors are pinned to $+1$ and
contribute $1$).  The proof writes the boundary restriction as a per-vertex pinning factor,
applies the full configuration-space Fubini ($\texttt{Fintype.prod\_sum}$), and evaluates
the single-spin sums.  Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3,
eqs. (3.41)--(3.45), pp. 116--117.

\subsection{The $+$-boundary one-point function ratio
(\texttt{PlusOnePointRepresentation.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The high-temperature representation of the $+$-boundary
spin-product expectation $\langle\sigma_A\rangle^+_\Lambda$ (FV (3.46)).  The numerator
carries an extra spin-product factor $\sigma^A = \prod_{i\in A}\sigma_i$, which is folded
into the edge-product vertex powers,
$\sigma^A\,\prod_{e\in X}\sigma_i\sigma_j = \prod_v (\sigma_v)^{[v\in A] + \deg_X(v)}$
($\texttt{spinProduct\_mul\_prod\_edgeSpin\_eq\_prod\_pow}$), so the same pinned-boundary
parity collapse applies with the \emph{$A$-shifted} exponent.  The numerator
representation ($\texttt{numeratorBC\_plus\_spinProduct\_h\_zero\_closed}$) is
\[
  \sum_\sigma \sigma^A\,w^+_\Lambda(\sigma)
  \;=\; 2^{|\Lambda|}(\cosh\beta J)^{|E|}
    \sum_{\substack{X \subseteq E \\ [v\in A]+\deg_X(v)\ \mathrm{even}\ \forall v\in\Lambda}}
      (\tanh\beta J)^{|X|},
\]
the parity being even off $A$ and odd on $A\cap\Lambda$ (the set $E^{+;0}$ of FV (3.46) for
a singleton).  Dividing by $Z^+_\Lambda$, the common prefactor cancels, giving the ratio
\[
  \langle\sigma_A\rangle^+_\Lambda
  \;=\; \frac{\sum_{X\,:\,A\text{-shifted even}} (\tanh\beta J)^{|X|}}
             {\sum_{X\,:\,\mathrm{even}} (\tanh\beta J)^{|X|}}
\]
($\texttt{gibbsExpectationBC\_plus\_spinProduct\_h\_zero\_ratio}$; singleton form
$\texttt{gibbsExpectationBC\_plus\_singleSpin\_h\_zero\_ratio}$).  The denominator is
positive ($\texttt{evenSubgraphSum\_pos}$, from $Z^+_\Lambda > 0$).  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eqs. (3.46)--(3.47), pp. 116--117.

\subsection{The connected-component bound $\langle\sigma_i\rangle^+_\Lambda \le
\sum_C (\tanh\beta J)^{|C|}$ (\texttt{PlusOnePointConnectedBound.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Decomposes the $E^{+;0}$ numerator by the connected component
of the origin and bounds the one-point ratio, giving FV (3.48)
\[
  \langle\sigma_i\rangle^+_\Lambda \;\le\; \sum_{C} (\tanh\beta J)^{|C|},
\]
the sum over the connected components $C$ of the origin arising from the $E^{+;0}$
subgraphs (for $i \in \Lambda$, $0 \le \tanh\beta J$).

\textbf{Ingredients:} The component $\texttt{componentOfZero}\,X\,z$ is the union of the
edge-components ($\texttt{edgeComponent}$, from the cluster-expansion development) of the
$X$-edges incident to $z$.  It is closed under shared vertices
($\texttt{componentOfZero\_absorbs\_incident}$), so it shares no vertex with its complement
$X \setminus \texttt{componentOfZero}\,X\,i$; consequently (FV (3.47),
$\texttt{sdiff\_componentOfZero\_even\_on}$) the complement is even on $\Lambda$ --- the
odd parity at $i$ is entirely absorbed by the origin's component, leaving the rest even.

\textbf{Argument:} Fibre the numerator $\sum_{X \in E^{+;0}}(\tanh\beta J)^{|X|}$ over the
map $X \mapsto \texttt{componentOfZero}\,X\,i$ ($\texttt{Finset.sum\_fiberwise\_of\_maps\_to}$).
On each fibre $(\tanh\beta J)^{|X|} = (\tanh\beta J)^{|C|}(\tanh\beta J)^{|X \setminus C|}$
(card additivity over the disjoint union $C \sqcup (X \setminus C)$), and the complement map
$X \mapsto X \setminus C$ is injective into the even-on-$\Lambda$ subgraphs, so the fibre's
complement sum is at most the full even sum
($\texttt{Finset.sum\_le\_sum\_of\_subset\_of\_nonneg}$, using $0 \le \tanh\beta J$) --- the
ratio-by-1 of FV (3.48).  Dividing by $Z^+_\Lambda$ leaves only the component sum.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eqs. (3.47)--(3.48), pp. 117--118.

\subsection{Distance bound for edge-connected edge sets
(\texttt{EdgeSetDistance.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The graph-theoretic input to FV (3.49): a connected component
reaching a far vertex must have many edges.  For an edge-connected edge set
$X : \texttt{Finset}\,(\texttt{Sym2}\,\iota)$ with $X \subseteq G.\texttt{edgeFinset}$ and
vertices $u, v$ each incident to an edge of $X$,
\[
  G.\mathrm{dist}\,u\,v \;\le\; |X|
\]
($\texttt{dist\_le\_card\_of\_edgeConnected}$).

\textbf{Argument:} The edge-adjacency chains (\texttt{ReflTransGen (edgeAdjacentIn X)})
defining edge-connectedness lift to reachability in $\texttt{fromEdgeSet}\,\uparrow\!X$
($\texttt{reachable\_fromEdgeSet\_of\_reflTransGen}$, by induction on the chain, each
shared-vertex step giving an adjacency).  A shortest path between reachable endpoints is a
trail, so its edges are distinct and lie in $X$; hence its length --- and therefore the
distance --- is at most $|X|$ ($\texttt{fromEdgeSet\_dist\_le\_card}$, via
$\texttt{IsTrail}$ edge-nodup and $\texttt{Walk.bypass}$).  Transferring to the supergraph
$G$ uses $\texttt{fromEdgeSet}\,\uparrow\!X \le G$ and
$\texttt{Reachable.dist\_anti}$.  Specialised to the origin's component, when $X$ has an
edge at $z$ the vertex-component $\texttt{componentOfZero}\,X\,z$ is a single edge-component
($\texttt{componentOfZero\_eq\_edgeComponent}$), hence edge-connected, giving
$G.\mathrm{dist}\,z\,v \le |\texttt{componentOfZero}\,X\,z|$
($\texttt{dist\_le\_card\_componentOfZero}$).  Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017),
\S3.7.3, eq. (3.49), p. 118.

\subsection{Handshake parity and the second odd-degree vertex
(\texttt{EdgeSetHandshake.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The handshake lemma for edge subsets and its parity
consequence, the FV §3.7.3 mechanism that a contour from the origin reaches a second
odd-degree vertex (the boundary).  The handshake identity is
\[
  \sum_v (X.\texttt{filter}\,(v\in\cdot)).\texttt{card} \;=\; 2\,|X|
\]
($\texttt{sum\_filter\_card\_eq\_two\_mul\_card}$, for $X \subseteq G.\texttt{edgeFinset}$),
whence the set of odd-degree vertices has even cardinality
($\texttt{even\_card\_odd\_filter\_card}$, via
$\texttt{Finset.even\_sum\_iff\_even\_card\_odd}$).  Therefore odd degree at $z$ forces a
\emph{second} odd-degree vertex $j \ne z$ ($\texttt{exists\_ne\_odd\_filter\_card}$: the
odd-degree set is even and contains $z$, so is not the singleton $\{z\}$).  Combined with
the distance bound, if the origin's component has odd degree at $z$ then there is a
$j \ne z$ with $G.\mathrm{dist}\,z\,j \le |\texttt{componentOfZero}\,X\,z|$
($\texttt{exists\_dist\_le\_card\_componentOfZero}$); in the cubic-box $+$ setup that second
site is a boundary site at distance $\ge n$, forcing $|C| \ge n$.  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eqs. (3.48)--(3.49), pp. 117--118.

\subsection{Subtype-to-ambient distance transfer
(\texttt{InduceDistanceTransfer.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Converts an induced-box distance into the lattice $\ell^1$
distance, the geometric transfer needed for FV (3.49).  A walk in an induced subgraph
$G.\texttt{induce}\,s$ maps to a walk in $G$ of the same length (via the inclusion
homomorphism $\texttt{induceValHom} : G.\texttt{induce}\,s \to_g G$ and
$\texttt{Walk.length\_map}$), so the ambient distance is at most the induced one,
$G.\mathrm{dist}\,a\,b \le (G.\texttt{induce}\,s).\mathrm{dist}\,a\,b$
($\texttt{dist\_val\_le\_induce\_dist}$, for reachable $a, b$).  Specialised to the lattice
graph, $\texttt{latticeDistance}\,d\,a\,b \le (\texttt{inducedGraph}\,(\texttt{latticeGraph}\,d)\,\Lambda).\mathrm{dist}\,a\,b$
($\texttt{latticeDistance\_le\_induce\_dist}$).  Composing with the handshake partner
gives $\texttt{latticeDistance}\,d\,z\,j \le |\texttt{componentOfZero}\,X\,z|$ for the
second odd-degree vertex $j$
($\texttt{latticeDistance\_le\_card\_componentOfZero}$): the origin's component, reaching a
far lattice site, must have many edges --- the FV (3.49) $|C| \ge n$ geometry.  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eq. (3.49), p. 118.

\subsection{The origin component reaches the boundary, $|C| \ge n$
(\texttt{CubicBoxComponentSize.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The FV (3.49) geometric estimate: in the cubic box $B(m)$ with
$+$ boundary on the inner box $B(n)$, an $E^{+;0}$ subgraph's origin component satisfies
$n \le |\texttt{componentOfZero}\,X\,z|$ ($\texttt{card\_componentOfZero\_ge\_of\_E0}$).

\textbf{Argument:} A site outside $\texttt{cubicBox}\,d\,n$ is at lattice distance $\ge n+1$
from the origin, since some coordinate has absolute value $\ge n+1$
($\texttt{latticeDistance\_origin\_ge\_of\_not\_mem\_cubicBox}$).  By the handshake parity,
the origin's component has a second odd-degree vertex $j$; the component inherits even
parity off the origin on the interior ($\texttt{even\_filter\_card\_componentOfZero}$), so
$j$ cannot lie in the interior --- its site is outside $B(n)$.  Hence
$n + 1 \le \texttt{latticeDistance}\,d\,0\,j \le |C|$, the last step by the lattice distance
bound for the component ($\texttt{latticeDistance\_le\_card\_componentOfZero}$).  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eq. (3.49), p. 118.

\subsection{Degree bound on the walk count
(\texttt{WalkCountDegreeBound.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The counting input to FV (3.49) --- the number of walks of a
given length is degree-bounded, the source of the $(2d)^{2\ell}$ factor.  Writing
$\texttt{walksFromCount}\,G\,u\,k = \sum_v |\texttt{finsetWalkLength}\,k\,u\,v|$ for the
number of length-$k$ walks starting at $u$,
\[
  \texttt{walksFromCount}\,u\,k \;\le\; \Delta^k
\]
for a uniform degree bound $\Delta$ ($\texttt{walksFromCount\_le\_pow}$).  The proof is by
induction on $k$: each length-$(k{+}1)$ walk is a first edge to a neighbour followed by a
length-$k$ walk, so the count multiplies by at most the degree
($\texttt{Finset.card\_biUnion\_le}$ and $\texttt{card\_neighborSet\_eq\_degree}$).
Specialised to the induced cubic-lattice box graph (degree $\le 2d$),
$\texttt{walksFromCount}\,(\texttt{inducedGraph}\,(\texttt{latticeGraph}\,d)\,\Lambda)\,u\,k \le (2d)^k$
($\texttt{walksFromCount\_inducedLatticeGraph\_le}$), the $(2d)^{2\ell}$ factor of FV (3.49).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eq. (3.49), p. 118.

\subsection{Geometric series tail and exponential decay
(\texttt{GeometricTail.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The analytic input to the FV (3.49) decay
$\langle\sigma_0\rangle^+_{B(n)} \le \sum_{\ell\ge n}(4d^2\tanh\beta J)^\ell \le e^{-cn}$.
For $0 \le q < 1$ the geometric tail is
\[
  \sum_{\ell}' q^{n+\ell} \;=\; q^n (1-q)^{-1}
\]
($\texttt{tsum\_geometric\_tail}$, via $\texttt{tsum\_mul\_left}$ and
$\texttt{tsum\_geometric\_of\_lt\_one}$), which tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$
($\texttt{tendsto\_geometric\_tail}$).  Writing $q^n = \exp(n\log q)$
($\texttt{pow\_eq\_exp\_mul\_log}$) exhibits the $e^{-cn}$ form with $c = -\log q > 0$ for
$0 < q < 1$.  Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eq. (3.49), p. 118.

\subsection{Geometric domination of a counted sum
(\texttt{CountGeometricCapstone.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The analytic capstone of FV (3.49).  For a finite family $S$
with a size function $g \ge n$ and member-count $\#\{C : g(C)=\ell\} \le M^\ell$,
\[
  \sum_{C\in S} q^{g(C)} \;\le\; \frac{(Mq)^n}{1-Mq} \qquad (0 < Mq < 1)
\]
($\texttt{sum\_pow\_le\_geometric\_tail\_of\_count}$).  The proof groups $S$ by size
($\texttt{Finset.sum\_fiberwise\_of\_maps\_to}$), bounds each size class
$\#\cdot q^\ell \le M^\ell q^\ell = (Mq)^\ell$, factors out $(Mq)^n$ (every size $\ge n$),
and dominates the reindexed $\sum_\ell (Mq)^{\ell-n}$ by the geometric series
$\sum_k' (Mq)^k = (1-Mq)^{-1}$ ($\texttt{Summable.sum\_le\_tsum}$).  With $S$ the origin
components, $g = |\cdot|$, $M = (2d)^2$, $q = \tanh\beta J$, this gives
$\langle\sigma_0\rangle^+_{B(n)} \le (4d^2\tanh\beta J)^n/(1-4d^2\tanh\beta J) \to 0$,
reducing the high-temperature $m^*(\beta)=0$ to the counting bound
$\#\{C : |C|=\ell\} \le (2d)^{2\ell}$ (FV Lemma 3.38).  Reference: Friedli--Velenik
(Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eq. (3.49), p. 118.

\subsection{FV Lemma 3.38: closed walk crossing each edge twice
(\texttt{EdgeWalkExistence.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The Eulerian-type construction underlying the counting
injection.  A connected edge set $X$ (non-diagonal edges) admits a closed walk from any
incident vertex $z$ with $w.\texttt{edges.toFinset} = X$ and $w.\texttt{length} = 2|X|$
($\texttt{exists\_closed\_walk\_of\_edgeConnected}$).

\textbf{Argument:} Grow a connected prefix $P$ from a single $z$-edge, one incident edge at
a time.  The connectivity frontier ($\texttt{exists\_boundary\_edge}$: across any proper
nonempty $P \subsetneq X$, edge-connectedness yields an edge of $X \setminus P$ incident to
$P$ --- proved by walking the $\texttt{ReflTransGen}$ chain and locating where it leaves
$P$) supplies the next edge $e$, sharing a vertex $v$ with $P$.  Since $v$ lies on a
$P$-edge it is in the current walk's support
($\texttt{Walk.mem\_support\_of\_mem\_edges}$); splice the detour $v \to w \to v$ (the new
edge $e = s(v,w)$ traversed twice) at the first visit to $v$, using
$\texttt{Walk.takeUntil}$, $\texttt{dropUntil}$ and $\texttt{take\_spec}$.  The edge set
gains exactly $\{e\}$ and the length gains exactly $2$, and
$\texttt{isEdgeConnected\_insert}$ keeps the prefix connected, so the induction (on
$|X \setminus P|$) closes.  Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3,
Lemma 3.38, p. 117.

\subsection{Counting injection $\#\{C : |C|=\ell\} \le (2d)^{2\ell}$
(\texttt{EdgeWalkCounting.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The FV (3.49) counting bound, the last input to the
high-temperature $m^*(\beta)=0$.  Each connected edge set $C \ni z$ of size $\ell$ is sent,
via its FV-Lemma-3.38 closed walk transported into the ambient graph $G$
(by $\texttt{Walk.transfer}$, $\texttt{exists\_closed\_walk\_in\_supergraph}$), to a closed
walk of length $2\ell$ from $z$.  The map is injective --- $C$ is exactly the walk's edge
set --- so ($\texttt{card\_connected\_edge\_sets\_le}$, via
$\texttt{Finset.card\_le\_card\_of\_injOn}$)
\[
  \#\{C \text{ connected}, \ni z, |C|=\ell, C \subseteq G.\texttt{edgeFinset}\}
  \;\le\; \#\{\text{closed walks of length } 2\ell \text{ from } z\}.
\]
On the induced cubic-lattice box graph, the closed walks are at most
$\texttt{walksFromCount}\,z\,(2\ell) \le (2d)^{2\ell}$
($\texttt{card\_connected\_edge\_sets\_inducedLatticeGraph\_le}$, via
$\texttt{Finset.single\_le\_sum}$), the $(2d)^{2\ell}$ bound of FV (3.49).  Reference:
Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3, eq. (3.49), p. 118.

\subsection{High-temperature box magnetization decay
(\texttt{CubicBoxMagnetizationDecay.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The FV (3.49) capstone bound.  In the cubic box $B(m)$ with $+$
boundary on the inner box $B(n)$,
\[
  \langle\sigma_0\rangle^+ \;\le\; \frac{(4d^2\tanh\beta J)^n}{1 - 4d^2\tanh\beta J}
\]
for $0 < d$, $0 < \tanh\beta J$ and $4d^2\tanh\beta J < 1$
($\texttt{gibbsExpectationBC\_box\_singleSpin\_le}$).  The proof composes the component
bound $\langle\sigma_0\rangle^+ \le \sum_C (\tanh\beta J)^{|C|}$ (3.48), the size lower
bound $|C| \ge n$ ($\texttt{card\_componentOfZero\_ge\_of\_E0}$), the counting bound
$\#\{C : |C|=\ell\} \le (2d)^{2\ell} = (4d^2)^\ell$
($\texttt{card\_connected\_edge\_sets\_inducedLatticeGraph\_le}$ --- each origin component
being connected, contained in the box edges, and containing the origin via its odd-degree
$z$-edge), and the geometric capstone
($\texttt{sum\_pow\_le\_geometric\_tail\_of\_count}$ with $M=4d^2$, $q=\tanh\beta J$).  This
is the exponential decay of $\langle\sigma_0\rangle^+_{B(n)}$ as $n\to\infty$, the heart of
FV's high-temperature $m^*(\beta)=0$.  Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017),
\S3.7.3, eq. (3.49), p. 118.

\subsection{High-temperature $m^*(\beta)=0$ --- FV \S3.7.3 complete
(\texttt{HighTempZeroMagnetization.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The high-temperature half of the phase transition.  For
$0<d$, $0<\beta$, $0<J$ and $4d^2\tanh\beta J < 1$, the $+$-state spontaneous magnetization
vanishes,
\[
  m^*(\beta) = 0
\]
($\texttt{plusStateSpontaneousMagnetization\_eq\_zero\_of\_high\_temp}$).  The screened box
magnetizations converge to $m^*$ ($\texttt{tendsto\_plusMagnetization}$), and each is
bounded by $(4d^2\tanh\beta J)^n/(1-4d^2\tanh\beta J) \to 0$
($\texttt{gibbsExpectationBC\_box\_singleSpin\_le}$ via the bridge
$\texttt{plusBoxObsExpectation\_singleSpin\_eq}$, and $\texttt{tendsto\_geometric\_tail}$),
so $m^* \le 0$; with $m^* \ge 0$ this gives $m^*=0$.  This completes the entire FV \S3.7.3
high-temperature argument: the random-graph representation (3.41)--(3.45), the one-point
ratio (3.46)--(3.47), the component bound (3.48), and the Eulerian-counting / geometric
estimate (3.49) with Lemma 3.38.  Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.3,
pp. 116--118.

\subsection{Connected-droplet refinement of the Peierls bound
(\texttt{Peierls/ConnectedDroplet.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The low-temperature half (FV \S3.7.2, $m^*(\beta)>0$) sharpens
the Peierls contour sum by restricting it to \emph{connected} spin droplets, the foundation
of the volume-independent contour counting.  Writing
$\texttt{ReachableWithin}\,G\,T\,x\,y$ for reachability via a $G$-walk staying inside $T$,
the droplet $\texttt{downComponent}\,G\,\sigma\,i$ is the connected component of $i$ in the
down-spins.  The key contour fact ($\texttt{cutEdges\_downComponent\_subset\_phaseBoundary}$)
is that for $\sigma_i = -1$ every cut edge of the droplet lies in the phase boundary
$\partial\sigma$ --- a cut edge joins a droplet down-spin to a non-droplet vertex, which must
then be an up-spin.  The droplet is connected through $i$ by symmetry of
$\texttt{ReachableWithin}$ ($\texttt{isConnectedDroplet\_downComponent}$), giving the
connected refinement
\[
  \mathbf 1_{\sigma_i=-1} \;\le\;
  \sum_{\substack{S \ni i \\ S\ \mathrm{connected}}} \mathbf 1_{\mathrm{cut}(S)\subseteq\partial\sigma}
\]
($\texttt{indicator\_spin\_down\_le\_connected\_contour\_sum}$).  This restriction makes the
boundary map $S \mapsto \mathrm{cut}(S)$ tractable for the volume-independent count.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Connected-droplet \texorpdfstring{$+$}{+}-boundary Peierls bound
  (\texttt{Peierls/ConnectedDropletBound.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Feeding the connected-droplet indicator through the flip
involution gives the connected refinement of $\texttt{spontaneous\_magnetization\_plus}$:
\[
  \langle \mathbf 1_{\sigma_i=-1}\rangle^{+}_{B} \;\le\;
  \sum_{\substack{S \ni i,\ S\cap B = \emptyset \\ S\ \mathrm{connected}}}
    e^{-2\beta J\,|\mathrm{cut}(S)|}
\]
($\texttt{spontaneous\_magnetization\_plus\_connected}$).  The witnessing droplet
$\texttt{downComponent}\,G\,\sigma\,i$ is disjoint from the boundary $B$ because it lies in
the down-spins, while the $+$-boundary forces $B$ to up-spins.  The per-droplet Peierls
ratio bound ($\texttt{boltzmannWeight\_flipSet\_ratio}$, with the flip $\texttt{Config.flipSet}\,S$
preserving the $+$-boundary when $S\cap B=\emptyset$ and injective via
$\texttt{Config.flipSet\_injective}$) is identical to the unrestricted version; only the index
filter is narrowed to connected droplets.  This is the bound made volume-independently
countable by the connected restriction.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, Lemma 3.37, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The boundary determines a connected droplet
  (\texttt{Peierls/DropletInjective.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} To count connected droplets volume-independently, we first observe
that a connected droplet is recoverable from its edge boundary.  Membership in the cut is
$s(a,b)\in\mathrm{cut}(S) \iff G.\mathrm{Adj}\,a\,b \wedge (a\in S \leftrightarrow b\notin S)$
($\texttt{mem\_cutEdges\_iff}$); consequently a non-cut edge incident to $S$ cannot leave $S$
($\texttt{mem\_of\_adj\_not\_mem\_cutEdges}$).  Hence if $S$ is a connected droplet with
$i\in S$ and $\mathrm{cut}(S)=\mathrm{cut}(T)$ with $i\in T$, a within-$S$ walk from $i$ crosses
no boundary edge and stays inside $T$, giving $S\subseteq T$
($\texttt{isConnectedDroplet\_subset\_of\_cutEdges\_eq}$).  Antisymmetry yields
$\texttt{connectedDroplet\_eq\_of\_cutEdges\_eq}$, so the boundary map
$S\mapsto\mathrm{cut}(S)$ is \emph{injective} on connected droplets containing $i$
($\texttt{cutEdges\_injOn\_connectedDroplet}$).  Therefore the number of connected droplets
$S\ni i$ equals the number of edge sets $\mathrm{cut}(S)$
($\texttt{card\_connectedDroplet\_eq\_card\_cutEdges\_image}$), reducing the volume-independent
contour count to an edge-set count (to be closed by the dual-lattice walk-counting
$\texttt{card\_connected\_edge\_sets\_inducedLatticeGraph\_le}$).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Crossing parity of the cut (\texttt{Peierls/CutCrossingParity.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The Peierls surrounding-contour extraction rests on a discrete
Jordan/winding-parity fact.  Writing $\texttt{cutCrossings}\,G\,S\,w$ for the number of cut
edges of $S$ that a walk $w$ traverses (with multiplicity), one has
\[
  \mathrm{Even}\bigl(\texttt{cutCrossings}\,G\,S\,w\bigr) \iff (u\in S \leftrightarrow v\in S)
\]
($\texttt{even\_cutCrossings\_iff}$, by induction on $w$: each edge flips the parity iff it is a
cut edge, i.e. iff it changes side).  Consequently a walk from inside $S$ to outside $S$ crosses
the cut an \emph{odd} number of times ($\texttt{odd\_cutCrossings\_of\_mem\_not\_mem}$), so it
traverses at least one cut edge ($\texttt{exists\_mem\_edges\_mem\_cutEdges}$) and the cut is
nonempty whenever $S$ separates two reachable vertices
($\texttt{cutEdges\_nonempty\_of\_reachable\_not\_mem}$).  A walk from the enclosed origin out to
a far vertex \emph{outside} the droplet thus crosses the boundary an odd number of times and must
traverse a cut edge, detecting that the origin is enclosed.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Hole-filled droplet region (\texttt{Peierls/FilledRegion.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A connected droplet $S$ may have holes, making $\mathrm{cut}(S)$ a
disconnected union of inner and outer boundaries; counting contours volume-independently wants a
single connected contour.  Fixing a ground vertex $g\notin S$ (the outside anchor), the outside
component $\texttt{outsideComponent}\,G\,S\,g$ is the set of vertices reachable from $g$ without
entering $S$, and the filled region $\texttt{filledRegion}\,G\,S\,g := \mathrm{univ}\setminus
\texttt{outsideComponent}$ is $S$ together with all holes.  One has $S\subseteq F$
($\texttt{subset\_filledRegion}$), $g\notin F$ ($\texttt{ground\_not\_mem\_filledRegion}$), and
$i\in F$ ($\texttt{self\_mem\_filledRegion}$).  Crucially, holes are not adjacent to the outside,
so every boundary edge of $F$ has its $F$-side in $S$
($\texttt{mem\_droplet\_of\_mem\_filledRegion\_adj\_outside}$); filling therefore only removes
inner-boundary edges, and for $S=\texttt{downComponent}$ the filled boundary remains broken
bonds, $\mathrm{cut}(F)\subseteq\partial\sigma$
($\texttt{cutEdges\_filledRegion\_downComponent\_subset\_phaseBoundary}$).  The complement of $F$
is the single connected outside component, removing the inner boundaries; reducing
$\mathrm{cut}(F)$ to a single edge-connected contour is \emph{not} automatic for an abstract
graph (both sides may be connected with a disconnected cut) and needs the $d=2$ dual/planar
geometry, deferred.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Idempotence of hole-filling (\texttt{Peierls/FilledRegionIdempotent.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Hole-filling is idempotent, so $\texttt{filledRegion}$ is a
projection onto the \emph{filled regions} (those equal to their own filling), the index set of
the single-contour Peierls sum.  The outside component is unchanged by filling
($\texttt{outsideComponent\_filledRegion\_eq}$): a walk from $g$ avoiding $S$ stays inside the
outside component (its vertices are themselves in the outside, never in a hole), so it also
avoids $F=\texttt{filledRegion}\,G\,S\,g$, while conversely filling only enlarges the avoided set
(using $\texttt{reachableWithin\_mono}$).  Hence
$\texttt{filledRegion}(\texttt{filledRegion}\,S)=\texttt{filledRegion}\,S$
($\texttt{filledRegion\_idempotent}$), and writing
$\texttt{IsFilled}\,G\,g\,F := (\texttt{filledRegion}\,G\,F\,g = F)$ every filling satisfies it
($\texttt{isFilled\_filledRegion}$) with $g\notin F$
($\texttt{ground\_not\_mem\_of\_isFilled}$).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The filled region is connected (\texttt{Peierls/FilledRegionConnected.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Filling the holes of a connected droplet keeps it connected.  A walk
from outside $S$ to inside $S$ has a first crossing edge $a\to b$ ($a\notin S$, $b\in S$), with $a$
reached while staying outside $S$ ($\texttt{exists\_first\_entry}$).  A vertex reached from $x\in F$
avoiding $S$ is again in $F$ — it lies in $x$'s hole, never the outside, else $x$ itself would be
outside ($\texttt{mem\_filled\_of\_reachableWithin\_compl}$), so such walks stay in $F$
($\texttt{reachableWithin\_filled\_of\_reachableWithin\_compl}$).  Hence in a preconnected graph
the filled region of a nonempty connected droplet (with $g\notin S$) is a connected droplet
($\texttt{isConnectedDroplet\_filledRegion}$): every hole vertex reaches $S$ through its first-entry
edge, and $S$ is connected.  This is the hypothesis needed to count the filled boundary as a single
edge-connected contour.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The filled-connected Peierls bound (\texttt{Peierls/FilledConnectedBound.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Restricting the $+$-boundary Peierls bound to \emph{connected, filled}
droplets:
\[
  \langle \mathbf 1_{\sigma_i=-1}\rangle^{+}_{B} \;\le\;
  \sum_{\substack{S\ni i,\ S\cap B=\emptyset \\ S\ \mathrm{connected},\ S\ \mathrm{filled}}}
    e^{-2\beta J\,|\mathrm{cut}(S)|}
\]
($\texttt{spontaneous\_magnetization\_plus\_filled\_connected}$).  The witness is the \emph{filled}
down-spin component $\texttt{filledRegion}\,(\texttt{downComponent}\,\sigma\,i)\,g$, connected and
filled, with boundary in $\partial\sigma$.  The ground vertex $g$ lies on the connected boundary
$B$; for a $+$-configuration $B$ is all up-spins, so $B\subseteq\mathrm{outside}$ of the
down-droplet, giving $\mathrm{Disjoint}\,F\,B$.  Restricting to filled droplets makes each contour
a \emph{single} edge-connected curve, the form needed for the volume-independent count.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, Lemma 3.37, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{A walk's edges are edge-connected (\texttt{Peierls/WalkEdgesConnected.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The edge set of any walk is edge-connected.  The start vertex of a
nonempty walk lies in one of its edges ($\texttt{start\_mem\_some\_edge}$), so by induction each
$\texttt{cons}$ edge touches the rest of the walk at the shared vertex and
$\texttt{isEdgeConnected\_insert}$ applies; the empty case is vacuous
($\texttt{walk\_edges\_isEdgeConnected}$).  For the Peierls contour this says the dual edges
traversed by a dart orbit ($d.\texttt{tail}\to d.\texttt{head}\to\cdots$, the
$\texttt{orbitClosedWalk}$) form a single edge-connected contour — the input to the
volume-independent count via $\texttt{card\_connected\_edge\_sets\_inducedLatticeGraph\_le}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The complement of a filled region is connected (\texttt{Peierls/ComplConnected.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A filled region has $\mathrm{univ}\setminus F = \texttt{outside\-Component}
\,G\,F\,g$, a single complementary component.  Hence any two vertices outside $F$ are reachable from
one another within $\mathrm{univ}\setminus F$ (both lie in the outside component, connected through
$g$; $\texttt{reachableWithin\_compl\_of\_isFilled}$), so $\mathrm{univ}\setminus F$ is a connected
droplet ($\texttt{isConnectedDroplet\_compl\_of\_isFilled}$).  This is the first input to the
discrete Jordan single-curve theorem $\texttt{boundaryDart\_single\_orbit\_of\_connected\_filled}$:
together with the connectivity of $F$ it forces the boundary darts into a single orbit.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The same-orbit equivalence (\texttt{Peierls/SameOrbit.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Two boundary darts are in the same orbit when one is reached from the
other by iterating $\texttt{nextDart}$: $\texttt{SameOrbit}\,d\,e := \exists n,\ \texttt{nextDart}^{[n]}
\,d = e$.  Since $\texttt{nextDart}$ is a bijection of the finite dart type (every dart periodic),
this is an equivalence relation: reflexive ($n=0$), transitive (iterate-add), and symmetric (via
$\texttt{nextDart\_periodic}$, $\texttt{iterate\_mul}$ and $\texttt{iterate\_fixed}$).  With the
left/right site accessors $\texttt{BoundaryDart.left}/\texttt{right}$ this is the scaffolding for the
discrete Jordan single-curve theorem, which will place all darts of a connected, filled region in
one orbit.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{A dart orbit's dual edges are edge-connected (\texttt{Peierls/OrbitDualEdges.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The dual edges $s(e.\texttt{tail}, e.\texttt{head})$ of the darts in
one $\texttt{nextDart}$-orbit form an edge-connected set.  Consecutive darts $e$, $\texttt{nextDart}
\,e$ have dual edges sharing the pivot vertex $e.\texttt{head} = (\texttt{nextDart}\,e).
\texttt{tail}$, so the dual edge of $\texttt{nextDart}^{[k]}\,d$ is edge-adjacency-reachable from the
anchor $s(d.\texttt{tail}, d.\texttt{head})$ ($\texttt{orbit\_iterate\_dualEdge\_reachable}$), giving
$\texttt{orbitDualEdges\_isEdgeConnected}$.  This is one half of the contour count: once the discrete
Jordan single-curve theorem places all boundary darts of a connected filled region in one orbit,
the whole dual cut is this single edge-connected contour.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The whole dual cut is edge-connected, given one orbit
  (\texttt{Peierls/DualCutConnected.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The dual cut $\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F$ collects every boundary dart's
dual edge $s(d.\texttt{tail}, d.\texttt{head})$.  If all darts share one orbit ($\texttt{hone}$),
then $\texttt{dartOrbit}\,d = \mathrm{univ}$, so $\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F = \texttt{orbitDualEdges}
\,d$ ($\texttt{dartDualCut\_eq\_orbitDualEdges}$) and the whole dual cut is edge-connected
($\texttt{dartDualCut\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_single\_orbit}$, empty case vacuous).  This isolates the
hard planar input (single orbit) as a hypothesis: once
$\texttt{boundaryDart\_single\_orbit\_of\_connected\_filled}$ (the discrete Jordan crux) is
available, the whole dual cut is a single edge-connected contour, the form consumed by the
volume-independent count.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Boundary darts have faithful site coordinates
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitBase.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A local base lemma for the planned boundary-slide argument toward the
single-orbit (discrete Jordan single-curve) property; the nontrivial slide/reachability content is
not part of this file.  The slide would track a boundary dart by its two sites
$(d.\texttt{left}, d.\texttt{right})$, so the argument is well defined only if these coordinates are
faithful.  $\texttt{BoundaryDart.left\_sub\_right}$ records the geometry
$d.\texttt{left} - d.\texttt{right} = (\texttt{turnLeft}\,d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$ (the right
site is one step back along the left normal).  Hence equal sites force equal directions
($\texttt{dir\_eq\_of\_left\_right}$, since the left normal is determined by $\texttt{left} -
\texttt{right}$ and $\texttt{turnLeft}$, $\texttt{vec}$ are injective) and then equal tails (via
$\texttt{leftSite\_injective\_tail}$), giving $\texttt{ext\_of\_left\_right}$: a dart is determined by
its two sites.  Equivalently the site-pair embedding $d \mapsto (d.\texttt{left}, d.\texttt{right})$
is injective ($\texttt{siteMap\_injective}$).  The two sites are distinct
($\texttt{left\_ne\_right}$, as $\texttt{left} \in F$ and $\texttt{right} \notin F$), and equal sites
give same-orbit darts ($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_left\_right\_eq}$, the reflexive base case of the
target $\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_left\_right\_reachable}$).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Site evolution under \texttt{nextDart}
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitSlide.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The concrete geometric increments the planned boundary slide relies on:
how a boundary dart's two sites $(d.\texttt{left}, d.\texttt{right})$ change under one
$\texttt{nextDart}$ step, case by case on the turn taken.  A left turn keeps the left site fixed
($\texttt{left\_nextDart\_of\_turnLeft}$, pivot about the left), with the right site moving to the
head's straight left site ($\texttt{right\_nextDart\_of\_turnLeft}$).  Dually a right turn keeps the
right site fixed ($\texttt{right\_nextDart\_of\_turnRight}$, pivot about the right), with the left
site at the head's straight right site ($\texttt{left\_nextDart\_of\_turnRight}$).  A straight step
puts both sites at the head ($\texttt{left/right\_nextDart\_of\_straight}$).  The capstone
$\texttt{nextDart\_site\_step}$ records the complete site-increment trichotomy: one step keeps the
left site fixed, keeps the right site fixed, or advances both to the head.  Each identity is a
direct consequence of the four site identities of \texttt{NextDart.lean} together with
$\texttt{nextDart\_eq\_\{turnLeft,straight,turnRight\}}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Boundary darts and contact pairs
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitContact.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A \emph{contact pair} of $F$ is an ordered adjacent pair $(a, b)$ with
$a \in F$ and $b \notin F$.  The boundary darts of $F$ correspond exactly to its contact pairs --
the bridge the planned boundary slide (which moves along contact pairs) needs between the in/out-site
geometry and the orbit dynamics.  Forward: every dart presents a contact pair via
$(d.\texttt{left}, d.\texttt{right})$, whose sites are lattice-adjacent
($\texttt{BoundaryDart.adj\_left\_right}$, from $\texttt{leftSite\_rightSite\_adjacent}$).  Backward:
every contact pair is realised by a boundary dart with $d.\texttt{left} = a$, $d.\texttt{right} = b$
($\texttt{exists\_boundaryDart\_of\_contact}$, strengthening $\texttt{exists\_dart\_of\_cut}$ by using
membership to orient the unordered cut edge $s(a, b)$).  Combined with the faithfulness of
\texttt{SingleOrbitBase}, this is a bijection of darts with contact pairs.  The trivial wrappers
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_nextDart}$, $\texttt{sameOrbit\_iterate}$ record that a dart shares its orbit with
its forward iterates.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Fan boundary detection (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFan.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The \emph{fan} around a left site $p \in F$ is the set of boundary darts
with left site $p$.  A left turn keeps the left site fixed ($\texttt{left\_nextDart\_of\_turnLeft}$),
so iterating left turns rotates the dart around $p$; this file proves the \emph{boundary} of the fan.
$\texttt{left\_nextDart\_eq\_left\_iff\_turnLeft}$: a $\texttt{nextDart}$ step keeps the left site
fixed iff it takes the left turn.  The converse (the new content,
$\texttt{left\_nextDart\_ne\_left\_of\_not\_turnLeft}$) holds because a straight step shifts the left
site by $\texttt{dir.vec} \neq 0$ ($\texttt{Dir2.vec\_ne\_zero}$) and a right turn shifts it by
$\texttt{dir.vec} - (\texttt{turnLeft dir}).\texttt{vec} \neq 0$
($\texttt{Dir2.vec\_ne\_turnLeft\_vec}$, from $\texttt{vec\_injective}$ and
$\texttt{turnLeft\_ne\_self}$), using the translation-equivariance
$\texttt{leftSite\_add}$/$\texttt{rightSite\_add}$ ($\texttt{leftSite}\,(t + v)\,\delta =
\texttt{leftSite}\,t\,\delta + v$).  $\texttt{dir\_nextDart\_of\_turnLeft}$ records that a left turn
rotates the direction left.  These are the local building blocks (per a focused design pass) of the
fan rotation feeding $\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_left\_right\_reachable}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Left-fan prefix rotation (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFanPrefix.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A \emph{left-fan prefix} of length $n$ at a dart $d$ is a run of $n$
consecutive $\texttt{nextDart}$ steps each taking the left turn ($\texttt{BoundaryDart.LeftFanPrefix}$).
Since each step keeps the left site fixed, the whole prefix rotates the dart around that fixed left
site: $\texttt{left\_eq\_iterate\_of\_leftFanPrefix}$ leaves the left site unchanged
($(\texttt{nextDart}^{[n]} d).\texttt{left} = d.\texttt{left}$), while
$\texttt{dir\_eq\_iterate\_of\_leftFanPrefix}$ rotates the direction left $n$ times
($(\texttt{nextDart}^{[n]} d).\texttt{dir} = \texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir}$), and
$\texttt{right\_eq\_iterate\_of\_leftFanPrefix}$ then gives the right site
$d.\texttt{left} - (\texttt{turnLeft}\,(\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir})).\texttt{vec}$.  The
general bridge $\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_iterate\_left\_right\_eq}$ converts agreement of both sites
after $n$ steps into a same-orbit conclusion (the iterate equals the target, via
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_iterate}$ and $\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_left\_right\_eq}$).  These realise the fan
rotation feeding $\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_left\_right\_reachable}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Left-fan prefix completeness
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFanComplete.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The forward left-fan rotation is pinned down by the rotation it
performs.  $\texttt{eq\_iterate\_of\_leftFanPrefix\_of\_dir\_eq}$: if $e$ sits at the same left site
as $d$ ($e.\texttt{left} = d.\texttt{left}$) with direction $d.\texttt{dir}$ rotated left $k$ times
($e.\texttt{dir} = \texttt{turnLeft}^{[k]} d.\texttt{dir}$) and the first $k$ steps from $d$ are all
left turns ($\texttt{LeftFanPrefix}\,d\,k$), then $\texttt{nextDart}^{[k]} d = e$ exactly -- both
sites then agree (by $\texttt{left\_eq\_iterate}$ and $\texttt{right\_eq\_iterate}$) and a dart is
determined by its sites ($\texttt{ext\_of\_left\_right}$).  Hence such $d$ and $e$ lie in one orbit
($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_leftFanPrefix\_dir\_eq}$).  The prefix order is given by
$\texttt{leftFanPrefix\_zero}$ (vacuous), $\texttt{leftFanPrefix\_of\_le}$ (restriction), and
$\texttt{leftFanPrefix\_succ}$ (extend by one valid left turn).  This is the fan-rotation
completeness feeding $\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_left\_right\_reachable}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Left site stays $F$-reachable across one step
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitReach.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} As $\texttt{nextDart}$ advances, the left site stays inside $F$ and
reachable within $F$, regardless of the turn taken.  The combined
$\texttt{reachableWithin\_left\_nextDart}$ gives
$\texttt{ReachableWithin}\,(\texttt{latticeGraph}\,2)\,F\,d.\texttt{left}\,d.\texttt{nextDart.left}$;
by induction every dart on the forward orbit has its left site in the single $F$-component of
$d.\texttt{left}$ -- the $F$-side half of the orbit component invariant feeding
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_left\_right\_reachable}$.  Per case: a left turn keeps the left site fixed
(reflexive), a straight step advances it by one $F$-edge, and a right turn moves it by two $F$-edges
through the head sites.  The right-turn case uses $\texttt{leftSite\_head\_mem\_of\_not\_turnLeft}$
and $\texttt{rightSite\_head\_mem\_of\_not\_turnLeft\_not\_straight}$ (the head sites are forced into
$F$, extracted from the validity propagation of
$\texttt{right\_valid\_of\_not\_left\_not\_straight}$) together with
$\texttt{adj\_leftSite\_rightSite}$ (the two sites are lattice-adjacent).  The complement-side
counterpart is \emph{not} uniformly local (a left turn lacks a forced complement bridge) and is
handled separately via contact-pair chains.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The orbit's left sites lie in one $F$-component
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitOrbitReach.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Iterating the per-step $F$-reachability of \texttt{SingleOrbitReach}.
$\texttt{reachableWithin\_left\_iterate}$ shows the left site of any forward iterate of $d$ is
reachable within $F$ from $d.\texttt{left}$ (induction plus transitivity), so any dart $e$ in $d$'s
orbit has $e.\texttt{left}$ reachable within $F$ from $d.\texttt{left}$
($\texttt{reachableWithin\_left\_of\_sameOrbit}$ and its symmetric form), as does every $e$ in the
orbit finset ($\texttt{reachableWithin\_left\_of\_mem\_dartOrbit}$).  Contrapositively, two darts
with left sites in different $F$-components lie in different orbits
($\texttt{not\_sameOrbit\_of\_not\_reachableWithin\_left}$).  This confines each orbit to one
$F$-component of left sites -- the $F$-side necessary condition for the single-orbit property; forcing
a \emph{single} orbit additionally needs the complementary planar input via contact-pair chains.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Contact pairs as a type
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitContactPair.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The dart $\leftrightarrow$ contact-pair correspondence of
\texttt{SingleOrbitContact} packaged as a type.  $\texttt{ContactPair}\,F$ is the type of ordered
adjacent pairs $(\texttt{inSite} \in F, \texttt{outSite} \notin F)$.  $\texttt{ContactPair.toDart}$
(via $\texttt{exists\_boundaryDart\_of\_contact}$) realises a contact pair as a boundary dart with the
prescribed sites ($\texttt{toDart\_left}$, $\texttt{toDart\_right}$), and
$\texttt{BoundaryDart.toContactPair}$ takes a dart to its contact pair.  The round trips
$\texttt{toContactPair\_toDart}$ and $\texttt{toDart\_toContactPair}$ make the correspondence a
bijection (a dart is determined by its sites, $\texttt{ext\_of\_left\_right}$).  Working with contact
pairs -- rather than right sites -- is the route to the complement side of the single-orbit property:
the elementary contact steps that vary only the in- or out-site avoid the left-turn gap that breaks
the naive orbit-step complement invariant.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Right-fan boundary detection
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitRightFan.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Dual to the left fan (\texttt{SingleOrbitFan}): the \emph{right fan}
around a fixed right site $q \notin F$ is the set of boundary darts with right site $q$.  A right turn
keeps the right site fixed ($\texttt{right\_nextDart\_of\_turnRight}$), so iterating right turns
rotates the dart around $q$; this file proves the \emph{boundary} of that fan.
$\texttt{right\_nextDart\_eq\_right\_iff\_turnRight}$: a $\texttt{nextDart}$ step keeps the right site
fixed iff it takes the right turn.  The converse holds because a left turn moves the right site by the
nonzero diagonal $\texttt{dir.vec} + (\texttt{turnLeft dir}).\texttt{vec}$
($\texttt{Dir2.vec\_add\_turnLeft\_vec\_ne\_zero}$,
$\texttt{right\_nextDart\_ne\_right\_of\_turnLeft}$) and a straight step moves it by
$\texttt{dir.vec} \neq 0$ ($\texttt{right\_nextDart\_ne\_right\_of\_straight}$).  This is the
complement-side rotation needed for the ``vary in-site'' contact step.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Right-fan prefix rotation and completeness
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitRightFanPrefix.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Dual to \texttt{SingleOrbitFanPrefix}/\texttt{SingleOrbitFanComplete}.  A
\emph{right-fan prefix} of length $n$ at $d$ is a run of $n$ consecutive $\texttt{nextDart}$ steps
each taking the right turn ($\texttt{BoundaryDart.RightFanPrefix}$, with the structure lemmas
$\texttt{rightFanPrefix\_zero}$/$\texttt{\_of\_le}$/$\texttt{\_succ}$).  Each step keeps the right site
fixed, so the prefix rotates the dart around it: $\texttt{right\_eq\_iterate\_of\_rightFanPrefix}$
(right site unchanged), $\texttt{dir\_eq\_iterate\_of\_rightFanPrefix}$
($(\texttt{nextDart}^{[n]} d).\texttt{dir} = \texttt{turnRight}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir}$ via
$\texttt{dir\_nextDart\_of\_turnRight}$), and $\texttt{left\_eq\_iterate\_of\_rightFanPrefix}$ (the
resulting left site $d.\texttt{right} + (\texttt{turnLeft}\,(\texttt{turnRight}^{[n]}
d.\texttt{dir})).\texttt{vec}$).  The rotation pins the endpoint
($\texttt{eq\_iterate\_of\_rightFanPrefix\_of\_dir\_eq}$,
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_rightFanPrefix\_dir\_eq}$).  This is the complement-side counterpart of the
left-fan rotation, needed for the ``vary in-site'' contact step.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Contact steps and the orbit push-down
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitContactStep.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} $\texttt{ContactStep}\,c\,c'$ is a proof-carrying edge between contact
pairs, independent of the orbit dynamics: either the in-site is fixed and the realizing darts are
related by a \textbf{left-fan} prefix, or the out-site is fixed and they are related by a
\textbf{right-fan} prefix (constructors $\texttt{ContactStep.of\_leftFan}$/$\texttt{of\_rightFan}$).
By the fan completeness lemmas ($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_leftFanPrefix\_dir\_eq}$,
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_rightFanPrefix\_dir\_eq}$) each step sends the two realizing darts into one
orbit ($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_contactStep}$), so a finite chain does too
($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_contactStep\_chain}$), and at the level of darts
($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_dart\_contactStep\_chain}$, via the round trip).  This is the bridge that
will push the orbit-free planar connectivity of contact pairs down to the single-orbit property:
once $\texttt{ReflTransGen ContactStep}$ holds for a connected filled region, all boundary darts
share one orbit.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Contact moves: fans plus the slide
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitContactMove.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The two fan contact steps do not suffice to connect the contact graph (a
``domino'' region has fan moves only along its sides); the missing move is the \emph{slide} --
advancing one boundary step ($\texttt{nextDart}$), which translates the contact pair.  A
$\texttt{ContactMove}$ is a $\texttt{ContactStep}$ or $c' = c.\texttt{toDart.nextDart.toContactPair}$
(constructors $\texttt{ContactMove.of\_contactStep}$/$\texttt{of\_nextDart}$).  Crucially every
$\texttt{nextDart}$ step is itself a contact move ($\texttt{ContactMove.of\_nextDart}$), so following
the boundary is a contact-move chain.  Each move sends the realizing darts into one orbit
($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_contactMove}$, the slide case via $\texttt{sameOrbit\_nextDart}$), so any
chain does ($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_contactMove\_chain}$,
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_dart\_contactMove\_chain}$).  Together with the remaining planar connectivity
of the contact graph this gives the single-orbit property.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Local generators of contact-move connectivity
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitContactGen.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The elementary $\texttt{ContactMove}$s packaged as
$\texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}$ facts -- the local generators a global planar-connectivity
argument will chain.  A left-fan rotation about a fixed in-site
($\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_of\_same\_inSite\_leftFanPrefix}$), a right-fan rotation about a
fixed out-site ($\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_of\_same\_outSite\_rightFanPrefix}$), one boundary
slide ($\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_nextDart}$), and a whole forward orbit as one contact-move
chain ($\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_iterate}$, by induction on the slide).  These hold
unconditionally; assembling them into full connectivity for a connected filled region is the
remaining planar step -- only there do $F$-connectivity and filledness enter, to cross between
exposed wedges.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{One-step fan validity (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFanOne.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The base case of fan-prefix construction: a length-one fan prefix is
exactly a single valid turn.  $\texttt{leftFanPrefix\_one\_iff}$ gives
$d.\texttt{LeftFanPrefix}\,1 \iff \texttt{ValidAt}\,F\,d.\texttt{head}\,d.\texttt{dir.turnLeft}$ (a
valid left turn), and $\texttt{rightFanPrefix\_one\_iff}$ gives
$d.\texttt{RightFanPrefix}\,1 \iff (\lnot\texttt{ValidAt turnLeft} \land \lnot\texttt{ValidAt
straight})$ (a right turn), with the $\texttt{mpr}$ constructors $\texttt{leftFanPrefix\_one}$,
$\texttt{rightFanPrefix\_one}$.  These are the elementary generators a fan rotation (hence a contact
step) is built from when the global connectivity argument constructs prefixes from local validity.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Elementary single-turn steps
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitTurnStep.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The $k = 1$ specialisations of the fan completeness and contact-move
generators: a single valid turn between darts sharing a site.  At the dart level, two darts with the
same left site whose directions differ by one valid left turn are in the same orbit
($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_left\_turn\_step}$), dually for the right turn
($\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_right\_turn\_step}$).  At the contact-pair level these are one-edge
$\texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}$ facts ($\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_left\_turn}$,
$\texttt{\_right\_turn}$).  These are the atomic wedge rotations the global connectivity argument
applies step by step.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Contact-move connectivity equals same-orbit
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitContactEquiv.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The dart-level contact-move connectivity is \emph{exactly} the orbit
relation.  $\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_of\_sameOrbit}$ shows same orbit gives a contact-move
chain (the forward-orbit slide chain $\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_iterate}$); together with the
push-down $\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_dart\_contactMove\_chain}$ this gives
$\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_iff\_sameOrbit}$: $\texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}$ on the
contact pairs of two darts is equivalent to those darts being in the same orbit.  Hence proving that
all contact pairs of a connected filled region are contact-move connected is \emph{the same problem}
as the single-orbit property -- the planar connectivity is the whole remaining content, with no
further orbit bookkeeping.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Contact-move connectivity is symmetric
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitContactSymm.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Although a single $\texttt{ContactMove}$ is directed (a fan prefix or a
forward slide), the connectivity $\texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}$ is symmetric: via
$\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_iff\_sameOrbit}$ it agrees with the same-orbit relation, which is
symmetric.  Hence $\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_symm}$ (symmetry) and
$\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_equivalence}$ (an equivalence relation on contact pairs, with
reflexivity and transitivity from $\texttt{ReflTransGen}$).  This lets the global planar-connectivity
argument route in either direction.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Straight-slide transport and fan reach
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitTransport.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Two free transport facts the global connectivity argument uses.
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_straight\_slide}$: when $\texttt{nextDart}$ goes straight at $d$ (left turn
invalid, straight valid) and $d'$ carries the straight head sites, $d$ and $d'$ are in the same orbit
(the new dart is determined by its sites).  $\texttt{exists\_orbit\_dart\_at\_left\_with\_dir}$: a
left-fan prefix from $d$ reaching direction $\delta$ produces an orbit dart at the same left site
with direction $\delta$.  Both are immediate from the existing orbit/fan lemmas; the only genuinely
new ingredient still missing for full connectivity is the existence of a left-fan prefix reaching the
exit direction of the exposed wedge.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The left-fan validity criterion
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitWedge.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The local condition controlling how far a left fan turns.
$\texttt{leftFan\_next\_turnLeft\_valid\_iff}$: after a left-fan prefix of length $n$, the next left
turn is valid iff $d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec} \notin F$,
the lattice point one step from the fixed left site in the current rotated direction.  The $F$-side
conjunct of validity is automatic (the left site is the fixed $F$-vertex $d.\texttt{left}$, via
$\texttt{leftSite\_head\_turnLeft}$ and $\texttt{d.left\_mem}$), so only the out-side membership
matters ($\texttt{rightSite\_head\_turnLeft\_eq\_leftSite\_head}$ and $\texttt{leftSite\_add}$).  This
reduces the wedge-existence question to a purely local membership condition on the neighbours of
$d.\texttt{left}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Left-fan reach through a complement arc
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitWedgeReach.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Using the validity criterion
$\texttt{leftFan\_next\_turnLeft\_valid\_iff}$, a left-fan prefix exists for as long as the successive
out-sites stay outside $F$.  $\texttt{leftFanPrefix\_of\_outSites\_not\_mem}$: if each out-site
$d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[i]} d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$ for $i < n$ lies outside
$F$, then $d.\texttt{LeftFanPrefix}\,n$ (induction, each step's validity from the membership).
Consequently $\texttt{exists\_orbit\_dart\_left\_rotated\_of\_outSites}$: $d$'s orbit contains a dart
at the same left site with direction $\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir}$.  This is the (purely
local) wedge-existence: rotating left through an exposed complement arc reaches every direction in the
arc, with no global filledness hypothesis -- the global argument later supplies the arc condition.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Same-site darts across a complement arc
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitSameLeftArc.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The wedge reach turned into a same-orbit statement.
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_same\_left\_arc}$: if $d$, $d'$ have the same left site,
$d'.\texttt{dir} = \texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir}$, and the arc out-sites
$d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[i]} d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$ for $i < n$ all lie outside
$F$, then $d$ and $d'$ are in the same orbit.  This is the same-vertex connectivity: all boundary
darts exposed in one complement wedge at a fixed $F$-vertex lie in one orbit.  The auxiliary
$\texttt{BoundaryDart.ext\_of\_left\_dir}$ records that a dart is determined by its left site and
direction.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Orbit advance to an adjacent vertex
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitAdvance.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Combining a left-fan rotation with one straight slide.
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_iterate\_succ\_left}$: if the first $n$ steps from $d$ are left turns and the
$n$-th iterate then goes straight, the $(n+1)$-th iterate is in $d$'s orbit and its left site is the
adjacent $F$-vertex $d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$.  This is
how the boundary orbit moves from one $F$-vertex to a neighbour: rotate to point along the chosen
exposed edge, then slide across it -- the per-edge transport step of the global connectivity
argument.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Membership form of the orbit advance
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitAdvanceMem.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The per-edge transport $\texttt{sameOrbit\_iterate\_succ\_left}$ restated
purely in terms of $F$-membership of the local sites -- the form the global filled-region argument
supplies.  $\texttt{sameOrbit\_advance\_of\_membership}$: if the out-sites
$d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[i]} d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$ for $i < n$ lie outside $F$
(fan rotates), the $n$-th rotated step $d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]}
d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$ lies inside $F$ (halts the fan and gives the straight $F$-side), and the
straight out-site $\texttt{rightSite}\,(\texttt{nextDart}^{[n]} d).\texttt{head}\,(\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]}
d.\texttt{dir})$ lies outside $F$, then $d$'s orbit reaches a dart at the adjacent $F$-vertex
$d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$.  The validity conditions are
derived from these memberships via $\texttt{leftFan\_next\_turnLeft\_valid\_iff}$ and
$\texttt{leftSite\_add}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Single orbit from contact-pair connectivity
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFromConnected.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The capstone reduction.
$\texttt{boundaryDart\_single\_orbit\_of\_contactPair\_connected}$: if every two contact pairs of $F$
are joined by a chain of contact moves ($\forall c\,c',\ \texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}\,c\,c'$),
then every two boundary darts are in the same orbit -- the $\texttt{hone}$ input of the Peierls bound.
The single-orbit property is now reduced to the orbit-free planar connectivity of the contact graph,
the only remaining content, via the dart-level push-down
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_dart\_contactMove\_chain}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Contact-move advance to an adjacent vertex
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitAdvanceConn.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The membership-driven orbit advance lifted to contact-move connectivity.
$\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_advance}$: under the three local membership conditions of
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_advance\_of\_membership}$, the contact pair of $d$ is contact-move connected
($\texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}$) to the contact pair of $\texttt{nextDart}^{[n+1]} d$, whose
in-site is the adjacent $F$-vertex $d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]}
d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$ (via $\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_of\_sameOrbit}$).  This is the
per-edge step the global $F$-path connectivity argument chains, now stated entirely at the
contact-graph level.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Reduction of connectivity to a basepoint
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitBasepoint.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A standard connectivity reduction using the symmetry of contact-move
connectivity.  $\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_of\_basepoint}$: if every contact pair reaches one
fixed basepoint $c_0$ by contact moves, then any two contact pairs are connected (via
$c \to c_0 \to c'$, using $\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_symm}$).  This turns the global
$\texttt{hconn}$ goal ($\forall c\,c',\ \texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}\,c\,c'$) into the simpler
$\forall c,\ \texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}\,c\,c_0$ -- ``every boundary contact pair reaches a
fixed one'', the form the $F$-path argument establishes.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Single orbit from basepoint connectivity
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFromBasepoint.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Composing the basepoint reduction with the connectivity capstone.
$\texttt{boundaryDart\_single\_orbit\_of\_contactPair\_basepoint}$: if every contact pair of $F$
reaches one fixed basepoint $c_0$ by contact moves, then every two boundary darts are in the same
orbit (the $\texttt{hone}$ input).  This is the cleanest entry point for the remaining global
argument: supplying $\forall c,\ \texttt{ReflTransGen ContactMove}\,c\,c_0$ (a boundary walk back to a
fixed contact pair) yields $\texttt{hone}$ directly.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Chaining the per-edge advance along an $F$-path
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitInSitePath.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The $F$-path induction at the contact-graph level.
$\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_of\_inSite\_reachable}$: given a per-edge advance (for any contact
pair $c$ and any $F$-neighbour $a'$ of $c.\texttt{inSite}$, a contact pair $c'$ at $a'$ connected to
$c$ by contact moves), from any contact pair $c$ one reaches a connected contact pair at any in-site
$a'$ reachable within $F$ from $c.\texttt{inSite}$ ($\texttt{ReflTransGen}$ induction over the
within-$F$ path).  This is the chaining half of the basepoint connectivity; supplying the per-edge
advance (from the wedge construction) and the same-vertex wedge then closes the global argument.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Basepoint connectivity from the geometric inputs
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitToBasepoint.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Assembling the $F$-path chaining into basepoint connectivity, isolating
the three geometric inputs the global filled-region argument must supply.
$\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_to\_basepoint}$: given a per-edge advance $\texttt{hstep}$,
same-vertex wedge connectivity $\texttt{hsame}$ (joining contact pairs sharing an in-site), and
$F$-reachability $\texttt{hreach}$ of every in-site to $c_0.\texttt{inSite}$ (from connectedness of
$F$), every contact pair reaches the fixed basepoint $c_0$ by contact moves: walk the in-site back to
the basepoint vertex ($\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_of\_inSite\_reachable}$), then rotate within
the basepoint wedge.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Single orbit from the geometric inputs
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitGeometric.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The full reduction capstone.
$\texttt{boundaryDart\_single\_orbit\_of\_geometric\_inputs}$: the single-orbit $\texttt{hone}$ input
of the Peierls bound follows from exactly three geometric inputs about $F$ with a basepoint contact
pair $c_0$ -- a per-edge advance ($\texttt{hstep}$), same-vertex wedge connectivity
($\texttt{hsame}$), and $F$-reachability of every in-site to $c_0.\texttt{inSite}$
($\texttt{hreach}$).  It composes $\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_to\_basepoint}$ with
$\texttt{boundaryDart\_single\_orbit\_of\_contactPair\_basepoint}$.  The remaining work is supplying
these three inputs from connectedness and filledness of $F$ -- the orbit/contact machinery is
otherwise complete.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Same-in-site contact pairs across an arc
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitSameInSite.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The same-vertex wedge connectivity at the contact-graph level.
$\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_same\_inSite\_arc}$: if $c$, $c'$ share an in-site,
$c'.\texttt{toDart.dir} = \texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} c.\texttt{toDart.dir}$, and the arc out-sites
$c.\texttt{inSite} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[i]} c.\texttt{toDart.dir}).\texttt{vec}$ for $i < n$ lie
outside $F$, then $c$ and $c'$ are joined by contact moves (via
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_of\_same\_left\_arc}$, $\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_of\_sameOrbit}$, and
the dart $\leftrightarrow$ contact-pair round trip).  This is the building block of the
$\texttt{hsame}$ input of $\texttt{boundaryDart\_single\_orbit\_of\_geometric\_inputs}$; the global
argument supplies the arc condition so that any two contact pairs at a vertex are connected.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Single orbit from connected-$F$ inputs
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitConnectedInputs.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The $\texttt{hreach}$ input is exactly within-$F$ connectivity, since
every contact-pair in-site lies in $F$.  $\texttt{reachable\_inSite\_of\_connected}$ supplies the
$\texttt{hreach}$ input from $F$-connectivity, and
$\texttt{boundaryDart\_single\_orbit\_of\_connected\_inputs}$ then gives $\texttt{hone}$ from a
per-edge advance $\texttt{hstep}$, same-vertex wedge connectivity $\texttt{hsame}$, and within-$F$
connectivity of $F$ -- the form in which the connectedness of the spin droplet enters.  Only the
per-edge advance and same-vertex inputs (the wedge/filled geometry) then remain.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Transferring connectivity from a box droplet to its image
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitConnTransfer.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The within-$F$ connectivity input supplied from the box.
$\texttt{reachableWithin\_image\_val}$: a within-$S$ path in $\texttt{Ambient.inducedGraph}\,G\,\Lambda$
maps under $\texttt{Subtype.val}$ to a within-$S.\texttt{image Subtype.val}$ path in $G$
($\texttt{ReflTransGen}$ induction, the induce adjacency being $G.\texttt{Adj}$ on values and
membership transferring via $\texttt{Finset.mem\_image\_of\_mem}$).  Hence
$\texttt{reachableWithin\_image\_of\_isConnectedDroplet}$: a connected droplet $S$ in the box yields a
within-image-connected set in the ambient graph.  With $G = \texttt{latticeGraph}\,2$ this is exactly
the $F$-connectivity $\texttt{hreach}$ input for $F = S.\texttt{image Subtype.val}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The left turn is a 4-cycle on directions
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitDirCycle.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} $\texttt{Dir2}$ is $\texttt{Fin}\,4$ and $\texttt{turnLeft}$ is
$\cdot + 1$, a 4-cycle.  $\texttt{Dir2.exists\_turnLeft\_iterate\_lt\_four}$: for any
$\texttt{dir}\,\delta$, there is $k < 4$ with $\texttt{turnLeft}^{[k]}\,\texttt{dir} = \delta$ (by
$\texttt{fin\_cases}$ enumeration over the 16 direction pairs).  This is the rotational backbone of
the wedge argument: a left fan can be aimed at any of the four lattice directions in at most three
steps.  Per a focused codex design review, the discrete-Jordan single-orbit input is most tractably
completed via the contact-pair route (no planar/Euler infrastructure, which Mathlib lacks); this is
one of its $\texttt{Dir2}$-enumeration ingredients.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{First exposed direction hitting $F$
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFirstHit.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Rotating left, $a + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[k]} \texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$
sweeps the four neighbours of $a$.  $\texttt{exists\_first\_turnLeft\_mem}$: if some rotation
($k < 4$) lands inside $F$, there is a \emph{first} index $n < 4$ whose rotated point lies in $F$
while every earlier rotation lands outside $F$ ($\texttt{Nat.find}$ with
$\texttt{Nat.find\_min}$/$\texttt{find\_spec}$/$\texttt{find\_le}$).  The intermediate ``outside'' run
is exactly the cleared complement arc the wedge advance needs, and the landing point is the adjacent
$F$-vertex the orbit slides to -- producing the arc-and-stop data for
$\texttt{sameOrbit\_advance\_of\_membership}$ from pure membership.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{An $F$-neighbour is hit by a rotation
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitHitAdjacent.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The precondition of $\texttt{exists\_first\_turnLeft\_mem}$ is met
whenever $a$ has an $F$-neighbour.  $\texttt{exists\_turnLeft\_hit\_of\_adjacent\_mem}$: if $a'$ is an
$F$-vertex adjacent to $a$, then some left rotation $a + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[k]}
\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$ ($k < 4$) lands in $F$ ($a' = a + \delta.\texttt{vec}$ for one of the four
directions, reached by $\texttt{Dir2.exists\_turnLeft\_iterate\_lt\_four}$).  Combined with
$\texttt{exists\_first\_turnLeft\_mem}$ this turns ``$a$ has an $F$-neighbour'' into the
cleared-arc-and-stop data of the wedge advance.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Orbit successor dichotomy at a first hit
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitDichotomy.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} After the left fan stops at the first rotation landing in $F$, the next
$\texttt{nextDart}$ step is a contact move, and its left site is fixed by one membership test on the
straight out-site $r = \texttt{rightSite}\,(\texttt{nextDart}^{[n]} d).\texttt{head}\,(\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]}
d.\texttt{dir})$.  $\texttt{firstHit\_nextDart\_inSite\_dichotomy}$: if $r \notin F$ the orbit slides
straight to the $F$-neighbour $d.\texttt{left} + (\texttt{turnLeft}^{[n]} d.\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$;
if $r \in F$ it turns right (a concave corner) with successor left site $r$.  This makes the orbit's
actual successor explicit but does \emph{not} discharge the single-orbit crux: since contact-move
connectivity equals same-orbit ($\texttt{reflTransGen\_contactMove\_iff\_sameOrbit}$), ``the orbit
visits every boundary contact pair of a filled connected component'' \emph{is} the discrete-Jordan
single-curve property, which the contact-pair bookkeeping relocates but does not remove.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Degree-two faces of the contour
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitDegTwo.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A characterisation of the $\texttt{squareSplitCount} = 2$ faces -- the
``ordinary'' faces of the Peierls contour where the curve passes through once (vs empty faces, count
$0$, and crossing faces, count $4$).  $\texttt{cyclic4\_xor\_count\_eq\_two\_iff}$: four cyclic
membership bits have two sign changes iff they are neither all equal (empty) nor strictly alternating
(crossing), by $\texttt{decide}$.  $\texttt{squareSplitCount\_eq\_two\_iff}$ transports this to the
unit square at $c$.  This isolates the crossing faces (count $4$) as the only obstruction to the
single-orbit property, the next step toward the discrete-Jordan argument (the contact-pair route
having been confirmed to relocate, not remove, the discrete Jordan crux).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The face-degree trichotomy of the contour
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFaceDeg.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Completing the characterisation of the three contour face types by
$\texttt{squareSplitCount}$ ($0$/$2$/$4$).  $\texttt{squareSplitCount\_eq\_zero\_iff}$: an
\emph{empty} face has all four corners on the same side of $F$;
$\texttt{squareSplitCount\_eq\_four\_iff}$: a \emph{crossing} face has strictly alternating corners;
with $\texttt{squareSplitCount\_eq\_two\_iff}$ (degree-two, ordinary) these decide each face's type
