from the four corner memberships (boolean facts $\texttt{cyclic4\_xor\_count\_eq\_zero\_iff}$ and
$\texttt{\_four\_iff}$, by $\texttt{decide}$).  This is the case basis for analysing how
$\texttt{nextDart}$ routes the contour through each face, toward the discrete-Jordan single-orbit
argument.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{A crossed edge carries a boundary dart
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitDartEdge.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} $\texttt{edgeCrosses}\,F\,s(a,b)$ holds exactly when one of $a, b$ lies in
$F$ and the other does not (xor of the endpoint memberships).
$\texttt{exists\_dart\_of\_edgeCrosses}$: either way the adjacent crossed pair is the primal cut edge
of some boundary dart (orienting it with $F$ on the left), packaging $\texttt{exists\_dart\_of\_cut}$
in the symmetric $\texttt{edgeCrosses}$ form via a case split on which endpoint lies in $F$
($\texttt{Sym2.eq\_swap}$ for the reversed orientation).  This is the bridge from the contour's cut
sides (counted by $\texttt{squareSplitCount}$) to the boundary darts whose orbits the single-orbit
argument tracks.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Dart site coordinates at a dual vertex
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFaceDart.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Explicit values of $\texttt{leftSite}$ and $\texttt{rightSite}$ for a
dart based at the dual vertex $c$ as the four directions rotate.  $\texttt{leftSite\_eq\_cases}$ (by
$\texttt{rfl}$, the definition) and $\texttt{rightSite\_eq\_cases}$ (by $\texttt{fin\_cases}$ and the
left-normal step) exhibit the four $\texttt{primalCutEdge}\,c\,\texttt{dir}$ as exactly the four sides
of the unit square at $c$ (bottom, right, top, left in $\texttt{dir} = -e_1, e_0, e_1, -e_0$ order).
This is the geometric input relating the contour's face degree ($\texttt{squareSplitCount}$) to the
dual-cut degree at $c$ in the discrete-Jordan argument.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{A crossed cut edge is a valid dart, one orientation
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitEdgeValid.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} $\texttt{edgeCrosses}\,F\,(\texttt{primalCutEdge}\,c\,\texttt{dir})$ says
the cut edge crossed by $\texttt{dir}$ at the dual vertex $c$ separates $F$.
$\texttt{edgeCrosses\_primalCutEdge\_iff}$: by the dart reversal identities
($\texttt{leftSite\_reverse}$, $\texttt{rightSite\_reverse}$), this holds exactly when either the dart
$(c, \texttt{dir})$ is valid ($F$ on its left) or the opposite dart $(c + \texttt{dir.vec},
\texttt{dir} + 2)$ is ($F$ on the other side), by a 4-way membership split.  This is the orientation
correction for counting incident cut directions as boundary darts (a cut edge with $F$ on the right
is realised by the reversed dart based at the neighbour) -- the degree-two face being two incident
cut directions, not two darts based at $c$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The face degree counts incident cut directions
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitFaceCard.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} $\texttt{squareSplitCount\_eq\_card\_cut\_dirs}$:
$\texttt{squareSplitCount}\,F\,c$ equals the number of directions $\texttt{dir}$ whose cut edge
$\texttt{primalCutEdge}\,c\,\texttt{dir}$ at the dual vertex $c$ is crossed by $F$.  The four
$\texttt{primalCutEdge}\,c\,\texttt{dir}$ are exactly the four sides of the unit square at $c$ (via
$\texttt{leftSite\_eq\_cases}$/$\texttt{rightSite\_eq\_cases}$ and four $\texttt{Sym2.eq\_swap}$s), so
the cut-side count is the dual-cut degree at $c$ (proof: $\texttt{card\_filter}$ with
$\texttt{sum\_congr}$ converting the filter's Prop-$\texttt{ite}$ to a Bool-$\texttt{ite}$,
$\texttt{Fin.sum\_univ\_four}$, then matching).  This identifies the contour's local even degree
($\texttt{square\_split\_count\_even}$) as a graph degree -- the bridge to the cycle structure of the
$\texttt{nextDart}$ orbits in the discrete-Jordan argument.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The Eulerian property of the dual cut
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitEulerian.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Transporting the contour's local even/$0$-$2$-$4$ degree facts
(\texttt{ContourEven}) through $\texttt{squareSplitCount\_eq\_card\_cut\_dirs}$ gives the
\textbf{Eulerian property} of the dual cut at the graph level: at every dual vertex $c$ the number
$\texttt{cutDirs}\,F\,c$ of incident cut directions is even ($\texttt{card\_cut\_dirs\_even}$), at most
four ($\texttt{card\_cut\_dirs\_le\_four}$), and in fact $0$, $2$, or $4$
($\texttt{card\_cut\_dirs\_eq}$).  Even degree everywhere is exactly the hypothesis under which a
finite graph decomposes into edge-disjoint cycles -- the combinatorial heart of identifying the
$\texttt{nextDart}$ orbits as the cycles of the contour in the discrete-Jordan argument.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Cut directions are boundary darts
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitCutDirDart.lean})}

This identifies the Eulerian degree $\texttt{cutDirs}\,F\,c$ with actual boundary darts.
$\texttt{mem\_cutDirs\_iff}$: a direction $\texttt{dir} \in \texttt{cutDirs}\,F\,c$ iff the dart
$(c, \texttt{dir})$ is valid ($\texttt{ValidAt}\,F\,c\,\texttt{dir}$, with $F$ on its left) \emph{or}
its reverse $(c + \texttt{dir}.\texttt{vec},\ \texttt{dir} + 2)$ is (with $F$ on its right), via
$\texttt{edgeCrosses\_primalCutEdge\_iff}$.  The corollaries
$\texttt{mem\_cutDirs\_of\_validAt}$ / $\texttt{mem\_cutDirs\_of\_validAt\_reverse}$ (either
orientation lands in $\texttt{cutDirs}$), $\texttt{not\_mem\_cutDirs\_iff}$ (non-membership is the
absence of an incident dart either way), $\texttt{dir\_mem\_cutDirs\_tail}$ (a
$\texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F$'s direction is a cut direction at its tail), and
$\texttt{cutDirs\_eq\_empty\_iff}$ / $\texttt{card\_cut\_dirs\_eq\_zero\_iff}$ (zero degree is no
incident boundary dart) turn the even-degree count into a count of the contour darts passing through
$c$, the link from the Eulerian property to the $\texttt{nextDart}$ orbits.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The degree-two pairing of the contour
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitDegTwoPairing.lean})}

At a \textbf{degree-two} dual vertex the contour passes through without branching (one dart in, one out), and a local pairing glues
the boundary darts into cycles.  $\texttt{dir\_add\_two\_mem\_cutDirs\_head}$: the incoming dart
$d$'s reverse $d.\texttt{dir} + 2$ is a cut direction at $d.\texttt{head}$ (the reversed dart
$(d.\texttt{head} + (d.\texttt{dir}+2).\texttt{vec},\ (d.\texttt{dir}+2)+2)$ is $d$ itself, hence
valid).  $\texttt{nextDart\_dir\_cases}$: the successor turns left, goes straight, or turns right
($d.\texttt{dir}+1,\ d.\texttt{dir},\ d.\texttt{dir}+3$); $\texttt{nextDart\_dir\_mem\_cutDirs\_head}$:
its direction is a cut direction at $d.\texttt{head}$ (its tail);
$\texttt{nextDart\_dir\_ne\_dir\_add\_two}$: it never reverses the incoming dart, since
$d.\texttt{dir}+2$ is none of those three.  Therefore
$\texttt{cutDirs\_head\_eq\_of\_squareSplitCount\_eq\_two}$: when
$\texttt{squareSplitCount}\,F\,d.\texttt{head} = 2$ the cut set is exactly the pair
$\{d.\texttt{dir}+2,\ d.\texttt{nextDart}.\texttt{dir}\}$ (two distinct cut directions in a
degree-two set), so the incoming and outgoing darts share an orbit
($\texttt{BoundaryDart.sameOrbit\_nextDart}$: $d.\texttt{SameOrbit}\,d.\texttt{nextDart}$).  This is
the degree-two case of the discrete-Jordan cycle structure.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The degree-four crossing of the contour
  (\texttt{Peierls/SingleOrbitDegFourPairing.lean})}

At a \textbf{degree-four} dual vertex all four sides are cut
($\texttt{cutDirs\_eq\_univ\_of\_squareSplitCount\_eq\_four}$) and the four corner sites strictly
alternate across $F$ (a checkerboard crossing).  Under the left-hand rule the contour
\textbf{rounds the corner}, the convention that keeps it from crossing itself.
$\texttt{validAt\_head\_turnLeft\_iff}$: the left turn at the head is valid iff the straight-ahead
left site is outside $F$ (its left site is the incoming left site, always in $F$, and its right site
is that straight left site, via $\texttt{leftSite\_head\_turnLeft}$ and
$\texttt{rightSite\_head\_turnLeft\_eq\_leftSite\_head}$).
$\texttt{validAt\_head\_turnLeft\_of\_squareSplitCount\_eq\_four}$: at a crossing the left turn is
valid -- the checkerboard alternation ($\texttt{squareSplitCount\_eq\_four\_iff}$) together with the
incoming dart's validity forces the straight left site out of $F$ (by $\texttt{fin\_cases}$ on the
direction).  $\texttt{nextDart\_dir\_eq\_turnLeft\_of\_squareSplitCount\_eq\_four}$: hence
$\texttt{nextDart}$ takes the left turn; $\texttt{nextDart\_pairs\_squareSplitCount\_four}$ bundles
the local pairing ($d.\texttt{SameOrbit}\,d.\texttt{nextDart}$,
$d.\texttt{nextDart}.\texttt{tail} = d.\texttt{head}$,
$d.\texttt{nextDart}.\texttt{dir} = d.\texttt{dir}.\texttt{turnLeft}$).  With the degree-two pairing
this completes the local case analysis for the cycle structure of the $\texttt{nextDart}$ orbits.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, Figure 3.11, p.~111 (corner-rounding rule);
pp.~109--116.

\subsection*{Edge-adjacency inside the whole dual cut
  (\texttt{Peierls/DualCutEdgeAdjacency.lean})}

Foundation for proving the dual cut $\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F$ of a connected filled region is
edge-connected \emph{directly}, without the strictly stronger single-orbit (discrete-Jordan)
hypothesis.  \textbf{Decoupling observation:} at a degree-four crossing the four incident cut edges
share the crossing vertex, so they are pairwise edge-adjacent \emph{across distinct
$\texttt{nextDart}$-orbits} -- edge-connectivity sits strictly below single-orbitness.  A strategic
audit shows the single-orbit input $\texttt{hone}$ is consumed at exactly one site
($\texttt{PeierlsContourCount.lean}$, supplying $\texttt{IsEdgeConnected}$), so the whole conditional
$m^*>0$ reduces to $\texttt{IsEdgeConnected}\,(\texttt{dualCut})$.
$\texttt{dartDualEdge\_mem\_dartDualCut}$: a boundary dart's dual edge lies in the dual cut.
$\texttt{edgeAdjacentIn\_dartDualCut\_of\_shared}$: two cut edges sharing a vertex are edge-adjacent
(the cross-orbit link).  $\texttt{orbitDualEdges\_subset\_dartDualCut}$: one orbit's dual edges sit
inside the dual cut.  $\texttt{reachable\_dartDualCut\_of\_sameOrbit}$: same-orbit darts' edges are
reachable in the whole dual cut, lifting the within-orbit reachability along the subset via
$\texttt{edgeAdjacentIn\_mono}$.  $\texttt{edgeAdjacentIn\_dartDualCut\_nextDart}$: a dart and its
successor share the pivot vertex $d.\texttt{head} = d.\texttt{nextDart}.\texttt{tail}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Dual-cut dart reachability}

File: \texttt{Peierls/DartDualReachable.lean}.  This packages the per-pair content of
edge-connectedness as a relation and proves the interface reduction needed before replacing the
single-orbit hypothesis $\texttt{hone}$.  $\texttt{DartReachable}\,F\,d\,e$ holds when the dual
edges $s(d.\texttt{tail}, d.\texttt{head})$ and $s(e.\texttt{tail}, e.\texttt{head})$ are joined by
a chain of shared-vertex steps $\texttt{edgeAdjacentIn}\,(\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F)$; it is an
equivalence ($\texttt{DartReachable.refl}$, $\texttt{DartReachable.symm}$ from
$\texttt{reflTransGen\_edgeAdjacentIn\_symmetric}$, and $\texttt{DartReachable.trans}$).
$\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_shared}$: darts sharing a dual vertex are reachable in one step (the
cross-orbit link).  $\texttt{dartReachable\_trans\_shared}$: extend a reachability by a shared-vertex
step (the F-path chaining primitive).  $\texttt{dartReachable\_nextDart}$: a dart and its
$\texttt{nextDart}$ successor are reachable.  $\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_sameOrbit}$: same-orbit
darts are reachable -- a comparison wrapper, so it is \emph{not} the intended bridge of the
unconditional route.
\textbf{Reduction:} $\texttt{dartDualCut\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_dartReachable}$ and
$\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_isEdgeConnected}$ identify pairwise dart reachability with
$\texttt{IsEdgeConnected}\,(\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F)$ at the dart interface.  The remaining geometric
obligation is to show that any two boundary darts of a connected, filled region are reachable by the
F-path / shared-vertex argument rather than by discrete-Jordan single-orbitness.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{F-path induction for dual-cut dart reachability
(\texttt{Peierls/DartReachableFPath.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A path-induction interface that turns reachability \emph{inside} the
region $F$ into $\texttt{DartReachable}$, the shape the F-path / shared-vertex shadow argument
produces.  The geometric core is \emph{not} proved here; it is isolated as explicit geometric
obligations.  The relation $\texttt{ReachableWithinSubtype}$ reindexes
$\texttt{ReachableWithin}$ on the subtype $\{x // x \in F\}$, so anchors are required only for
sites of $F$.  Fix an anchor map $\varphi : \{x // x \in F\} \to \texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_reachableWithinSubtype}$ and
    $\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_reachableWithin}$: given a per-edge step
    $\texttt{hstep} : \forall a\,b,\ G.\texttt{Adj}\,a.1\,b.1 \to
    \texttt{DartReachable}\,F\,(\varphi\,a)\,(\varphi\,b)$, a within-$F$ walk $a \rightsquigarrow b$
    ($\texttt{ReachableWithin}\,G\,F$) lifts to $\texttt{DartReachable}\,F\,(\varphi\,a)\,
    (\varphi\,b)$ by $\texttt{ReflTransGen}$ induction folding through $\texttt{DartReachable.trans}$.
  \item $\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_reachableWithin\_shadow}$: the same with the per-edge step given
    as a shared dual vertex $\exists v,\ v \in s((\varphi\,a).\texttt{tail}, (\varphi\,a).
    \texttt{head}) \wedge v \in s((\varphi\,b).\texttt{tail}, (\varphi\,b).\texttt{head})$,
    discharged through $\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_shared}$ (the ``shadow'' form).
  \item $\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_anchored}$: adding $\texttt{hanchor} : \forall d,\
    \texttt{DartReachable}\,F\,d\,(\varphi\,\langle d.\texttt{left}, d.\texttt{left\_mem}
    \rangle)$ and $F$-connectivity gives pairwise reachability of \emph{all} boundary darts via
    $d \rightsquigarrow \varphi(d.\texttt{left}) \rightsquigarrow \varphi(e.\texttt{left})
    \rightsquigarrow e$.
  \item $\texttt{dartDualCut\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_anchored}$: composing with
    $\texttt{dartDualCut\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_dartReachable}$ yields
    $\texttt{IsEdgeConnected}\,(\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F)$ from $(\varphi, \texttt{hanchor},
    \texttt{hstep})$ plus $F$-connectivity.
\end{itemize}
Remaining open: the construction of $\varphi$, $\texttt{hstep}$, and $\texttt{hanchor}$.  The
one-edge shadow step is local, while $\texttt{hanchor}$ is a same-left-site reachability input that
may require nontrivial wedge/arc geometry beyond a single local degree case.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Cardinality of the dual cut (\texttt{Peierls/DartDualCutCard.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The dual-edge map $d \mapsto s(d.\texttt{tail}, d.\texttt{head})$ is
\emph{injective} on $\texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F$ ($\texttt{dartDualEdge\_injective}$): if two darts
share a dual edge with the same orientation they are equal ($\texttt{BoundaryDart.ext'}$); the
reverse orientation forces $d.\texttt{dir}.\texttt{vec} = -e.\texttt{dir}.\texttt{vec}$, whence
$d.\texttt{dir} = e.\texttt{dir} + 2$ ($\texttt{Dir2.vec\_add\_two}$, $\texttt{Dir2.vec\_injective}$)
and the reverse left site equals the original right site ($\texttt{leftSite\_reverse}$),
contradicting $\texttt{left\_mem}$ versus $\texttt{right\_not\_mem}$.  Hence
$|\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F| = |\texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F|$ ($\texttt{dartDualCut\_card}$), the size
$r$ fed into the volume-independent contour count.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The dual-cut support box and its subtype lift (\texttt{Peierls/DualSupport.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The contour count $\texttt{card\_connected\_edge\_sets\_inducedLattice%
Graph\_le}$ lives over a finite \emph{subtype} $\uparrow\!\Lambda$, so the ambient dual cut is
restricted to the finite support box $\texttt{dualSupport}\,F$ collecting every dart's tail and head
($\texttt{tail\_mem\_dualSupport}$, $\texttt{head\_mem\_dualSupport}$).  The lifted cut
$\texttt{dualCutSub}\,F \subseteq \mathrm{Sym}_2\,\uparrow\!(\texttt{dualSupport}\,F)$ lies in the
induced lattice graph's edge finset ($\texttt{dualCutSub\_subset\_edgeFinset}$, via
$\texttt{SimpleGraph.induce\_adj}$ and $\texttt{BoundaryDart.tail\_adj\_head}$), and the lift is
injective (factoring through $\mathrm{Sym}_2.\texttt{map}\,\texttt{Subtype.val}$), so
$|\texttt{dualCutSub}\,F| = |\texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F|$ ($\texttt{dualCutSub\_card}$).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Edge-connectivity of the subtype-lifted dual cut
  (\texttt{Peierls/DualCutSubConnected.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Edge-connectivity transfers across the injective subtype lift
$\mathrm{Sym}_2.\texttt{map}\,\texttt{Subtype.val}$: if the image of $Y$ is edge-connected, so is
$Y$ ($\texttt{isEdgeConnected\_of\_image\_map\_subtype}$).  A shared ambient vertex of two lifted
edges is a coercion, hence pulls back into $\uparrow\!\Lambda$, and a reachability chain lifts by
$\texttt{ReflTransGen}$ induction.  Since the lift's image is exactly $\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F$
($\texttt{dualCutSub\_image\_map\_val}$), the subtype dual cut is edge-connected given one orbit
($\texttt{dualCutSub\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_single\_orbit}$), the form
$\texttt{card\_connected\_edge\_sets\_le}$ consumes.  The same transfer is also provided for the
anchored dart-reachability route
($\texttt{dualCutSub\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_anchored}$).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The dual cut over a common box (\texttt{Peierls/DualCutInBox.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The contour count ranges over a \emph{fixed} box $\Lambda_d$, so the
per-region support box must be promoted into a common box $\Lambda_d \supseteq \texttt{dualSupport}
\,F$.  Forward edge-connectivity transfers under any injective $\mathrm{Sym}_2.\texttt{map}\,f$
($\texttt{isEdgeConnected\_image\_map}$): a shared vertex and a reachability chain
both map forward.  Mapping $\texttt{dualCutSub}\,F$ along the injective inclusion
$\uparrow\!(\texttt{dualSupport}\,F) \hookrightarrow \uparrow\!\Lambda_d$
($\texttt{supportIncl}$) gives $\texttt{dualCutInBox}$, which carries the three count-ready
properties to the common box: edge-finset membership
($\texttt{dualCutInBox\_subset\_edgeFinset}$), cardinality $|\texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F|$
($\texttt{dualCutInBox\_card}$), and edge-connectivity given one orbit
($\texttt{dualCutInBox\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_single\_orbit}$).  The wrapper
$\texttt{dualCutInBox\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_anchored}$ gives the same common-box target from the
anchored $\texttt{DartReachable}$ data, matching the connectivity form consumed by the Peierls
contour count.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The contour count capstone (\texttt{Peierls/ContourCount.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} FV (3.49) specialized to the droplet family.  over any droplet type, if a family $D$ of
droplets maps \emph{injectively} to connected size-$r$ edge cuts inside the induced lattice graph
over a box $\Lambda_d$, each through a fixed anchor vertex $z$, then $\#D \le (2\cdot 2)^{2r}$
($\texttt{card\_droplets\_le\_of\_cut\_connected}$).  This is the direct consequence of the
walk-counting bound $\texttt{card\_connected\_edge\_sets\_inducedLatticeGraph\_le}$, the geometric
inputs (injectivity, connectivity, anchor) isolated as hypotheses; the single-anchor form is summed
over $r+1$ ray anchors downstream.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The dual edge determines the primal cut edge (\texttt{Peierls/DualToPrimal.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} A boundary dart crosses one primal cut edge $\texttt{primalCutEdge}
\,t\,\delta = s(\texttt{leftSite}, \texttt{rightSite})$.  This primal edge depends only on the
dart's \emph{dual} edge $s(t, t+\delta.\texttt{vec})$, independent of orientation: the reverse dart
swaps the left and right sites ($\texttt{rightSite\_reverse}$ complements $\texttt{leftSite\_%
reverse}$), but the unordered primal edge is unchanged ($\texttt{Sym2.eq\_swap}$).  Hence equal dual
edges give equal primal cut edges ($\texttt{primalCutEdge\_congr\_of\_dualEdge\_eq}$) --- the
well-definedness bridge from dual-cut equality to primal-cut equality used in the contour
injectivity (with $\texttt{isFilled\_eq\_of\_cutEdges\_eq}$).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The dual cut determines the primal cut (\texttt{Peierls/DartPrimalCut.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The \emph{primal cut} $\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,F$ collects every
boundary dart's primal cut edge.  A dual-cut inclusion induces a primal-cut inclusion
($\texttt{dartPrimalCut\_subset\_of\_dartDualCut\_subset}$): each primal edge's dart has a dual edge
in the larger dual cut, matched by some dart there, whose primal edge coincides by
$\texttt{primalCutEdge\_congr\_of\_dualEdge\_eq}$.  Hence equal dual cuts give equal primal cuts
($\texttt{dartPrimalCut\_eq\_of\_dartDualCut\_eq}$), the middle link of the contour injectivity
chain $\texttt{dartDualCut}\,{=}\Rightarrow\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,{=}\Rightarrow\mathrm{cut}\,{=}
\Rightarrow F\,{=}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Common-box dual cut determines the primal cut
  (\texttt{Peierls/DualCutInBoxInjective.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Mapping the common-box dual cut $\texttt{dualCutInBox}$ back down by
$\mathrm{Sym}_2.\texttt{map}\,\texttt{Subtype.val}$ recovers $\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F$
($\texttt{dualCutInBox\_image\_map\_val}$; the two subtype maps compose to the support inclusion's
coercion via $\mathrm{Sym}_2.\texttt{map\_map}$).  Hence equal common-box dual cuts over the same
box force equal ambient dual cuts ($\texttt{dartDualCut\_eq\_of\_dualCutInBox\_eq}$), and therefore
equal primal cuts ($\texttt{dartPrimalCut\_eq\_of\_dualCutInBox\_eq}$) --- the upper half of the
contour injectivity chain.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Every cut edge is crossed by a boundary dart (\texttt{Peierls/DartOfCut.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The reverse of $\texttt{primalCutEdge}$.  A 2D lattice neighbour is one
of the four axis shifts $\pm e_0, \pm e_1$ ($\texttt{latticeGraph2\_adj\_cases}$, from $\sum_i
|a_i-b_i| = 1$).  Hence given $a \in F$, $b \notin F$ adjacent, some boundary dart of $F$ has primal
cut edge $s(a, b)$ ($\texttt{exists\_dart\_of\_cut}$): the dart's direction and tail are recovered
from the offset $b - a$ by inverting the $\texttt{leftSite}$/$\texttt{rightSite}$ formulas (four
cases).  This is the surjective ($\supseteq$) half of the dart--cut bijection.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The primal cut is the lattice cut (\texttt{Peierls/DartCutChar.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Combining the two halves of the dart--cut correspondence, an edge lies
in $\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,F$ exactly when it joins an $F$-vertex to a non-$F$-vertex
($\texttt{mem\_dartPrimalCut\_iff}$): the $\subseteq$ direction reads off each dart's
$\texttt{left\_mem}$/$\texttt{right\_not\_mem}$ (its endpoints are adjacent,
$\texttt{leftSite\_adj\_rightSite}$, differing by the unit vector $(\texttt{turnLeft}\,
\texttt{dir}).\texttt{vec}$); the $\supseteq$ direction is $\texttt{exists\_dart\_of\_cut}$.  Thus
$\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,F$ \emph{is} the lattice cut of $F$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Cardinality of the primal cut (\texttt{Peierls/DartPrimalCutCard.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The left site is the tail shifted by a direction constant
($\texttt{leftSite\_eq\_tail\_add}$: $\texttt{leftSite}\,t\,\texttt{dir} = t +
\texttt{leftSite}\,0\,\texttt{dir}$), so $\texttt{leftSite}\,\cdot\,\texttt{dir}$ is injective in the
tail.  Hence the primal-cut-edge map $d \mapsto \texttt{primalCutEdge}\,d.\texttt{tail}\,
d.\texttt{dir}$ is \emph{injective} ($\texttt{dartPrimalEdge\_injective}$): same orientation
determines the dart ($\texttt{Dir2.turnLeft}$/$\texttt{Dir2.vec}$ injective, tail injectivity),
reverse orientation puts $F$ on both sides.  Therefore $|\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,F| =
|\texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F|$ ($\texttt{dartPrimalCut\_card}$): the primal cut, dual cut, and dart
count share the common size $r$, matching $|\texttt{dualCutInBox}|$ to $|\mathrm{cut}\,(G,S)|$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The dual-cut size equals the box cut size
  (\texttt{Peierls/DualCutCardBridge.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} For a neighbour-closed box droplet $S$, $|\texttt{dualCutInBox}| =
|\mathrm{cut}\,(G,S)|$ ($\texttt{dualCutInBox\_card\_eq\_cutEdges}$), by chaining
$|\texttt{dualCutInBox}| = |\texttt{BoundaryDart}| = |\texttt{dartPrimalCut}| = |\texttt{liftBoxCut}|
= |\mathrm{cut}\,(G,S)|$ (via $\texttt{dualCutInBox\_card}$, $\texttt{dartPrimalCut\_card}$, the box
bridge $\texttt{dartPrimalCut\_image\_val\_eq\_liftBoxCut}$, and $\texttt{liftBoxCut\_card}$).  So
the dual-cut size $r$ fed into the contour count coincides with the Peierls bound's
$|\mathrm{cut}\,(G,S)|$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Membership in the lifted box cut (\texttt{Peierls/LiftBoxCutChar.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} An ambient edge lies in $\texttt{liftBoxCut}\,\Lambda\,F$ iff it is the
subtype lift $s(\uparrow\!a, \uparrow\!b)$ of a box edge with $a \in F$, $b \notin F$
($\texttt{mem\_liftBoxCut\_iff}$; the $\texttt{edgeCrosses}$ xor selects the orientation via
$\mathrm{Sym}_2.\texttt{eq\_swap}$, and box adjacency unfolds through
$\texttt{SimpleGraph.induce\_adj}$).  This oriented form mirrors $\texttt{mem\_dartPrimalCut\_iff}$,
so the two can be matched in the dart--cut box bridge.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The ambient primal cut is the lifted box cut (\texttt{Peierls/BoxBridge.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} For a box droplet $F : \texttt{Finset}\,\uparrow\!\Lambda$ that is
\emph{neighbour-closed} (every lattice neighbour of an $F$-vertex lies in $\Lambda$, automatic when
$F$ is separated from the box boundary), $\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,(F.\texttt{image}\,
\texttt{Subtype.val}) = \texttt{liftBoxCut}\,\Lambda\,F$
($\texttt{dartPrimalCut\_image\_val\_eq\_liftBoxCut}$).  The inclusion $\texttt{liftBoxCut}
\subseteq \texttt{dartPrimalCut}$ needs no hypothesis; the reverse uses neighbour-closure so the
non-$F$ endpoint is itself a box vertex.  This bridges the ambient dual-cut/dart machinery to the
box parity injectivity $\texttt{isFilled\_eq\_of\_cutEdges\_eq}$, completing the contour injectivity
chain $\texttt{dualCutInBox}\,{=}\Rightarrow\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,{=}\Rightarrow\texttt{liftBoxCut}
\,{=}\Rightarrow\mathrm{cut}\,{=}\Rightarrow F\,{=}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The lifted box cut is injective (\texttt{Peierls/LiftBoxCutInjective.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} In a preconnected box graph, $\texttt{liftBoxCut}\,\Lambda$ is injective
on $\{F \mid g \notin F\}$ ($\texttt{liftBoxCut\_injOn}$): equal lifted cuts give equal box cuts
($\mathrm{Sym}_2.\texttt{map}\,\texttt{Subtype.val}$ injective via $\texttt{Finset.image\_%
injective}$), which $\texttt{eq\_of\_cutEdges\_eq}$ (the winding-parity argument) turns into equal
regions.  This is the final link of the contour injectivity chain.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Contour injectivity: a droplet is determined by its dual cut
  (\texttt{Peierls/ContourInjective.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Assembling the three links --- $\texttt{dualCutInBox}\,{=}\Rightarrow
\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,{=}$, the box bridge $\texttt{dartPrimalCut}\,{=}\,\texttt{liftBoxCut}$
under neighbour-closure, and $\texttt{liftBoxCut}$ injectivity --- a neighbour-closed
($\texttt{NeighbourClosed}$), ground-avoiding box droplet in a preconnected box graph is uniquely
determined by its common-box dual cut ($\texttt{box\_droplet\_eq\_of\_dualCutInBox\_eq}$, via
$\texttt{box\_droplet\_eq\_of\_dartPrimalCut\_eq}$).  This is the injectivity input of the contour
count capstone $\texttt{card\_droplets\_le\_of\_cut\_connected}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The axis ray exits a finite region (\texttt{Peierls/RayExit.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The Peierls anchor walks along the $+e_0$ ray $\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k =
i + k\,e_0$ ($\texttt{ray0\_succ}$, $\texttt{ray0\_apply\_zero}$, $\texttt{ray0\_injective}$,
$\texttt{ray0\_adj\_succ}$).  A finite region $F \ni i$ has a \emph{first exit}
($\texttt{exists\_first\_exit}$): an index $k$ with $\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k \in F$ and
$\texttt{ray0}\,i\,(k{+}1) \notin F$ (the ray cannot stay in the finite $F$; take $\texttt{Nat.find}$
of the first non-membership).  The exit edge $\{\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k, \texttt{ray0}\,i\,(k{+}1)\}$ is
a cut edge, the basis of the anchor pinning the contour to the fixed sequence $z_k =
\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The ray-exit anchor dart (\texttt{Peierls/RayAnchorDart.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} At a $+e_0$ exit point $a$ ($a \in F$, $a + e_0 \notin F$), the concrete
dart $\texttt{e0ExitAnchorDart}$ has $\texttt{tail} = a - e_1$, $\texttt{dir} = e_1$, and
\emph{head} $= a$; its dual edge $s(a-e_1, a)$ contains $a$
($\texttt{e0ExitAnchorDart\_tail}$, $\texttt{e0ExitAnchorDart\_dir}$,
$\texttt{e0ExitAnchorDart\_head}$, $\texttt{e0ExitAnchorDart\_anchor\_mem}$).  Composing with
$\texttt{exists\_first\_exit}$, the dual cut of a finite $F \ni i$ passes through some ray point
($\texttt{exists\_ray\_anchor\_dartDualCut}$:
$\exists k,\ \exists e \in \texttt{dartDualCut}\,F,\ \texttt{ray0}\,i\,k \in e$) --- the Peierls
anchor (ambient form), pinning the dual contour to the fixed sequence $\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The ray anchor in the common box (\texttt{Peierls/RayAnchorBox.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Lifting the ambient ray anchor to the count-ready common-box dual cut.
The $+e_0$ exit dart has \emph{head} exactly the exit point $a$
($\texttt{exists\_e0\_exit\_anchor\_dart\_head}$).  Hence for a finite box droplet $F \ni i$ with
$\texttt{dualSupport}\,F \subseteq \Lambda_d$, there is $k$ with $\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k \in \Lambda_d$
and an edge of $\texttt{dualCutInBox}$ containing the subtype anchor vertex $\langle\texttt{ray0}\,
i\,k, \cdot\rangle$ ($\texttt{exists\_ray\_anchor\_dualCutInBox}$).  The anchor vertex lies in the box
automatically (it is a dart head, hence in $\texttt{dualSupport}\,F \subseteq \Lambda_d$), equals
$\texttt{supportIncl}\,(\texttt{dartHeadSub}\,d)$, and sits on the dart's lifted dual edge.  This is
the count-ready anchor $\exists e \in \mathrm{cut},\ z \in e$ for
$\texttt{card\_droplets\_le\_of\_cut\_connected}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Ray-exit anchor darts as a site-indexed map
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorDart.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} For every site $a \in F$, the chosen $+e_0$ first-exit index
$\texttt{rayExitIndex}\,F\,a\,h_a$ keeps every earlier ray point in $F$
($\texttt{rayExitIndex\_below}$); in particular
$\texttt{ray0}\,a\,(\texttt{rayExitIndex}\,F\,a\,h_a) \in F$, while its successor lies outside $F$
($\texttt{rayExitIndex\_mem}$ and $\texttt{rayExitIndex\_succ\_not\_mem}$).  The corresponding
boundary dart $\texttt{rayExitAnchorDart}\,F\,a\,h_a$ is the concrete $+e_0$ exit dart at that site:
its tail is one $e_1$ step below the chosen exit point, its direction is $e_1$, its head is the
chosen exit point, and that point lies on its dual edge
($\texttt{rayExitAnchorDart\_tail}$, $\texttt{rayExitAnchorDart\_dir}$,
$\texttt{rayExitAnchorDart\_head}$, $\texttt{rayExitAnchorDart\_anchor\_mem}$).  Its dual edge lies in
$\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F$ ($\texttt{rayExitAnchorDart\_dualEdge\_mem}$).  The map
$\texttt{rayExitAnchorDartMap}\,F : \{x // x \in F\} \to \texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F$ packages these
choices in exactly the subtype-indexed shape needed for the later anchored $\texttt{DartReachable}$
data, including map-level tail, direction, head, and anchor-membership lemmas for the later
$\texttt{hshadow}$ input.  This file only supplies the canonical ray-exit anchor map; the anchoring
and one-edge shadow obligations remain separate geometric inputs.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Ray-exit anchor stability along ray prefixes
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorPrefix.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Along a fixed $+e_0$ ray before its chosen first exit, later prefix
sites see the same exit edge.  The ray identity $\texttt{ray0\_add}$ reindexes a ray whose origin
has already been shifted along the same ray.  The uniqueness lemmas
$\texttt{first\_exit\_below\_unique}$ and $\texttt{rayExitIndex\_eq\_of\_first\_exit}$ make the
strengthened first-exit specification rigid, so $\texttt{rayExitIndex\_shift}$ subtracts the prefix
offset and $\texttt{ray0\_rayExitIndex\_shift}$ identifies the shifted and original exit sites.
Consequently $\texttt{rayExitAnchorDart\_shift}$ and
$\texttt{rayExitAnchorDartMap\_prefix\_eq}$ show that prefix sites choose the same ray-exit anchor
dart, while $\texttt{rayExitAnchorDart\_prefix\_shared}$ and
$\texttt{rayExitAnchorDartMap\_prefix\_shared}$ package the same fact as a shared-dual-vertex input
for later $\texttt{hshadow}$ assembly.  This is only ray-prefix stability; the full adjacent-site
shadow condition and the $\texttt{hanchor}$ reachability input remain separate geometric tasks.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Horizontal ray-exit anchor shadow steps
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorStep.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} This file repackages ray-prefix stability as the one-step horizontal
part of the later $\texttt{hshadow}$ input.  The identity $\texttt{ray0\_one}$ rewrites one ray
step as $x + e_0$.  A small lower-bound lemma for the first exit index then shows that this first
step is before the chosen exit whenever it remains in $F$.  Consequently the file provides
shared-dual-vertex witnesses for $x$ with $\texttt{ray0}\,x\,1$, for the forward horizontal step
$x \mapsto x+e_0$, and, by coordinate cancellation, for the backward horizontal step
$x \mapsto x-e_0$.  These lemmas cover only the horizontal
same-ray cases; the vertical/frontier shadow cases and the $\texttt{hanchor}$ reachability input
remain separate.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Ray-exit adjacency shadow case reduction
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorAdjacency.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} This file packages the two-dimensional nearest-neighbour case split
around the horizontal ray-exit shadow lemmas.  For adjacent sites $x,y \in F$,
$\texttt{rayExitAnchorDartMap\_adj\_shared\_or\_vertical}$ proves that either the two ray-exit
anchor edges already share a dual vertex, or $y$ is one of the vertical shifts $x \pm e_1$.
The horizontal $x \pm e_0$ branches are discharged by the one-step results above.  The vertical
and frontier shadow cases, and the $\texttt{hanchor}$ reachability input, remain separate.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Ray-exit adjacency route with vertical obligations}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorAdjacencyRoute.lean} consumes the adjacency case reduction at the
route level.
The predicate $\texttt{RayExitVerticalStep}\,F$ names the remaining oriented vertical transport
input: for $y = x \pm e_1$, the ray-exit anchors of $x$ and $y$ are connected by
$\texttt{DartReachable}$.  The main adjacency lemma closes an arbitrary adjacent-site step by using
the horizontal shared-vertex lemmas in the $x \pm e_0$ branches and the vertical input in the
remaining branches.  The resulting ambient, subtype, common-box, and contour-count wrappers carry
this narrowed input through the anchored route, keeping $\texttt{hanchor}$,
$\texttt{RayExitVerticalStep}$, and ordinary within-$F$ connectivity explicit.  The point of this
interface is to avoid overclaiming a direct shared vertex in the vertical cases, where the two
first-exit anchor edges may require a longer dual-cut chain.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Equal-index vertical ray-exit steps}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalEqual.lean} closes the safe part of the vertical input left
by the adjacency route.  The coordinate lemma
\(\texttt{ray0\_add\_unitVec2\_one}\) says that shifting the start of a \(+e_0\) ray by \(+e_1\)
shifts every ray point by \(+e_1\).  Hence, if \(b=a+e_1\) and the two ray-exit indices agree,
the anchor edge for \(a\) has endpoints \(\texttt{ray0}\,a\,k-e_1\) and
\(\texttt{ray0}\,a\,k\), while the anchor edge for \(b\) has endpoints
\(\texttt{ray0}\,a\,k\) and \(\texttt{ray0}\,a\,k+e_1\).  The two edges therefore share the lower
exit point.  This is formalized by
\(\texttt{rayExitAnchorDartMap\_add\_e1\_shared\_of\_index\_eq}\).

The remaining predicate \(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictStep}\,F\) asks only for upward
\(+e_1\) pairs whose first-exit indices are unequal.  The wrapper
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStep\_of\_strictStep}\) recovers the earlier
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStep}\): equal-index upward cases use the shared vertex, and downward
cases are handled by applying the upward statement in the reverse order and using symmetry of
\(\texttt{DartReachable}\).  The ambient, subtype, common-box, and contour-count wrappers expose
the stricter input while still leaving the genuinely unequal-index vertical geometry open.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Connected-droplet strict ray-exit route}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictConnected.lean} removes one purely structural input from
the strict ray-exit route in the Peierls count setting.  The strict wrappers of the previous file
still require ordinary connectivity inside
\(F = S.\mathrm{image}\,\texttt{Subtype.val}\).  But for a box droplet
\(S : \texttt{Finset}\,\Lambda\), the Peierls hypotheses already include connectedness of \(S\) in
the induced box graph.  The lemma
\(\texttt{rayExit\_image\_conn\_of\_isConnectedDroplet}\) is the specialization of
\(\texttt{reachableWithin\_image\_of\_isConnectedDroplet}\) to \(\texttt{latticeGraph}\,2\), turning
that box connectedness into the required within-image reachability.

The connected wrappers thread this supplied connectivity through the ray-exit route:
\begin{Verbatim}
dartReachable_of_rayExitVerticalStrict_connected
dualCutInBox_isEdgeConnected_of_rayExitVerticalStrict_connected
peierls_contour_count_rayExit_verticalStrict_connected
\end{Verbatim}
The remaining explicit geometric inputs are still
\(\texttt{hanchor}\) and \(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictStep}\); the strict unequal-index vertical
chain and the same-left-site anchor reachability are not proved here.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Ordered strict ray-exit cases}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictOrdered.lean} splits the remaining strict vertical
ray-exit input by first-exit-index order.  The previous
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictStep}\) handles upward \(+e_1\) pairs with unequal indices in one
block.  The ordered interface names the two later geometric cases separately:
\begin{Verbatim}
RayExitVerticalStrictLtStep
RayExitVerticalStrictGtStep
\end{Verbatim}
The lemma \(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictStep\_of\_orderedStep}\) recovers the previous strict
input by trichotomy for natural numbers.

The ordered wrappers thread this refinement through the same strict route, including the connected
count consumer \(\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_verticalStrictOrdered\_connected}\).
The proof obligations remain explicit: this file does not prove either ordered frontier chain and
does not prove the same-left-site anchor reachability \(\texttt{hanchor}\).
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Endpoint bridge darts for strict vertical ray-exit cases}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridge.lean} proves the first boundary dart forced at
the near endpoint of each ordered strict vertical case.  If \(b=a+e_1\) and the lower ray exits
first, then \(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtBridgeDart}\) is the horizontal \(+e_0\) boundary dart
at the lower first-exit point: its left site is the upper successor, still in \(F\), and its right
site is the lower successor, outside \(F\).  The lemma
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_rayExitAnchorDartMap\_ltBridgeDart}\) connects the lower ray-exit anchor
to this bridge by a shared dual vertex.

If the upper ray exits first, \(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictGtBridgeDart}\) is the horizontal
\(-e_0\) boundary dart below the upper first-exit point: its left site is the lower successor,
still in \(F\), and its right site is the upper successor, outside \(F\).  The lemma
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_rayExitAnchorDartMap\_gtBridgeDart}\) connects the upper ray-exit anchor
to this bridge by a shared dual vertex.

These lemmas are endpoint bridges only.  A finite set may re-enter a ray after the first exit, so
the file deliberately does not assert that the whole vertical strip between the two exit indices is
a straight boundary chain.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Bridge-chain inputs for strict vertical ray-exit cases}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeChain.lean} consumes the endpoint bridge darts
and restates the remaining ordered strict vertical obligations as post-bridge chain inputs.  In the
lower-exits-first case, \(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtBridgeChain}\) asks for reachability from
the lower-first bridge dart to the upper ray-exit anchor.  The endpoint lemma supplies the preceding
step from the lower ray-exit anchor to that bridge, so transitivity recovers
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtStep}\).

In the upper-exits-first case, \(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictGtBridgeChain}\) asks for reachability
from the lower ray-exit anchor to the upper-first bridge dart.  The endpoint lemma supplies
reachability from the upper ray-exit anchor to that bridge; after symmetry, transitivity recovers
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictGtStep}\).  The combined theorem
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictOrderedStep\_of\_bridgeChainStep}\) then supplies the ordered strict
input consumed by the existing ray-exit route.

The connected count wrapper
\(\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_verticalStrictBridgeChain\_connected}\) keeps the
same-left-site anchor reachability explicit, uses the bridge-chain input for the remaining vertical
frontier geometry, and continues to obtain ordinary within-image connectivity from
\(\texttt{IsConnectedDroplet}\).  This is still an interface reduction; it does not prove the
post-bridge frontier chains.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Gap-reduced bridge-chain inputs for strict vertical ray-exit cases}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeGap.lean} removes the adjacent-index subcase from
the remaining bridge-chain input.  If the lower ray exits first and the upper first-exit index is
exactly one more than the lower first-exit index, then the lower endpoint bridge dart shares its
head with the upper ray-exit anchor.  Thus
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_ltBridgeDart\_rayExitAnchorDartMap\_of\_succ}\) closes that
post-bridge chain by a single shared-vertex step.

The upper-exits-first adjacent-index case is symmetric:
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_rayExitAnchorDartMap\_gtBridgeDart\_of\_succ}\) connects the lower
ray-exit anchor to the upper endpoint bridge dart when the lower first-exit index is exactly one
more than the upper first-exit index.

The new input
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictBridgeGapChainStep}\) therefore only covers genuine gaps, where the
first-exit indices differ by at least two.  The count wrappers
\(\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_verticalStrictBridgeGapChain}\) and
\(\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_verticalStrictBridgeGapChain\_connected}\) thread this
narrower input to the same count consumer, either from explicit within-\(F\) connectivity or from
\(\texttt{IsConnectedDroplet}\).  This still does not assume that a ray remains outside after first
exit; it only proves the endpoint-adjacent case.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Straight strip chains for strict vertical ray-exit gaps
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeStrip.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeStrip.lean} closes the next concrete subcase of
the genuine-gap bridge input.  In the lower-exits-first case, if every lower ray point between the
two first-exit indices is outside \(F\), the horizontal darts
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtStripDart}\) form a finite strip from the lower endpoint bridge to
the upper ray-exit anchor.  Consecutive strip darts share the intermediate lower ray point, and the
terminal strip dart shares the upper anchor tail.  This gives
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_ltBridgeDart\_rayExitAnchorDartMap\_of\_strip}\).

The upper-exits-first case is the reversed analogue: if every upper ray point in the interval is
outside \(F\), the darts \(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictGtStripDart}\) form a finite chain from the
lower ray-exit anchor down to the upper endpoint bridge, giving
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_rayExitAnchorDartMap\_gtBridgeDart\_of\_strip}\).

The new input \(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripGapChainStep}\) therefore only covers
genuine gaps which are not straight strips.  The wrappers
\(\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_verticalStrictBridgeNonStripGapChain}\) and
\(\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_verticalStrictBridgeNonStripGapChain\_connected}\)
thread this narrower input to the count consumer.  The argument is local to the finite interval
between the two first-exit indices; it does not assume global ray monotonicity after first exit.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Frontier entries for non-strip strict ray-exit gaps
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStrip.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStrip.lean} prepares the remaining
non-strip genuine-gap case.  If the lower-exits-first gap is not a straight strip, then some
lower ray point in the finite interval between the two first-exit indices belongs to \(F\);
\(\texttt{exists\_ltGap\_nonStrip\_mem}\) extracts such a point.  The upper-exits-first case is
handled by \(\texttt{exists\_gtGap\_nonStrip\_mem}\).  The indices
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtFirstFrontierIndex}\) and
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictGtFirstFrontierIndex}\) choose the first such re-entry point by
\(\texttt{Nat.find}\).

The first re-entry index is strictly after the first outside successor, since that successor is
outside \(F\) by the first-exit property.  Minimality then shows that the predecessor ray point is
outside \(F\).  Thus the horizontal primal edge between
\(\texttt{ray0}\,i\,(n-1)\notin F\) and \(\texttt{ray0}\,i\,n\in F\) is a cut edge.  The generic
dart \(\texttt{ray0ReentryDart}\) crosses this edge with direction \(-e_1\), and the specialized
darts \(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierDart}\) and
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictGtFrontierDart}\) provide the canonical entry darts for the next
\(\texttt{nextDart}\) frontier-chain step.  The file also exposes tail, direction, and head
shape lemmas for \(\texttt{ray0ReentryDart}\) and for the lower and upper specialized frontier
darts, complementing the existing left-site and right-site descriptions.  This remains a
finite-interval statement and does not assume ray monotonicity after first exit.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Frontier-split inputs for non-strip strict ray-exit gaps
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripFrontier.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripFrontier.lean} refines the remaining
non-strip bridge-gap input by factoring it through the first re-entry darts constructed above.
The lower-exits-first input \(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtBridgeFrontierChain}\) asks for a
chain from the endpoint bridge dart to
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierDart}\), followed by a chain from that frontier dart to
the upper ray-exit anchor.  The upper-exits-first input
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictGtBridgeFrontierChain}\) is oriented as in the existing upper
route: the lower ray-exit anchor reaches \(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictGtFrontierDart}\), and
that frontier dart reaches the upper endpoint bridge dart.

The theorem
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripGapChainStep\_of\_frontierChainStep}\) recovers the
previous non-strip input by transitivity through the explicit frontier dart.  The accompanying
route and count wrappers thread this frontier-split data to the connected-droplet Peierls count
consumer.  This is still an interface reduction for the later \(\texttt{nextDart}\) local-turn
proof; it does not assume ray monotonicity after first exit.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{NextDart inputs for non-strip strict ray-exit frontier chains
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripNextDart.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripNextDart.lean} gives the frontier-split
input a direct traversal form.  The generic lemma
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_nextDart\_iterate}\) proves that a boundary dart reaches each forward
\(\texttt{nextDart}\) iterate in the \(\texttt{DartReachable}\) relation, and
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_nextDart\_iterate\_eq}\) turns a forward-iterate equality into the
corresponding reachability statement.  This avoids routing the argument through
\(\texttt{SameOrbit}\) or \(\texttt{ContactMove}\).

The lower input
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtBridgeFrontierNextDartChain}\) asks for two forward iterate
witnesses: from the lower endpoint bridge to
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierDart}\), and from that frontier dart to the upper
ray-exit anchor.  The upper input
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictGtBridgeFrontierNextDartChain}\) asks for the analogous witnesses
from the lower ray-exit anchor to \(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictGtFrontierDart}\), and from that
frontier dart to the upper endpoint bridge.  The recovery theorem
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictBridgeFrontierChainStep\_of\_nextDartChainStep}\) and the route/count
wrappers thread this stricter input to the connected-droplet count consumer.  The local turn proof
for these iterates remains the next geometric task.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Turn-certificate inputs for non-strip strict ray-exit frontier chains
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripTurn.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripTurn.lean} refines the NextDart input
by naming the local left/straight/right turn data that compute each step of the frontier
traversal.  The generic certificate \(\texttt{NextDartTurnStep}\) records one application of the
boundary-dart turning rule, and \(\texttt{NextDartTurnChain}\) records a finite chain of such
certificates.  The bridge theorem
\(\texttt{exists\_nextDart\_iterate\_eq\_of\_turnChain}\) recovers an explicit forward
\(\texttt{nextDart}\) iterate witness from the chain, and
\(\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_turnChain}\) gives the corresponding dual-cut reachability.

The lower and upper non-strip inputs are strengthened to
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtBridgeFrontierTurnChain}\) and
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictGtBridgeFrontierTurnChain}\).  These assumptions supply local turn
chains for the four frontier legs: lower bridge to lower frontier, lower frontier to the upper
ray-exit anchor, lower ray-exit anchor to upper frontier, and upper frontier to upper bridge.
Recovery wrappers convert the turn-chain input back to the NextDart input, so the common-box and
connected-droplet count route ends at
\(\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_verticalStrictBridgeFrontierTurnChain\_connected}\).

This remains an interface reduction.  The concrete geometric proof of those turn certificates,
and the separate same-left-site anchor reachability input, remain open.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Concrete lower strip turn step for non-strip ray-exit chains
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripTurnStep.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The file
\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchorVerticalStrictBridgeNonStripTurnStep.lean} starts to discharge the
turn-chain input by proving concrete local steps along the lower horizontal strip.  The lemma
\(\texttt{nextDartTurnChain\_ltBridgeDart\_ltStripDart\_base}\) identifies the lower endpoint
bridge dart with the first lower strip dart as a trivial turn chain.  The lemma
\(\texttt{validAt\_ltStripDart\_straight\_succ}\) shows that the straight candidate after a lower
\(+e_0\) strip dart is valid when the next upper ray point is still in \(F\) and the next lower ray
point is outside \(F\).  The lemma
\(\texttt{not\_validAt\_ltStripDart\_turnLeft\_succ}\) shows that the left-turn candidate is
blocked because its right site is that same upper ray point in \(F\).

Together these facts give
\(\texttt{nextDartTurnStep\_ltStripDart\_succ}\): consecutive lower strip darts are connected by a
certified straight \(\texttt{nextDart}\) step.  This is a concrete local turn certificate for the
non-strip frontier-chain route and does not assume monotonicity of the ray after its first exit.
The lemma \(\texttt{nextDartTurnChain\_ltStripDart\_iterate}\) lifts these one-step certificates to
a finite lower strip \(\texttt{NextDartTurnChain}\), matching the turn-chain interface introduced
above.  The terminal step before the first lower re-entry is a right turn:
\(\texttt{not\_validAt\_ltStripDart\_turnLeft\_frontier}\) and
\(\texttt{not\_validAt\_ltStripDart\_straight\_frontier}\) show that the left-turn and straight
candidates are blocked by \(F\)-sites, while
\(\texttt{validAt\_ltStripDart\_turnRight\_frontier}\) supplies the valid right-turn candidate.
Thus \(\texttt{nextDartTurnStep\_ltStripDart\_frontier}\) connects the last lower strip dart to
the first lower re-entry frontier dart.  The generic chain helpers
\(\texttt{nextDartTurnChain\_of\_eq}\) and
\(\texttt{nextDartTurnChain\_trans}\) transport and compose turn chains, and
\(\texttt{nextDartTurnChain\_ltBridgeDart\_ltFrontierDart}\) combines the lower bridge base, the
finite lower strip chain, and the terminal right turn into a single certified chain from the lower
endpoint bridge dart to the first lower frontier dart.  Consequently
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierAnchorTurnChain}\) names only the remaining lower leg from
the first lower frontier dart to the upper ray-exit anchor, and
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtBridgeFrontierTurnChain\_of\_frontierAnchorTurnChain}\) recovers
the full lower turn-chain input from that smaller assumption.  The wrapper
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictBridgeFrontierLtReducedTurnChainStep}\) packages the resulting
full non-strip input with only the lower side reduced: the lower component is the smaller
frontier-anchor assumption, while the upper-exits-first component remains the existing
turn-chain input.  The corresponding route and contour-count wrappers simply recover the old
turn-chain input before reusing the previous Peierls count route.  The further split input
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierAnchorSplitTurnChain}\) factors the remaining lower
frontier-anchor leg through the ray-exit anchor of the first lower frontier site, packaged by
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierSite}\).  Its recovery theorem and the
\(\texttt{LtAnchorSplit}\) route/count wrappers compose the two split legs and then reuse the
lower-reduced route.  The next site-anchor input
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierSiteAnchorTurnChain}\) removes the first of those two
split legs from the local turn-chain assumptions: the shape lemma
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierDart\_left\_frontierSite}\) identifies the frontier
dart's left site with the packaged first lower frontier site, so the existing anchoring input
\(\texttt{hanchor}\) gives a \(\texttt{DartReachable}\) step to that site's ray-exit anchor.  The
\(\texttt{LtSiteAnchor}\) route/count wrappers therefore leave only the frontier-site anchor to
upper anchor turn chain as lower local input.  The upper-prefix site
\(\texttt{rayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierUpperSite}\) is the point on the upper ray at the same
frontier index.  It lies before the upper first exit, and
\(\texttt{rayExitAnchorDartMap\_ltFrontierUpperSite\_eq}\) identifies its ray-exit anchor with
the original upper site's anchor by ray-prefix stability.  Thus
\(\texttt{RayExitVerticalStrictLtFrontierUpperSiteAnchorTurnChain}\) and the
\(\texttt{LtUpperSiteAnchor}\) route/count wrappers split the remaining lower local input through
this upper-prefix site.  The next reachable split weakens that final lower leg to
\(\texttt{DartReachable}\), which is the form consumed by the edge-connected route.  If the
frontier site and upper-prefix site have equal ray-exit indices, the existing equal-index vertical
straight-step certificate proves the upward anchor pair is a local straight turn, and the
shared-vertex lemma closes the reachable leg; the strict-reachable input only covers the
unequal-index subcase for those two intermediate sites.  The ordered split then separates that
remaining strict subcase according to which intermediate site's ray-exit index is smaller, exposing
two local-order obligations for later geometry.  The residual-order refinement then uses prefix
stability on the upper ray to rewrite the upper-prefix site's local first-exit index as the
remaining upper ray length after the first lower frontier index.  The residual-gap refinement then
removes the adjacent residual comparisons: in the lower-first residual case it composes the lower
frontier anchor to the lower bridge dart with the adjacent lower-first bridge-to-upper-anchor
shared-vertex step, and in the upper-first residual case it composes the adjacent lower-anchor to
upper-first-bridge step with the reverse of the upper anchor to upper-first bridge step.  Thus the
remaining residual input starts only at genuine residual gaps.  The residual-non-strip refinement
then removes the straight residual strip cases by reusing the existing finite lower-first and
upper-first strip-chain lemmas for the local frontier-site/upper-prefix-site pair.  The remaining
lower input starts only at non-strip residual gaps.  The residual-bridge refinement then moves that
remaining local residual input from the two endpoint anchors to the corresponding local bridge leg:
the lower-first case uses the automatic lower anchor-to-bridge shared-vertex step, while the
upper-first case uses the reverse of the automatic upper anchor-to-bridge step.  This is still an
interface reduction.  The residual-frontier refinement then splits that local residual bridge leg
through the first residual re-entry frontier dart of the local frontier-site/upper-prefix-site
pair: the lower-first residual bridge-to-frontier leg is the concrete turn-chain certificate
already proved for lower non-strip gaps, while the post-frontier lower leg and both upper-first
frontier legs remain explicit inputs.  The residual-site-anchor refinement then uses the existing
anchoring input to consume the residual lower frontier-dart-to-frontier-site-anchor leg, so the
remaining lower residual input starts at the ray-exit anchor of that residual frontier site.  It
then introduces the residual upper-prefix site for this local residual pair and uses ray-prefix
stability on the residual upper ray to identify that target anchor with the original residual
upper anchor.  The next strict refinement discharges the equal-index residual
frontier-site/upper-prefix-site subcase by the existing shared-vertex lemma, leaving only the
unequal-index strict subcase explicit.  The following ordered refinement splits that strict
residual upper-prefix-site input into local residual ray-exit index increasing and decreasing
subcases.  The next residual-index ordered refinement rewrites the local residual upper-prefix
site index as the residual upper ray length for the local residual pair.  The following
residual-gap refinement discharges adjacent local residual-index comparisons by the existing
lower-first and upper-first vertical bridge shared-vertex lemmas.  The residual non-strip
refinement then discharges straight local residual strips by reusing the existing finite
strip-chain lemmas on the local residual pair.  The residual-bridge refinement moves the
remaining local residual upper-prefix-site residual input to bridge data for the local
residual pair, using automatic endpoint anchor-to-bridge steps in the lower-first and
upper-first subcases.  The residual-frontier refinement then splits the lower local
residual bridge leg through the first local residual re-entry frontier dart, using the
already proved lower bridge-to-frontier turn-chain certificate while leaving the
post-frontier lower local residual leg and the upper-first residual frontier legs explicit.
The residual-site refinement then uses the existing anchoring input to consume the lower
local residual frontier-dart-to-frontier-site-anchor leg, so the remaining lower local
residual input starts at the ray-exit anchor of the local residual frontier site.
The residual-frontier-upper refinement then introduces the local residual upper-prefix
site for this remaining local residual pair and uses ray-prefix stability to identify
its anchor with the original local residual upper anchor.
The residual-frontier-upper strict refinement then discharges the equal-index local
residual frontier-upper subcase by the existing shared-vertex lemma, leaving only the

The residual-frontier-upper ordered refinement then splits that remaining unequal-index

The residual-index frontier-upper refinement then rewrites the local residual

The residual-gap frontier-upper refinement then discharges adjacent local

The residual non-strip frontier-upper refinement then discharges straight local

The residual bridge frontier-upper refinement then moves the remaining local

The residual frontier split for the frontier-upper stage then routes the remaining

The residual frontier-site split for the frontier-upper stage then consumes the

The residual upper-prefix-site split for the frontier-upper stage then introduces

The residual non-strip ordered residual upper-prefix-site split for the

The residual bridge ordered residual upper-prefix-site split for the

The residual frontier ordered residual upper-prefix-site split for the

The residual frontier-site ordered residual upper-prefix-site split for the

The residual upper-prefix-site ordered residual upper-prefix-site split for the

\subsection*{The ray-exit anchored route
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitAnchoredRoute.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} This file specializes the abstract anchored reachability route to the
concrete ray-exit anchor map $\texttt{rayExitAnchorDartMap}\,F$.  The wrappers
$\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_rayExitAnchored}$,
$\texttt{dartDualCut\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_rayExitAnchored}$,
$\texttt{dualCutSub\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_rayExitAnchored}$, and
$\texttt{dualCutInBox\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_rayExitAnchored}$ carry the specialization through the
ambient, subtype, and common-box dual cuts.  The contour-count wrapper
$\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_anchored}$ fixes each droplet's anchor map to
$\texttt{rayExitAnchorDartMap}$ while keeping the remaining inputs explicit: every boundary dart
must reach the ray-exit anchor of its left site, adjacent sites of $F$ must have reachable ray-exit
anchors, and ordinary within-$F$ connectivity chains those local steps.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The ray-exit shadow route
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitShadowRoute.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} This file narrows the per-edge input of the ray-exit anchored route.
Instead of asking directly for $\texttt{DartReachable}$ between the anchors of adjacent sites, it
asks for a shared dual vertex of the two ray-exit anchor edges.  The lemma
$\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_rayExitShadow}$ turns that shadow into pairwise dart reachability using
$\texttt{dartReachable\_of\_shared}$; the corresponding ambient, subtype, and common-box wrappers
are $\texttt{dartDualCut\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_rayExitShadow}$,
$\texttt{dualCutSub\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_rayExitShadow}$, and
$\texttt{dualCutInBox\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_rayExitShadow}$.  The contour-count wrapper
$\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_rayExit\_shadow}$ keeps $\texttt{hanchor}$,
$\texttt{hshadow}$, and ordinary within-$F$ connectivity explicit.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The ray first-exit distance is bounded by the cut size
  (\texttt{Peierls/RayExitBound.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The $+e_0$-ray first-exit distance $k$ satisfies $k <
|\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F|$, \emph{without} contour connectivity
($\texttt{firstExit\_lt\_dartDualCut\_card}$).  At the first exit all $\texttt{ray0}\,i\,0, \dots,
\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k$ lie in $F$ ($\texttt{exists\_first\_exit\_below}$); from each $\texttt{ray0}\,i
\,t$ a $+e_1$ ray exits $F$ ($\texttt{exists\_first\_exit\_ray1}$), giving a boundary dart
($\texttt{exists\_e1\_exit\_dart}$, $\texttt{tail} = q$) with tail $x$-coordinate $i_0 + t$.  These
$k+1$ darts are distinct (different tail $x$-coordinate), so $k+1 \le |\texttt{BoundaryDart}\,F| =
|\texttt{dartDualCut}\,F|$.  This bounds the Peierls ray anchors to the fixed sequence $z_0, \dots,
z_r$, making the contour count \emph{volume-independent}.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The bounded ray anchor (\texttt{Peierls/RayAnchorBound.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Combining the ray anchor
($\texttt{exists\_ray\_anchor\_dualCutInBox}$) with the first-exit distance bound
($\texttt{firstExit\_lt\_dartDualCut\_card}$) at a \emph{single} first-exit index $k$, a finite box
droplet $F \ni i$ has an anchor $\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k$ on its common-box dual cut with $k <
|\texttt{dualCutInBox}|$ (using $|\texttt{dualCutInBox}| = |\texttt{dartDualCut}|$)
($\texttt{exists\_ray\_anchor\_lt\_card}$).  This is the input to the contour count's anchor-cover,
pinning each droplet to one of the $r$ fixed ray anchors $z_0, \dots, z_{r-1}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The ray anchor set (\texttt{Peierls/RayAnchorSet.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The fixed set $\texttt{rayAnchorSet}\,\Lambda_d\,i\,r$ of dual-box
vertices equal to $\texttt{ray0}\,i\,k$ for some $k < r$.  It has at most $r$ elements
($\texttt{rayAnchorSet\_card\_le}$, its image under $\texttt{Subtype.val}$ lies in
$(\texttt{range}\,r).\texttt{image}\,(\texttt{ray0}\,i)$), and every box droplet $F \ni i$ with
$|\texttt{dualCutInBox}| = r$ has an anchor in it ($\texttt{rayAnchorSet\_cover}$, from
$\texttt{exists\_ray\_anchor\_lt\_card}$).  This supplies the anchor set $Z$, the cover, and
$|Z| \le r$ of $\texttt{contour\_count\_le}$, yielding $r \cdot 16^r$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The Peierls contour count (\texttt{Peierls/PeierlsContourCount.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Assembling all the supply lemmas, the number of neighbour-closed,
ground-avoiding, \emph{single-orbit} box droplets $S \ni i$ with box edge cut of size $r$ is at most
$r \cdot (2\cdot 2)^{2r} \le 32^r$, volume-independently ($\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count}$).  The
dual cut function $\texttt{cut}\,S = \texttt{dualCutInBox}$ (via $\texttt{dif}$) is injective
($\texttt{box\_droplet\_eq\_of\_dualCutInBox\_eq}$), edge-connected
($\texttt{dualCutInBox\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_single\_orbit}$, from $\texttt{hone}$), of size $r$
($\texttt{dualCutInBox\_card\_eq\_cutEdges}$), and anchored in $\texttt{rayAnchorSet}$
($\texttt{rayAnchorSet\_cover}$); feeding these to $\texttt{contour\_count\_le}$ and
$\texttt{rayAnchorSet\_card\_le}$ bounds the count.  The variant
$\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_anchored}$ replaces the single-orbit connectivity supply by
per-droplet anchored $\texttt{DartReachable}$ data and
$\texttt{dualCutInBox\_isEdgeConnected\_of\_anchored}$, giving the count-consumer form for the direct
edge-connectedness route.  The single-orbit (discrete Jordan) input enters only through the
connectivity supply.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The contour count as a power bound (\texttt{Peierls/PeierlsContourCountPow.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Absorbing the polynomial factor $\ell \le 2^\ell$ into $\ell \cdot
16^\ell \le 32^\ell$, the number of size-$\ell$ droplets is at most $(32 : \mathbb{R})^\ell$ (given
$\texttt{hone}$, $\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_pow}$).  This is exactly the
$\texttt{hcount} : \forall \ell,\ \#\{C : g\,C = \ell\} \le M^\ell$ hypothesis (with $M = 32$) of the
geometric tail estimate $\texttt{sum\_pow\_le\_geometric\_tail\_of\_count}$, the bridge from the
contour count to the low-temperature sum $\sum_r 32^r e^{-2\beta J r} \to 0$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The Peierls low-temperature droplet sum (\texttt{Peierls/PeierlsSum.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Feeding the $32^\ell$ contour count
($\texttt{peierls\_contour\_count\_pow}$) into the geometric tail estimate
$\texttt{sum\_pow\_le\_geometric\_tail\_of\_count}$, the droplet sum $\sum_S e^{-2\beta J\,
|\mathrm{cut}\,S|}$ is at most $(32 q)^n / (1 - 32 q)$ with $q = e^{-2\beta J}$, whenever $32 q < 1$
(low temperature) and $n$ lower-bounds the cut sizes ($e^{-2\beta J r} = (e^{-2\beta J})^r$ via
$\texttt{Real.exp\_nat\_mul}$, $\texttt{peierls\_sum\_le}$).  As $\beta \to \infty$ this tail
vanishes ($n \ge 1$), giving $m^*(\beta) > 0$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The finite-volume Peierls bound on the down-spin probability
  (\texttt{Peierls/PeierlsPlusGibbs.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Combining the filled-connected Peierls bound
($\texttt{spontaneous\_magnetization\_plus\_filled\_connected}$) with the geometric tail estimate
$\texttt{peierls\_sum\_le}$, the $+$-state probability that $\sigma_i = -1$ is at most
$32 q / (1 - 32 q)$ ($q = e^{-2\beta J}$, low temperature $32 q < 1$,
$\texttt{peierls\_plusGibbs\_le}$), provided every filled connected droplet is neighbour-closed
($\texttt{hne}$), has dual support in $\Lambda_d$ ($\texttt{hdual}$), and is a single boundary-dart
orbit ($\texttt{hone}$).  The cut-size lower bound $n = 1$ comes from
$\texttt{cutEdges\_nonempty\_of\_connected}$ (a droplet $S \ni i$, $g \notin S$ is a proper nonempty
subset of a preconnected graph).  As $\beta \to \infty$ this vanishes --- the finite-volume input to
$m^*(\beta) > 0$.  The single-orbit (discrete Jordan) input enters only through $\texttt{hone}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The down-spin probability vanishes at low temperature
  (\texttt{Peierls/PeierlsTendsto.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The $+$-expectation of a nonnegative observable is $\ge 0$
($\texttt{plusGibbsExpectation\_nonneg}$, from $(Z^+)^{-1} \ge 0$ and $\texttt{boltzmannWeight} > 0$).
Hence for a fixed box $\Lambda$ (with the neighbour-closed / dual-support / single-orbit droplet
hypotheses), $\mu^+_\Lambda(\sigma_i = -1) \to 0$ as $\beta \to \infty$
($\texttt{peierls\_plusGibbs\_tendsto\_zero}$), by squeezing the finite-volume Peierls bound
$\texttt{peierls\_plusGibbs\_le}$ between $0$ and the vanishing geometric tail
$\texttt{peierls\_low\_temp\_tail\_tendsto\_zero}$ (with $C = 32$).  The analytic core of
$m^*(\beta) > 0$; the single-orbit input enters only through $\texttt{hone}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Magnetization versus down-spin probability (\texttt{Peierls/PlusGibbsSign.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The $+$-expectation of the constant $1$ is $1$
($\texttt{plusGibbsExpectation\_one}$, normalization $(Z^+)^{-1} Z^+ = 1$).  Since $\texttt{Spin.sign}
\,\mathbb{R}\,(\sigma_i) = 1 - 2\,[\sigma_i = -1]$ pointwise ($+1$ up, $-1$ down), by linearity
$\mu^+(\sigma_i) = 1 - 2\,\mu^+(\sigma_i = -1)$ ($\texttt{plusGibbsExpectation\_sign\_eq}$).  This
converts the Peierls down-spin bound into a lower bound on the magnetization ($1 - \mu^+(\sigma_i) =
2\,\mu^+(\sigma_i = -1)$), the link from $\texttt{PeierlsInfinite}$'s liminf structure to
$m^*(\beta) > 0$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Monotonicity of the $+$-Gibbs expectation (\texttt{Peierls/PlusGibbsMono.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} $F_1 \le F_2$ pointwise implies $\mu^+(F_1) \le \mu^+(F_2)$
($\texttt{plusGibbsExpectation\_mono}$; positive weights and partition function).  In particular
$\mu^+(\sigma_i) \le 1$ ($\texttt{plusGibbsExpectation\_sign\_le\_one}$, since $\texttt{Spin.sign}
\,\mathbb{R}\,(\sigma_i) \le 1$ pointwise and $\mu^+(1) = 1$).  This upper bound supplies the
coboundedness needed to push the per-stage Peierls bound to the infinite-volume liminf.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Pushing a pointwise bound through the liminf (\texttt{Peierls/LiminfBound.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} If $1 - a_n \le M$ and $a_n \le 1$ for all $n$, then $1 - \liminf a \le
M$ ($\texttt{one\_sub\_liminf\_le}$): the lower bound $1 - M \le a_n$ lifts to $1 - M \le \liminf a$
via $\texttt{Filter.le\_liminf\_of\_le}$, with $a_n \le 1$ supplying the coboundedness
$\texttt{isCoboundedUnder\_ge\_of\_eventually\_le}$.  The abstract step taking the per-stage Peierls
bound to the infinite-volume liminf.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The infinite-volume Peierls magnetization bound (\texttt{Peierls/PeierlsLiminf.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Under per-stage neighbour-closure, dual-support, and \emph{single-orbit}
($\texttt{hone}$) hypotheses for the boxes $\Lambda.\texttt{volume}\,n$ of an exhaustion, the genuine
$+$-state magnetization $\texttt{plusGibbsExpectationLiminf}(\sigma_i)$ satisfies $1 -
\mu^+(\sigma_i) \le 2\cdot 32 q / (1 - 32 q)$ ($\texttt{peierls\_plusGibbsLiminf\_le}$).  Each stage
gives $1 - \mu^+_n(\sigma_i) = 2\mu^+_n(\downarrow) \le 64 q/(1-32q)$ ($\texttt{peierls\_plusGibbs\_le}$
and $\texttt{plusGibbsExpectation\_sign\_eq}$) and $\mu^+_n(\sigma_i) \le 1$; $\texttt{one\_sub\_%
liminf\_le}$ pushes this to the liminf.  This \emph{replaces the volume-dependent count of}
$\texttt{prop\_5\_4\_2\_plusGibbsExpectationLiminf\_bound}$ \emph{with the volume-independent contour
count}.  As $\beta \to \infty$ the bound vanishes, so $\mu^+(\sigma_i) \to 1$ --- the spontaneous
magnetization is positive, $m^*(\beta) > 0$, the Peierls phase transition.  The single-orbit
(discrete Jordan) input enters only through the per-stage $\texttt{hone}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Positivity of the spontaneous magnetization
  (\texttt{Peierls/PeierlsMagnetizationPos.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} When the low-temperature tail $2\cdot 32 q / (1 - 32 q) < 1$ (large
$\beta$), the infinite-volume bound $1 - \mu^+(\sigma_i) \le 2\cdot 32 q / (1 - 32 q)$
($\texttt{peierls\_plusGibbsLiminf\_le}$) forces $0 < \mu^+(\sigma_i)$
($\texttt{peierls\_plusGibbsLiminf\_pos}$).  This is the \emph{Peierls phase transition}: spontaneous
magnetization $m^*(\beta) > 0$ at low temperature ($\beta_c < \infty$), modulo the per-stage
single-orbit input $\texttt{hone}$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{Counting by anchor cover (\texttt{Peierls/ContourCountCover.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} The combinatorial core of the contour count.  If every element of a
finite family $D$ satisfies $P\,a\,z$ for \emph{some} anchor $z \in Z$, and each anchor class
$\{a \in D \mid P\,a\,z\}$ has at most $M$ elements, then $|D| \le |Z| \cdot M$
($\texttt{card\_le\_of\_anchor\_cover}$, via $\texttt{Finset.biUnion}$ cover, $\texttt{card\_%
biUnion\_le}$, and the constant sum).  With the $r$ ray anchors $z_0, \dots, z_{r-1}$ (first-exit
bound $k < r$) and per-anchor count $M = 16^r$, this gives the volume-independent contour bound
$r \cdot 16^r \le 32^r$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The contour count assembly (\texttt{Peierls/ContourCountAssembly.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} Combining the per-anchor count
$\texttt{card\_droplets\_le\_of\_cut\_connected}$ ($\le (2d)^{2r}$ per fixed anchor) with the
anchor-cover principle $\texttt{card\_le\_of\_anchor\_cover}$ (over the $r$ ray anchors $Z$), over any droplet type, a
droplet family $D$ mapping injectively to connected size-$r$ edge cuts (each through some anchor in
$Z$) has $|D| \le |Z| \cdot (2\cdot 2)^{2r}$ ($\texttt{contour\_count\_le}$).  The geometric inputs
(injectivity, connectivity, per-anchor membership, anchor set $Z$) are isolated as hypotheses; the
single-orbit Jordan input enters only via $\texttt{IsEdgeConnected}\,(\texttt{cut}\,S)$.  With
$|Z| = r$ this is the volume-independent bound $r \cdot 16^r \le 32^r$.
Reference: Friedli--Velenik (Cambridge, 2017), \S3.7.2, (3.49), pp. 109--116.

\subsection*{The cut determines the region (\texttt{Peierls/CutDeterminesRegion.lean})}

\par\noindent\textbf{Role:} In a preconnected graph, a vertex set $F$ avoiding a fixed ground
vertex $g$ is completely determined by its edge cut.  Reading a walk $w:g\to v$, the winding
parity gives $v\in F \iff \mathrm{Odd}(\texttt{cutCrossings}\,G\,F\,w)$
