proved by expanding the doubled integrand into four product pieces and separating
each via \texttt{integral\_prod\_mul}. Hence if the doubled integral is
non-negative then $\langle F\rangle\langle G\rangle\le\langle FG\rangle$
(\texttt{vectorExpectation\_mul\_le\_of\_doubled\_nonneg}), the truncated-pair
positivity of (4.7.6)--(4.7.7). The doubled-integral non-negativity is supplied,
via the duplicate-variable rotation, by the doubled-rotated cone. Reference:
Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S4.7, Theorem 4.7.1, pp.~70--71.

\paragraph{The \S4.7 block $\sqrt2$-rotation (4.3.2) is measure-preserving.} The
\S4.7 duplicate-variable rotation is the \emph{block} $\sqrt2$-rotation given by
the formulas (4.3.2) applied to the pair $(t,q)$ and its duplicate $(t',q')$:
$\alpha=(t+t')/\sqrt2$, $\beta=(t-t')/\sqrt2$, $\gamma=(q+q')/\sqrt2$,
$\delta=(q'-q)/\sqrt2$, mixing the two copies coordinate by coordinate (the
$t$-pair into $(\alpha,\beta)$, the $q$-pair into $(\gamma,\delta)$). This is the
rotation for which the doubled field is $\sqrt2\,(h^1\alpha+h^2\gamma)$ --- so the
doubled field constants $\sqrt2\beta h^1,\sqrt2\beta h^2\ge0$ for $\beta,h^1,h^2\ge0$
--- and for which the difference observables expand with non-negative coefficients,
as the duplicate-variable proof of (4.7.6)--(4.7.8) requires. (It is \emph{not} the
Hadamard rotation $\texttt{phi4Alpha},\dots$ of \S4.3 used in
\texttt{twoCompPotential\_double\_eq}, which mixes all four coordinates and realises
the scalar $\varphi^4$ doubled potential.) All entries of \texttt{rotMatrix} are
$0$ or $\pm\sqrt2/2$ (\texttt{sqrt2\_half\_mul\_self}: $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot
\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=\tfrac12$), with orthonormal rows, so $M M^{\mathsf T}=1$
(\texttt{rotMatrix\_mul\_transpose}), $\det^2=1$, $|\det|=1$. Through
\texttt{LinearMap.det\_toLin'} and
\texttt{Measure.map\_linearMap\_addHaar\_eq\_smul\_addHaar} ($|\det^{-1}|=1$), the
linear map $\texttt{rotLin}=\texttt{Matrix.toLin'}\,\texttt{rotMatrix}$ is
measure-preserving (\texttt{measurePreserving\_rotLin}); applied site-wise via
\texttt{volume\_preserving\_pi} on $(\iota\to\mathrm{Fin}\,4\to\mathbb{R})$
(\texttt{measurePreserving\_rotLinPi}). This is the linchpin connecting the doubled
Gibbs integral to the doubled-rotated cone. Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed.,
\S4.3, (4.3.2), p.~59; \S4.7, pp.~70--71.

\paragraph{Rotation algebra (4.3.5) and the doubled potential.} The block
coordinates $\texttt{bAlpha}\,t\,t'=(t+t')/\sqrt2$, $\texttt{bBeta}\,t\,t'=(t-t')/
\sqrt2$, $\texttt{bGamma}\,q\,q'=(q+q')/\sqrt2$, $\texttt{bDelta}\,q\,q'=(q'-q)/
\sqrt2$; the single-site coordinate vector $\texttt{dCoord}\,\xi\,\xi'\,i=
![t_i,q_i,t_i',q_i']$, rotated by \texttt{rotLin}, yields
$(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)=(\texttt{bAlpha},\texttt{bBeta},\texttt{bGamma},
\texttt{bDelta})$ (\texttt{rotLin\_dCoord}). The doubled-interaction identity (4.3.5)
$t_it_j+q_iq_j+t_i't_j'+q_i'q_j'=\alpha_i\alpha_j+\beta_i\beta_j+\gamma_i\gamma_j
+\delta_i\delta_j$ (\texttt{doubled\_dot\_eq\_rot}, via \texttt{linear\_combination}
on $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=\tfrac12$) shows the doubled
ferromagnetic interaction stays ferromagnetic in the rotated coordinates. The
doubled-potential identity $P(t,q)+P(t',q')=\texttt{twoCompEvenPart}\,
\alpha\,\beta\,\gamma\,\delta-4A\,\alpha\beta\gamma\delta$
(\texttt{twoCompPotential\_double\_block}, the block analogue of
\texttt{twoCompPotential\_double\_eq} with the \emph{same} even part
\texttt{twoCompEvenPart} matching \texttt{rotSiteDensity}) shows the doubled
potential is even plus ferromagnetic. Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed.,
\S4.3, (4.3.2), (4.3.5); \S4.7, pp.~70--71.

\paragraph{The doubled Gibbs weight factorises through the block rotation.}
Writing $\mathrm{cfg}\,i=\texttt{rotLin}(\texttt{dCoord}\,\xi\,\xi'\,i)$ for the
block rotation of the doubled configuration $(\xi,\xi')$, the product of the two
single-copy Gibbs weights is the doubled-rotated weight
\[
  W(\xi)\,W(\xi')=\exp\!\Big(\beta J\textstyle\sum_e \texttt{edgeDot4}\,\mathrm{cfg}\,e\Big)
    \cdot\prod_i \texttt{siteWeight4}\,A\,\sigma\,(\sqrt2\beta h^1)\,(\sqrt2\beta h^2)\,(\mathrm{cfg}\,i)
\]
(\texttt{vectorWeight\_mul\_eq\_rot}). This combines the per-edge interaction
identity $\sum_e(\xi\cdot\xi+\xi'\cdot\xi')=\sum_e\texttt{edgeDot4}\,\mathrm{cfg}$
(\texttt{doubled\_vEdgeDot\_eq\_edgeDot4}, the $\mathrm{Sym2}$-lift of (4.3.5)), the
field identity $\beta h^1(t_i+t_i')+\beta h^2(q_i+q_i')=\sqrt2\beta h^1\alpha_i
+\sqrt2\beta h^2\gamma_i$ (\texttt{sqrt2\_mul\_sqrt2\_half}: $\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2/2=1$),
and the potential identity \texttt{twoCompPotential\_double\_block}, assembled per
site by \texttt{doubled\_site\_exponent} and combined through \texttt{Real.exp\_add}
/ \texttt{Real.exp\_sum}. The doubled field constants $\sqrt2\beta h^1,\sqrt2\beta
h^2\ge0$ are exactly the non-negative field hypotheses of
\texttt{dRotInteraction\_nonneg}. This is the weight side of the duplicate-variable
change of variables for (4.7.6)--(4.7.8). Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S4.7,
Theorem 4.7.1, pp.~70--71.

\paragraph{The duplicate-variable change of variables and the doubled-integral
engine.} The combined map $(\xi,\xi')\mapsto(i\mapsto\texttt{rotLin}(\texttt{dCoord}
\,\xi\,\xi'\,i))$, sending the doubled configuration to its block-rotated form, is
packaged as a measurable equivalence $\texttt{combinedEquiv}:(\texttt{VectorConfig}
\,\iota\times\texttt{VectorConfig}\,\iota)\simeq_{\mathrm m}(\iota\to\mathrm{Fin}\,4
\to\mathbb{R})$ and is measure-preserving (\texttt{measurePreserving\_combinedEquiv}).
It is assembled from the per-site reshuffle $\texttt{siteEquiv}$
(via \texttt{finTwoArrow}, \texttt{sumPiEquivProdPi}, \texttt{piCongrLeft}\,\texttt{finSumFinEquiv},
with underlying function $\texttt{siteEquiv}\,((t,q),(t',q'))=![t,q,t',q']$), the per-site
rotation \texttt{rotEquiv} (\texttt{rotLin} packaged as a \texttt{MeasurableEquiv} via
\texttt{Matrix.toLinearEquiv'}, with underlying function \texttt{rotLin}),
\texttt{arrowProdEquivProdArrow}, and \texttt{volume\_preserving\_pi}.
The capstone \texttt{doubled\_integral\_nonneg}: if
$(F(\xi)-F(\xi'))\,(G(\xi)-G(\xi')) = \texttt{dSpinEval}\,\mathrm{obs}\,(\texttt{rotLin}
\circ\texttt{dCoord})$ for a non-negative-coefficient $\mathrm{obs}$, then
\[
  0 \le \int\!\!\int (F(\xi)-F(\xi'))\,(G(\xi)-G(\xi'))\,W(\xi)\,W(\xi'),
\]
proved by the change of variables
(\texttt{measurePreserving\_combinedEquiv.integral\_comp'}), the weight factorization
(\texttt{vectorWeight\_mul\_eq\_rot}), and the doubled-rotated cone non-negativity
(\texttt{dRotInteraction\_nonneg}). This is the engine of the second/third
inequalities; combined with the GKS-II doubling consequence it yields the headlines
(4.7.6)--(4.7.8) once the difference-observable non-negative-coefficient expansion is
supplied. Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S4.7, Theorem 4.7.1, pp.~70--71.

\paragraph{The second/third inequalities (4.7.6)--(4.7.8) and Corollary 4.7.2.} In the
block rotation the single-copy spins are recovered by $t_i=(\alpha_i+\beta_i)/\sqrt2$,
$t_i'=(\alpha_i-\beta_i)/\sqrt2$, $q_i=(\gamma_i-\delta_i)/\sqrt2$,
$q_i'=(\gamma_i+\delta_i)/\sqrt2$ (\texttt{vSpinT\_eq\_rot}, \dots). Hence the difference
of a $t$- (resp.\ $q$-) monomial across the duplicate is $(\sqrt2/2)^{|A|}$ times the
difference $\texttt{plusProd}-\texttt{minusProd}$ of the $\pm$ products of the rotated
coordinates on slots $0,1$ (resp.\ $2,3$) (\texttt{tMon\_diff}, \texttt{qMon\_diff}).
The crucial combinatorial fact is that $\texttt{plusProd}-\texttt{minusProd}=
\prod_i(X_{i,s}+X_{i,t})-\prod_i(X_{i,s}-X_{i,t})$ has \emph{non-negative coefficients}
--- proved by mutual induction with the even sum
(\texttt{nncoeffs\_evenSum\_oddDiff}), since
$\prod(a+b)-\prod(a-b)=2\sum_{|S|\text{ odd}}\prod_{S}b\prod_{A\setminus S}a$. Therefore
the product of two such differences is $\texttt{dSpinEval}$ of a
non-negative-coefficient polynomial, and \texttt{doubled\_integral\_nonneg} gives the
doubled-integral positivity. Combined with the GKS-II doubling consequence
\texttt{vectorExpectation\_mul\_le\_of\_doubled\_nonneg} this yields
\[
  \langle t^A\rangle\langle t^B\rangle\le\langle t^A t^B\rangle\ (4.7.6),\quad
  \langle q^A\rangle\langle q^B\rangle\le\langle q^A q^B\rangle\ (4.7.7),\quad
  \langle t^A q^B\rangle\le\langle t^A\rangle\langle q^B\rangle\ (4.7.8),
\]
(\texttt{vectorExpectation\_t\_mul\_le}, \texttt{\_q\_mul\_le}, \texttt{\_t\_mul\_q\_le};
the last via the $-q^B$ reflection and \texttt{vectorExpectation\_neg}). Integrability of
the monomials against the Gibbs weight is supplied through the \texttt{genMonomial} bridge.
The pairwise specializations $A=\{i\}$, $B=\{j\}$ give Corollary 4.7.2
(\texttt{vectorExpectation\_\{t,q,t\_q\}\_pair\_le}). This completes Theorem 4.7.1.
Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S4.7, Theorem 4.7.1, Cor 4.7.2, pp.~70--71.

\section{Pure and mixed phases (\texttt{PhaseTransition.lean})}

Formalization of Glimm--Jaffe, \S5.1 (pp.~72--74).

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{truncated2\_le\_one}]
For ferromagnetic parameters: $0 \le \langle\sigma_i;\sigma_j\rangle \le 1$.
The lower bound is GKS-II. The upper bound: $\langle\sigma_i\sigma_j\rangle \le 1$
and $\langle\sigma_i\rangle\langle\sigma_j\rangle \ge 0$ by GKS-I.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{mixed\_phase\_truncated2}; eq.~(5.1.5)]
$M^2 - (M(2\alpha - 1))^2 = 4\alpha(1-\alpha)M^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{mixed\_phase\_pure\_iff}]
For $0 \le \alpha \le 1$ and $M \ne 0$:
$4\alpha(1-\alpha)M^2 = 0$ iff $\alpha = 0$ or $\alpha = 1$.
\end{theorem}

These formalize the algebraic content of \S5.1: the truncated 2-point
function measures the deviation from a pure phase, and
its asymptotic value $4\alpha(1-\alpha)M^2$ vanishes iff the state is pure.

\subsection{Mean field theory (\S5.2)}

The mean field free energy density for the Ising model
(Glimm--Jaffe, \S5.2, eq.~(5.2.3)) is
$\varphi(m) = -\frac{1}{2}Jzm^2 - hm + \beta^{-1}\,\mathrm{entropy}(m)$.

\begin{definition}[\texttt{meanFieldEnergy}]
The interaction part: $-\frac{1}{2}Jzm^2 - hm$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{meanFieldEnergy\_neg}]
At $h = 0$: $\varphi(-m) = \varphi(m)$ (spin-flip symmetry).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{meanField\_zero\_solution}]
$m = 0$ is always a solution of the mean field equation
$m = \tanh(\beta(Jzm + h))$ when $h = 0$, since $\tanh(0) = 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{tanh\_odd}]
$\tanh(-x) = -\tanh(x)$: if $m^*$ solves the mean field equation
at $h = 0$, so does $-m^*$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Symmetry breaking (\S5.3)}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{magnetization}]
The order parameter: $M(i) = \langle\sigma_i\rangle$ (eq.~(5.3.5)).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{susceptibility}]
$\chi(i) = \sum_j \langle\sigma_i;\sigma_j\rangle = \sum_j \texttt{truncated2}(i,j)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{susceptibility\_nonneg}]
$\chi(i) \ge 0$ for ferromagnetic parameters, by \texttt{truncated2\_nonneg}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{magnetization\_zero\_at\_h\_zero}]
$M(i) = 0$ when $h = 0$: the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry is unbroken in finite
volume. Uses \texttt{correlation\_odd\_vanish}.
\end{theorem}

Symmetry breaking occurs only in the infinite volume limit:
$M_+ = \lim_{h \downarrow 0} \langle\sigma_i\rangle_h > 0$ for $\beta > \beta_c$.
The concavity $d^2 M/dh^2 \le 0$ for $h \ge 0$ follows from the GHS inequality
(Cor.~4.3.4), as noted on p.~80 of \cite{glimm-jaffe}.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{$\mathbb{Z}_2$ $h$-symmetry across the tower}{Z2 h-symmetry across the tower}}

The reflection $h \mapsto -h$ combined with the global spin-flip
$\sigma \mapsto -\sigma$ is a symmetry of the Ising Hamiltonian. The
statements in this subsubsection are derived from this symmetry in
combination with the basic \texttt{correlation} / \texttt{magnetization}
/ \texttt{susceptibility} definitions; the citation to
Glimm--Jaffe~\S5.3, pp.~77--80 (2nd ed., Springer, 1987) is at the
section level, as background for the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ $h$-symmetry
framework, rather than as a source of each individual closed form.
On correlations, the framework yields the capstone identity:
\begin{theorem}[\texttt{correlation\_neg\_h}, PR~\#754]
$\langle \sigma^A \rangle_{(J,-h,\beta)}
 = (-1)^{|A|}\,\langle \sigma^A \rangle_{(J,h,\beta)}$.
\end{theorem}
\noindent The proof uses the flip reindexing of numerator and denominator:
\texttt{hamiltonian\_neg\_h} gives $H_{(J,-h,\beta)}(\sigma)
= H_{(J,h,\beta)}(\sigma.\mathrm{flip})$, \texttt{spinProduct\_flip}
gives $\prod_{i\in A}\sigma.\mathrm{flip}(i) = (-1)^{|A|}\prod_{i\in A}\sigma(i)$,
and \texttt{partitionFunction\_neg\_h} shows $Z(-h) = Z(h)$.

Specializations:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{magnetization\_neg\_h}: $M(-h) = -M(h)$ ($|A|=1$).
\item \texttt{truncated\{2,3,4\}\_neg\_h} (PRs~\#755--\#758): the Ursell
      coefficients inherit the parity of their total degree. E.g.\
      \texttt{truncated2\_neg\_h} gives $\langle\sigma_i;\sigma_j\rangle(-h)
      = \langle\sigma_i;\sigma_j\rangle(h)$ for $i\neq j$ (even total).
\item \texttt{correlation\_eq\_abs\_h\_of\_even\_card} (PR~\#760): for
      $|A|$ even, $\langle\sigma^A\rangle_{|h|} = \langle\sigma^A\rangle_{h}$.
\end{itemize}
The Ambient $\Lambda$-layer, along-exhaustion, and infinite-volume
counterparts (even $|A|$ in the $\infty$-volume case, since
$\sup(-f) \ne -\sup(f)$ for odd $|A|$) appear in PRs~\#762--\#766.

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{susceptibility\_neg\_h}, PR~\#767]
$\chi(\langle J,-h,\beta\rangle; i) = \chi(\langle J,h,\beta\rangle; i)
 - 2\,M(\langle J,h,\beta\rangle; i)$.
\end{theorem}
\noindent The off-diagonal sum $\sum_{j\neq i}\texttt{truncated2}(i,j)$ is
invariant by \texttt{truncated2\_neg\_h}; the diagonal term, via the
Finset collapse $\{i,i\}=\{i\}$, contributes $\texttt{truncated2}(-h,i,i)
- \texttt{truncated2}(h,i,i) = -2\,M(h)$ by the $|A|=1$ case of
\texttt{correlation\_neg\_h}.

Under ferromagnetism ($0\le J$, $0<\beta$), the magnetization at $|h|$
coincides with the absolute value:
\begin{theorem}[\texttt{abs\_magnetization\_eq\_magnetization\_abs\_h}, PR~\#769]
$|M(\langle J,h,\beta\rangle;i)| = M(\langle J,|h|,\beta\rangle;i)$
under $0\le J$, $0<\beta$.
\end{theorem}
\noindent The $\Lambda$-layer counterpart is
\begin{theorem}[\texttt{abs\_magnetization\LeanLambda\_eq\_magnetization\LeanLambda\_abs\_h}, PR~\#772]
$|M_\Lambda(\langle J,h,\beta\rangle;i)| = M_\Lambda(\langle J,|h|,\beta\rangle;i)$
under $0\le J$, $0<\beta$, for any finite volume $\Lambda \subseteq V$ and
any site $i \in \Lambda$. Proved by the same
\texttt{abs\_choice}-based case split, using
\texttt{magnetization\LeanLambda\_nonneg} (ferromagnetic, via GKS-I at
$\Lambda$-level) and \texttt{magnetization\LeanLambda\_neg\_h}.
\end{theorem}
\noindent The along-exhaustion counterpart (pointwise per stage) is
likewise an equality, and it is the bridge to the infinite-volume
statement:
\begin{theorem}[\texttt{abs\_magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_eq\_magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_abs\_h}, PR~\#773]
For every exhaustion stage $n$,
$|M_\text{along}(\langle J,h,\beta\rangle;i,n)|
= M_\text{along}(\langle J,|h|,\beta\rangle;i,n)$
under $0 \le J$, $0 < \beta$. Same case split via
\texttt{abs\_choice}, using
\texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_nonneg} and the new helper
\texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_neg\_h} (specialization of
\texttt{correlationAlongExhaustion\_neg\_h} at $A = \{i\}$).
\end{theorem}

The naive lift to the thermodynamic-limit $M_\infty$ \emph{fails} as an
equality for this project's sup-based definition
$M_\infty := \sup_n M_\text{along}(n)$. The failure mode is the
odd-$|A|$ obstruction already flagged in
\texttt{correlationInfinite\_neg\_h\_of\_even\_card}: at $h < 0$
ferromagnetic, covered stages give $M_\text{along}(n) \le 0$
(via \texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_neg\_h} plus the finite/\(\Lambda\)
ferromagnetic positivity at $|h|$), so the supremum is bounded above
by the contributions of any \emph{missed} stages (where
$M_\text{along}(n) = 0$ by the ``if $A \subseteq \Lambda_n$ then
$\ldots$ else $0$'' convention). Concretely, if there exists
$n$ with $i \notin \Lambda_n$, then $M_\infty(h) = 0$ but
$M_\infty(|h|) > 0$, so the equality fails. Since
\texttt{Exhaustion} does not require such a missed stage, this is an
obstruction/example rather than a universal identity; still, the
equality cannot hold in general under this definition.
Glimm--Jaffe's standard thermodynamic limit
(e.g.\ $\pm$BC or $h \to 0^\pm$) restores the equality; upgrading the
definition is out of scope here.

What does survive is the one-sided inequality, which is the natural
$\infty$-volume odd-$|A|$ result compatible with the sup-based setup:
\begin{theorem}[\texttt{abs\_magnetizationInfinite\_le\_magnetizationInfinite\_abs\_h}, PR~\#773]
$|M_\infty(\langle J,h,\beta\rangle;\,i)|
 \le M_\infty(\langle J,|h|,\beta\rangle;\,i)$
under $0 \le J$, $0 < \beta$. Proved via $\mathtt{abs\_le}$ plus two
$\mathtt{ciSup}$-level pointwise comparisons driven by the along-exhaustion
pointwise equality above.
\end{theorem}

Two further $\infty$-volume sign-control statements pin down the
$h \le 0$ behavior of the sup-based $M_\infty$:
\begin{theorem}[\texttt{magnetizationInfinite\_nonpos\_of\_nonpos\_h}, PR~\#774]
Under $0 \le J$, $0 < \beta$, $h \le 0$, and any exhaustion,
$M_\infty(\langle J, h, \beta\rangle; i) \le 0$.
\end{theorem}
\noindent Proof: rewrite $M_\infty = \sup_n M_\text{along}(n)$; each
covered stage is $\le 0$ by \texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_neg\_h}
plus nonnegativity at $-h$ (ferromagnetic, since $-h \ge 0$), and each
uncovered stage is $0$; close with $\mathtt{ciSup\_le}$.

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{magnetizationInfinite\_eq\_zero\_of\_exists\_stage\_not\_mem}, PR~\#774]
Under $0 \le J$, $0 < \beta$, $h \le 0$, and the extra hypothesis that
some stage misses $i$ (i.e.\ $\exists n_0,\ i \notin \Lambda_{n_0}$),
$M_\infty(\langle J, h, \beta\rangle; i) = 0$.
\end{theorem}
\noindent Proof: the previous theorem gives $M_\infty \le 0$; the
missed stage contributes $M_\text{along}(n_0) = 0 \le M_\infty$ via
\texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_le\_magnetizationInfinite};
close with \texttt{le\_antisymm}.

Further ``$\Lambda$-layer susceptibility'' and
``$\infty$-volume susceptibility'' refinements are tracked in
issue~\#770.

Finally, a closed form for $\chi$ at $|h|$ that does \emph{not} require
ferromagnetism:
\begin{theorem}[\texttt{susceptibility\_eq\_abs\_h}, PR~\#771]
$\chi(\langle J,|h|,\beta\rangle;i)
 = \chi(\langle J,h,\beta\rangle;i)
   + M(\langle J,|h|,\beta\rangle;i) - M(\langle J,h,\beta\rangle;i)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Case $|h| = h$ ($h\ge 0$): $M(|h|) = M(h)$ so the correction vanishes;
both sides equal $\chi(h)$. Case $|h| = -h$ ($h\le 0$): by
\texttt{susceptibility\_neg\_h}, $\chi(-h) = \chi(h) - 2\,M(h)$, and by
\texttt{magnetization\_neg\_h}, $M(-h) = -M(h)$, so the RHS equals
$\chi(h) + (-M(h)) - M(h) = \chi(h) - 2\,M(h)$, matching the LHS.
\end{proof}
\noindent Under ferromagnetism, combining with
\texttt{abs\_magnetization\_eq\_magnetization\_abs\_h} gives the
non-negative closed form
$\chi(|h|) - \chi(h) = |M(h)| - M(h) = 2\max\{0,-M(h)\}$.

\begin{definition}[\texttt{susceptibility\LeanLambda}, PR~\#776]
For $\Lambda \subseteq V$ a finite volume in an infinite ambient $V$ and
$i : \uparrow\Lambda$,
\[
  \chi_\Lambda(G, \Lambda, p; i)
  := \chi\bigl(\mathrm{inducedGraph}\ G\ \Lambda,\ p;\ i\bigr)
  = \sum_{j : \uparrow\Lambda}\mathrm{truncated2}\bigl(\mathrm{inducedGraph}\ G\ \Lambda,\ p;\ i, j\bigr).
\]
This is the $\Lambda$-layer counterpart of \texttt{susceptibility}, matching
the \texttt{magnetization\LeanLambda} / \texttt{correlation\LeanLambda} pattern at the ambient
lattice layer.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{susceptibility\LeanLambda\_eq\_abs\_h}, PR~\#776 (A-4, issue~\#770)]
For all $J, h, \beta \in \mathbb R$ and $i : \uparrow\Lambda$,
\[
  \chi_\Lambda(\langle J, |h|, \beta\rangle; i)
  = \chi_\Lambda(\langle J, h, \beta\rangle; i)
    + M_\Lambda(\langle J, |h|, \beta\rangle; i) - M_\Lambda(\langle J, h, \beta\rangle; i),
\]
unconditionally (no ferromagnetic hypothesis required).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Direct lift of \texttt{susceptibility\_eq\_abs\_h} (PR~\#771) along
$\chi_\Lambda := \chi(\mathrm{inducedGraph}\ G\ \Lambda)$ and
$M_\Lambda = M(\mathrm{inducedGraph}\ G\ \Lambda)$. Bundled helpers
\texttt{susceptibility\LeanLambda\_apply}, \texttt{susceptibility\LeanLambda\_nonneg}
(ferromagnetic), \texttt{susceptibility\LeanLambda\_neg\_h}
($\chi_\Lambda(-h) = \chi_\Lambda(h) - 2 M_\Lambda(h)$), and the
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ wrapper
\texttt{susceptibility\LeanLambda\_latticeGraph\_eq\_abs\_h} are included.
The concrete wrapper now lives in
\texttt{CorrelationSymmetry.lean}.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{susceptibilityAlongExhaustion}, PR~\#777]
For an exhaustion $\Lambda = (\Lambda_n)_{n : \mathbb N}$ of $V$, site $i : V$
and stage $n : \mathbb N$,
\[
  \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(i, n)
  := \begin{cases}
       \chi_{\Lambda_n}(G, \Lambda_n, p;\ \langle i, h_{in}\rangle) & \text{if } i \in \Lambda_n \\
       0 & \text{otherwise.}
     \end{cases}
\]
Along-exhaustion companion of $\chi_\Lambda$, mirroring
\texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion}. Prerequisite for a future
\texttt{susceptibilityInfinite}.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{susceptibilityAlongExhaustion\_eq\_abs\_h},
PR~\#777 (A-4b, issue~\#770)]
For all $J, h, \beta \in \mathbb R$, $i : V$ and $n : \mathbb N$,
\[
  \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(\langle J, |h|, \beta\rangle; i, n)
  = \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(\langle J, h, \beta\rangle; i, n)
    + M_{\mathrm{along}}(\langle J, |h|, \beta\rangle; i, n) - M_{\mathrm{along}}(\langle J, h, \beta\rangle; i, n),
\]
unconditionally (no ferromagnetic hypothesis required).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Case split on $i \in \Lambda_n$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Covered stage}: reduce to
    \texttt{susceptibility\LeanLambda\_eq\_abs\_h} (PR~\#776) at the lifted
    subtype site $\langle i, h_i\rangle$. The magnetization-side
    terms are converted via the helper
    \texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_of\_mem\_eq\_magnetization\LeanLambda},
    which upgrades the \texttt{liftFinset $\{i\}$}-form returned by
    \texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_of\_mem} (itself a singleton
    specialization of \texttt{correlationAlongExhaustion\_of\_subset})
    to the \texttt{magnetization\LeanLambda} form via the auxiliary
    \texttt{liftFinset\_singleton}.
  \item \emph{Uncovered stage}: all four terms are $0$ by the
    \texttt{\_of\_not\_mem} unfoldings, and the identity holds.
\end{itemize}
Bundled helpers: \texttt{susceptibilityAlongExhaustion\_apply},
\texttt{\_of\_mem}, \texttt{\_of\_not\_mem}, \texttt{\_nonneg}
(ferromagnetic), \texttt{\_neg\_h}
($\chi_{\mathrm{along}}(-h) = \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(h) - 2 M_{\mathrm{along}}(h)$),
and the $\mathbb Z^d$ wrapper
\texttt{susceptibilityAlongExhaustion\_latticeGraph\_eq\_abs\_h}. The concrete
wrapper now lives in
\texttt{CorrelationSymmetry.lean}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{susceptibilityAlongExhaustion\_le\_abs\_h},
PR~\#778 (A-4c, issue~\#770)]
For $0 \le J$, $0 < \beta$, any $h \in \mathbb R$, $i : V$ and $n : \mathbb N$,
\[
  \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(\langle J, h, \beta\rangle; i, n)
  \le \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(\langle J, |h|, \beta\rangle; i, n).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Case $|h| = h$ ($h \ge 0$): equality by $h = |h|$. Case $|h| = -h$
($h \le 0$): by PR~\#777's \texttt{susceptibilityAlongExhaustion\_eq\_abs\_h},
$\chi_{\mathrm{along}}(|h|) = \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(h) + M_{\mathrm{along}}(|h|) - M_{\mathrm{along}}(h)$.
$\mathrm{Ferromagnetic}\ \langle J, |h|, \beta\rangle$ holds by
$0 \le J$, $0 \le |h|$, $0 < \beta$, giving
$M_{\mathrm{along}}(|h|) \ge 0$. Via
\texttt{magnetizationAlongExhaustion\_neg\_h}, $M_{\mathrm{along}}(h) = -M_{\mathrm{along}}(|h|) \le 0$.
Thus the correction $M_{\mathrm{along}}(|h|) - M_{\mathrm{along}}(h) \ge 0$, and
$\chi_{\mathrm{along}}(|h|) \ge \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(h)$.
The concrete $\mathbb Z^d$ wrapper now lives in
\texttt{CorrelationSymmetry.lean}.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{susceptibilityInfinite}, PR~\#778]
For an exhaustion $\Lambda = (\Lambda_n)_{n : \mathbb N}$ of $V$ and a
site $i : V$,
\[
  \chi_\infty(G, \Lambda, p; i)
  := \sup_{n : \mathbb N} \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(G, \Lambda, p; i, n)
\]
(\texttt{ciSup} on $\mathbb R$: defaults to $0$ when the sequence is
unbounded above). Unlike $M$ and correlations which are bounded by $1$,
susceptibility is not automatically bounded; at the ferromagnetic
critical point, $\chi_{\mathrm{along}}$ diverges and the \texttt{ciSup}
default kicks in. Theorems comparing $\chi_\infty$ values typically
assume an explicit $\texttt{BddAbove}$ hypothesis in the unbounded
regime. Bundled: \texttt{\_eq\_ciSup}, \texttt{\_apply},
\texttt{\_nonneg} (ferromagnetic).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{susceptibilityInfinite\_le\_abs\_h},
PR~\#778 (A-5$'$, issue~\#770)]
For $0 \le J$, $0 < \beta$, any $h \in \mathbb R$, $i : V$, and under
the hypothesis that
$\{\chi_{\mathrm{along}}(\langle J, |h|, \beta\rangle; i, n) : n \in \mathbb N\}$
is bounded above,
\[
  \chi_\infty(\langle J, h, \beta\rangle; i)
  \le \chi_\infty(\langle J, |h|, \beta\rangle; i).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A-4c gives pointwise $\chi_{\mathrm{along}}(h) \le \chi_{\mathrm{along}}(|h|)$
at every $n$. The \texttt{BddAbove} hypothesis on the $|h|$-side and
pointwise comparison gives the same for the $h$-side. Apply
\texttt{ciSup\_mono} (mathlib).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{truncated2Infinite\_tendsto\_cofinite\_zero\_of\_summable},
PR~\#779]
For any ambient type $V$, graph $G$, exhaustion $\Lambda$, parameters
$p$, and fixed site $i : V$, if the function
$j \mapsto \mathrm{truncated2Infinite}\ G\ \Lambda\ p\ i\ j$ is summable
over $V$, then
\[
  \mathrm{Tendsto}\bigl(\lambda j,\ \mathrm{truncated2Infinite}\ G\ \Lambda\ p\ i\ j\bigr)
    \ \mathrm{Filter.cofinite}\ (\mathrm{nhds}\ 0).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Direct application of mathlib's \texttt{Summable.tendsto\_cofinite\_zero}.
\end{proof}
\noindent
\emph{Interpretation.} The summability hypothesis is a finiteness
condition on the two-point function summed over the free argument $j$;
in translation-invariant / connected-correlation settings (a pure phase
of a $\mathbb Z^d$ Ising model) it matches the physical ``finite
susceptibility'' condition expected away from the critical line, but in
the general ambient setup of the Lean statement it is simply the
real-analysis condition $\mathrm{Summable}$. $\mathrm{Filter.cofinite}$
on $V$ is the filter of cofinite subsets; on $\mathrm{Fin}\ d \to
\mathbb Z$ (with $d \ge 1$) bounded subsets are finite, so cofinite
aligns with the informal ``$|r| \to \infty$'' filter. This is therefore
a \emph{conditional} cluster decay statement (Glimm--Jaffe \S5.1).
Unconditional exponential decay (Simon--Lieb inequality) is not yet
formalized; this lemma is the elementary real-analysis step ready to be
composed with a future proof of summability. $\mathbb Z^d$ wrapper:
\texttt{truncated2Infinite\_latticeGraph\_tendsto\_cofinite\_zero\_of\_summable}.

\paragraph{$\ell^1$ lattice distance on $\mathbb Z^d$.}
As infrastructure for turning the above cofinite statement into a
distance-based statement (Epic~\#780), PR~\#781 introduces an
$\mathbb N$-valued $\ell^1$ distance on $\mathrm{Fin}\,d \to \mathbb Z$
defined by
\[
  d_{\mathrm{latt}}(x, y) \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,d}
    \lvert x_i - y_i \rvert_{\mathbb N}, \qquad
  \lvert \cdot \rvert_{\mathbb N} = \texttt{Int.natAbs}.
\]
The basic lemmas \texttt{latticeDistance\_self},
\texttt{latticeDistance\_comm},
\texttt{latticeDistance\_eq\_zero\_iff},
\texttt{latticeDistance\_triangle} give a full pseudo-metric structure,
and \texttt{latticeGraph\_adj\_iff\_latticeDistance\_eq\_one} ties the
new metric to the pre-existing adjacency relation
$\sum_i \lvert x_i - y_i\rvert = 1$ via the identity
$\lvert n \rvert = (\lvert n \rvert_{\mathbb N} : \mathbb Z)$.
The shortest-path metric agrees with this $\ell^1$ distance:
\texttt{latticeGraph\_dist\_eq\_latticeDistance} ($(\mathrm{latticeGraph}\,d).\mathrm{dist}\,x\,y
= \mathrm{latticeDistance}\,d\,x\,y$), using \texttt{latticeGraph\_connected},
the inductive geodesic step \texttt{latticeDistance\_exists\_adj\_step} (move one
coordinate toward $y$, reducing the distance by one), the geodesic walk
\texttt{latticeGraph\_exists\_walk\_length} (length $=$ distance, giving $\le$),
and the walk-length lower bound \texttt{latticeDistance\_le\_walk\_length} (giving $\ge$). The
companion Chebyshev ($\ell^\infty$) distance \texttt{latticeDistanceInf} $=
\max_i \lvert x_i - y_i\rvert$ is the lattice \emph{hyperplane separation} of
Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.5 (p.~312), in which the transfer matrix yields exponential
decay $e^{-m\cdot\mathrm{dist}}$. With \texttt{latticeDistanceInf\_self},
\texttt{latticeDistanceInf\_comm}, \texttt{latticeDistanceInf\_eq\_zero\_iff},
\texttt{latticeDistanceInf\_triangle}, and \texttt{latticeDistanceInf\_pos\_of\_ne}
(the $\ell^\infty$ pseudo-metric structure), together with
\texttt{latticeDistanceInf\_le\_latticeDistance}
($\ell^\infty \le \ell^1$), and \texttt{latticeDistance\_le\_card\_mul\_latticeDistanceInf}
($\lvert x-y\rvert_1 \le d\,\lvert x-y\rvert_\infty$), this records the geometric
input $\mathrm{dist} \ge \lvert x-y\rvert/a_0$ with $a_0 = d$ that converts
hyperplane-separation decay into $\ell^1$-distance decay at rate $m/d$. The
rate conversion itself (\texttt{ChebyshevRateBridge.lean}) is
\texttt{rate\_div\_card\_mul\_latticeDistance\_le} ($\tfrac{m}{d}\lvert x-y\rvert_1
\le m\lvert x-y\rvert_\infty$ for $m\ge 0$), \texttt{exp\_neg\_rate\_latticeDistanceInf\_le}
($e^{-m\lvert x-y\rvert_\infty} \le e^{-(m/d)\lvert x-y\rvert_1}$), and
\texttt{le\_exp\_neg\_rate\_latticeDistance\_of\_le\_exp\_neg\_latticeDistanceInf}
(a bound $c \le A e^{-m\lvert x-y\rvert_\infty}$ transfers to $c \le A
e^{-(m/d)\lvert x-y\rvert_1}$), exactly the step turning transfer-matrix decay
into the $e^{-m\cdot\mathrm{dist}}$ bound of Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.5. The bridge to
the project's $\ell^1$ machinery is \texttt{HasExponentialDecay\_of\_latticeDistanceInf\_bound}:
a hyperplane-separation decay $\lvert S^T_2(i,j)\rvert \le A e^{-m\lvert i-j\rvert_\infty}$
($i \ne j$) implies $\mathrm{HasExponentialDecay}\,d\,\Lambda\,p\,(m/d)$, feeding a
future transfer-matrix decay estimate into the $\mathrm{latticeMass}$ development
without the spectral operator. The
range is kept in $\mathbb N$ rather than in $\mathbb R$ to avoid
$\mathbb N$/$\mathbb Z$/$\mathbb R$ cast bookkeeping in the downstream
summability arguments (Simon--Lieb iteration) that this infrastructure
is meant to support. No mathlib
\texttt{PseudoMetricSpace} instance is registered at this stage.

\paragraph{1D Ising transfer matrix (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511 PR~1).}
The concrete instance of the Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1 transfer-matrix method is the
$2\times 2$ real matrix governing the one-dimensional Ising chain at zero
external field. With the two spin values $s : \mathrm{Fin}\,2 \to \mathbb R$,
$s_0 = +1$, $s_1 = -1$ (\texttt{spin1D}), the transfer matrix is
\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1D}$(a)_{ij} = e^{a\,s_i s_j}$ with $a = \beta J$, i.e.
$T(a) = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} e^a & e^{-a} \\ e^{-a} & e^a \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
It is symmetric (\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1D\_transpose}), entrywise positive
(\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1D\_pos}), with trace $2e^a$
(\texttt{trace\_isingTransferMatrix1D}) and determinant $e^{2a}-e^{-2a}$
(\texttt{det\_isingTransferMatrix1D}). The Hadamard vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$
are eigenvectors (\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1D\_mulVec\_hadamardTop} /
\texttt{...\_hadamardBot}) with eigenvalues
$\lambda_+ = e^a + e^{-a} = 2\cosh a$ (\texttt{transferEigenvalueTop}) and
$\lambda_- = e^a - e^{-a} = 2\sinh a$ (\texttt{transferEigenvalueBot}). The
spectral ratio $\lambda_-/\lambda_+ = \tanh a$
(\texttt{transferEigenvalue\_ratio}) is the source of the correlation decay rate
$-\log\tanh a$ for the ferromagnetic one-dimensional chain ($a = \beta J > 0$;
Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.5).

\paragraph{Transfer matrix with external field (\S17.1, Issue~\#3538 PR~1).}
The zero-field matrix extends to a general external field $h \ne 0$. Writing
$a = \beta J$, $b = \beta h$, the symmetric transfer matrix is
\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1DField}$(a,b)_{ij} =
\exp(a\,s_i s_j + \tfrac{b}{2}(s_i + s_j))$, explicitly
\[
  T(a,b) = \begin{pmatrix} e^{a+b} & e^{-a} \\ e^{-a} & e^{a-b} \end{pmatrix},
\]
symmetric (\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1DField\_transpose}), entrywise positive
(\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1DField\_pos}), with trace $2e^a\cosh b$
(\texttt{trace\_isingTransferMatrix1DField}) and determinant $e^{2a} - e^{-2a}$
(\texttt{det\_isingTransferMatrix1DField}). Unlike the zero-field case the
eigenvectors are no longer the fixed Hadamard pair, so the spectral data is
organised through the characteristic polynomial. With discriminant
$D(a,b) = e^{2a}\sinh^2 b + e^{-2a} > 0$
(\texttt{fieldTransferDiscriminant}, \texttt{fieldTransferDiscriminant\_pos}) the
eigenvalues are
\[
  \lambda_\pm = e^a\cosh b \pm \sqrt{D}
  \qquad (\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalueTop} / \texttt{Bot}),
\]
satisfying Vieta's relations $\lambda_+ + \lambda_- = \mathrm{tr}\,T = 2e^a\cosh b$
(\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalueTop\_add\_bot}) and $\lambda_+\lambda_- = \det T
= e^{2a} - e^{-2a}$ (\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalueTop\_mul\_bot}, using
$\sqrt{D}^2 = D$ and $\cosh^2 b = \sinh^2 b + 1$), hence the characteristic
equation $\lambda_\pm^2 = (\mathrm{tr}\,T)\,\lambda_\pm - \det T$
(\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalue\{Top,Bot\}\_sq}). The eigenvalues are ordered
$\lambda_- < \lambda_+$ (\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalueBot\_lt\_top}) and
positive, $0 < \lambda_+$ always and $0 < \lambda_-$ for $a > 0$
(\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalueTop\_pos},
\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalueBot\_pos}). At $b = 0$ the matrix and eigenvalues
reduce to the zero-field objects (\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1DField\_zero},
\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalue\{Top,Bot\}\_zero}). Foundational PR of the
general external-field 1D programme (Issue~\#3538); the partition function
$Z_N = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N$, free energy, magnetization $m(h)$, and
susceptibility $\partial_h m$ follow in later PRs.

\paragraph{Field partition function and free energy (\S17.1, Issue~\#3538 PR~2).}
With no Hadamard eigenbasis available for $h \ne 0$, the cyclic-chain partition
function $Z_N = \mathrm{Tr}\,T(a,b)^N$ is computed through the Cayley--Hamilton
recurrence. From \texttt{Matrix.aeval\_self\_charpoly} and
\texttt{Matrix.charpoly\_fin\_two} one gets
$T^2 = (\mathrm{tr}\,T)\,T - (\det T)\,\mathbb 1$
(\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1DField\_sq}), hence the matrix recurrence
$T^{N+2} = \mathrm{tr}\cdot T^{N+1} - \det\cdot T^N$
(\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1DField\_pow\_succ\_succ}) and, by linearity of the
trace, $s_{N+2} = \mathrm{tr}\cdot s_{N+1} - \det\cdot s_N$ with $s_N =
\mathrm{Tr}\,T^N$
(\texttt{trace\_isingTransferMatrix1DField\_pow\_succ\_succ}). The eigenvalue
powers $\lambda_\pm^N$ obey the same recurrence (the characteristic equation
$\lambda_\pm^2 = \mathrm{tr}\,\lambda_\pm - \det$) with the same initial data
$s_0 = 2 = \lambda_+^0 + \lambda_-^0$, $s_1 = \mathrm{tr} = \lambda_+ +
\lambda_-$, so two-step induction (\texttt{Nat.twoStepInduction}) gives
\[
  \mathrm{Tr}\,T(a,b)^N = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N
  \qquad (\texttt{trace\_isingTransferMatrix1DField\_pow}).
\]
For $a = \beta J > 0$ the subdominant ratio $\lambda_-/\lambda_+ \in [0,1)$
(\texttt{fieldTransferEigenvalue\_ratio\_\{nonneg,lt\_one\}}) gives
$(\lambda_-/\lambda_+)^N \to 0$
(\texttt{tendsto\_fieldTransferEigenvalue\_ratio\_pow}) and the free-energy
density $\tfrac1N \log(\lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N) \to \log\lambda_+$
(\texttt{tendsto\_log\_fieldEigenvalueSum\_div\_nat}), hence
$\tfrac1N \log\mathrm{Tr}\,T(a,b)^N \to \log\lambda_+$
(\texttt{tendsto\_log\_trace\_isingTransferMatrix1DField\_pow\_div\_nat}) --- the
free-energy density of the 1D Ising chain in a field. Issue~\#3538 PR~2; next:
magnetization $m(h)$ and susceptibility $\partial_h m$.

\paragraph{Field magnetization (\S17.1, Issue~\#3538 PR~3).}
The magnetization of the 1D Ising chain in a field is the field-derivative of the
free-energy density $\log\lambda_+$:
\[
  m(h) = \partial_b \log\lambda_+(a,b)
       = \frac{\sinh b}{\sqrt{\sinh^2 b + e^{-4a}}}
  \qquad (\texttt{fieldMagnetization}).
\]
The closed form rests on the discriminant factorisation $\sqrt{D} =
e^a\sqrt{\sinh^2 b + e^{-4a}}$ (\texttt{sqrt\_fieldTransferDiscriminant}, from
$D = e^{2a}(\sinh^2 b + e^{-4a})$ and $\sqrt{e^{2a}} = e^a$). Differentiating
$D$ (\texttt{hasDerivAt\_fieldTransferDiscriminant}, $\partial_b D =
e^{2a}\cdot 2\sinh b\cosh b$), then $\sqrt{D}$
(\texttt{HasDerivAt.sqrt}), $e^a\cosh b$ (\texttt{Real.hasDerivAt\_cosh}), and
$\log\lambda_+$ (\texttt{HasDerivAt.log}), the logarithmic derivative
$(\partial_b\lambda_+)/\lambda_+$ collapses to $\sinh b/\sqrt{\sinh^2 b +
e^{-4a}}$ (\texttt{hasDerivAt\_log\_fieldTransferEigenvalueTop}). The
magnetization vanishes at zero field, $m(a,0) = 0$
(\texttt{fieldMagnetization\_zero}) --- no spontaneous magnetization in one
dimension --- and is strictly sub-saturated, $|m| < 1$
(\texttt{abs\_fieldMagnetization\_lt\_one}), since $\sqrt{\sinh^2 b + e^{-4a}} >
|\sinh b|$ (the field gap $e^{-4a} > 0$). Issue~\#3538 PR~3; next: susceptibility
$\partial_h m$.

\paragraph{Field susceptibility (\S17.1, Issue~\#3538 PR~4).}
Differentiating the magnetization once more gives the susceptibility
\[
  \chi = \partial_b m
       = \frac{\cosh b\,e^{-4a}}{(\sinh^2 b + e^{-4a})^{3/2}}
  \qquad (\texttt{fieldSusceptibility}),
\]
strictly positive (\texttt{fieldSusceptibility\_pos}). By the quotient rule
(\texttt{HasDerivAt.div}) on $m = \sinh b/\sqrt{X}$ with $X = \sinh^2 b +
e^{-4a}$, using $(\sqrt{X})^2 = X$ and $X - \sinh^2 b = e^{-4a}$, the derivative
collapses to the closed form (\texttt{hasDerivAt\_fieldMagnetization}). The
physical susceptibility is $\partial_h m = \beta\,\chi$
(\texttt{hasDerivAt\_fieldMagnetization\_field}, chain rule through $b = \beta h$),
and at zero field $\chi(a,0) = e^{2a}$ (\texttt{fieldSusceptibility\_zero}), so
$\partial_h m|_0 = \beta e^{2a}$ --- the gap-enhanced zero-field susceptibility of
the 1D chain. This completes the exact solution of the 1D Ising chain in a field:
matrix $\to$ eigenvalues $\to$ partition function $\to$ free energy $\to$
magnetization $\to$ susceptibility (Issue~\#3538).

\paragraph{General finite layer transfer matrix (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The higher-dimensional transfer-matrix route begins with an abstract finite
layer state space $\Omega$. Given a one-layer weight $u:\Omega\to R$ and a
transition weight $k:\Omega\to\Omega\to R$, the file
\texttt{TransferMatrix/LayerTransfer.lean} defines
\[
  \texttt{layerTransferMatrix}\;u\;k\;(a,b) = u(b)\,k(a,b).
\]
For a periodic layer configuration $c:\mathrm{Fin}(m+1)\to\Omega$, the induced
closed-walk weight is
\[
  \prod_i u(c_{i+1})\,k(c_i,c_{i+1})
  \quad(\texttt{layerClosedWalkWeight\_eq\_prod}).
\]
The finite layer partition trace is the trace of the transfer-matrix power, and
the closed-walk trace identity gives
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}(T^{m+1})
   = \sum_{c:\mathrm{Fin}(m+1)\to\Omega}
      \prod_i u(c_{i+1})\,k(c_i,c_{i+1})
  \quad(\texttt{layerTransferPartition\_trace\_eq\_sum\_prod}).
\]
The same file also packages the one-insertion trace
$\operatorname{Tr}(D_fT^n)$ and the two-insertion trace
$\operatorname{Tr}(D_fT^aD_fT^b)$ through the marked layer weight
\texttt{layerMarkedClosedWalkWeight}; this wrapper uses the positive separation
hypothesis $0<b$ to hide the redundant nonzero total-length instance. These are
finite matrix identities over a
commutative semiring and contain no spectral gap, Perron--Frobenius theorem,
lattice hyperplane identification, thermodynamic limit, or exponential-decay
estimate. Those are the later hyperplane and spectral steps of Issue~\#3511.
Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306.

\paragraph{Finite cyclic layer Gibbs representation (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The Gibbs-sum side of the same finite layer abstraction is recorded in
\texttt{TransferMatrix/LayerGibbs.lean}. For a positive-length periodic stack
$c:\mathrm{Fin}\,N\to\Omega$,
\[
  \texttt{layerCyclicGibbsWeight}\;u\;k\;c
    = \prod_i u(c_{i+1})\,k(c_i,c_{i+1}),
\]
and \texttt{layerCyclicPartition} sums this weight over all such stacks. The
partition theorem
\texttt{layerCyclicPartition\_eq\_trace} identifies the Gibbs partition sum
with \texttt{layerTransferPartitionTrace} by reducing $N$ to $m+1$ and applying
the trace identity above. Positivity lemmas
\texttt{layerCyclicGibbsWeight\_pos} and
\texttt{layerCyclicPartition\_pos} package the strictly positive finite-volume
case.

For two insertions, \texttt{layerMarkedCyclicGibbsWeight} inserts the observable
$f$ at the sites $0$ and $a$ of a cycle of length $a+b$ with $0<b$, and
\texttt{layerTwoPointNumerator} sums the marked weights. The trace bridge
\[
  \texttt{layerTwoPoint}\;u\;k\;f
   = \frac{\operatorname{Tr}(D_fT^aD_fT^b)}{\operatorname{Tr}(T^{a+b})}
\]
is \texttt{layerTwoPoint\_eq\_trace\_ratio}. The entry points
\texttt{LayerState}\,S, \texttt{layerSpinAt}, and
\texttt{layerSpinTwoPoint\_eq\_trace\_ratio} specialise this abstract observable
to a spin at a fixed transverse site of a finite hyperplane layer. This is still
only the finite abstract hyperplane bridge: concrete $\mathbb{Z}^d$ box edge
factorisation, Perron--Frobenius theory, thermodynamic limits, and exponential
decay are intentionally left to later Issue~\#3511 steps. Reference:
Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306.

\paragraph{Finite cyclic layer cylinders (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
\texttt{TransferMatrix/LayerCylinder.lean} adds the concrete finite stack side
of the preceding abstraction. The cylinder site type is
\[
  \texttt{LayerCylinderSite}\;N\;S = \mathrm{Fin}\,N \times S,
\]
and \texttt{layerCylinderConfigEquiv} reindexes an ordinary spin configuration
on this product as a cyclic family of layer states
$\mathrm{Fin}\,N\to\texttt{LayerState}\,S$. The Ising-facing weights
\texttt{layerInternalWeight} and \texttt{layerTransitionWeight} package,
respectively, the transverse graph contribution plus field term inside one
layer, and the finite adjacent-layer pair contribution.

The concrete stack partition sum \texttt{layerCylinderPartition} is reindexed to
the abstract Gibbs layer sum by
\texttt{layerCylinderPartition\_eq\_layerCyclicPartition}, and hence to the
transfer trace by \texttt{layerCylinderPartition\_eq\_trace}. The specialisations
\texttt{isingLayerCylinderPartition\_eq\_layerCyclicPartition} and
\texttt{isingLayerCylinderPartition\_eq\_trace} apply this to the Ising internal
and transition weights. The same reindexing is available for same-transverse-site
two-point numerators:
\texttt{layerCylinderSpinTwoPointNumerator\_eq\_layerTwoPointNumerator} gives
\texttt{layerCylinderSpinTwoPoint\_eq\_layerSpinTwoPoint} and the trace-ratio
form \texttt{layerCylinderSpinTwoPoint\_eq\_trace\_ratio}. This remains a finite
periodic cylinder bridge; open-boundary boxes, Perron--Frobenius theory,
thermodynamic limits, and exponential decay are still later Issue~\#3511 steps.
Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306.

\paragraph{Finite layer-cylinder graph and stack-weight bridge (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
\texttt{TransferMatrix/LayerCylinderGraph.lean} adds the project-level graph
side of the finite periodic layer cylinder. For a transverse graph $H$ and a
finite set of directed transverse pairs $E$, the internal edge finset copies
$H.\texttt{edgeFinset}$ into each layer, and the transition edge finset contains
the unordered pairs
\[
  s((i,x),(i+1,y)) \qquad ((x,y)\in E).
\]
The graph \texttt{layerCylinderGraph} is the \texttt{SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet}
generated by the union of those two explicit finite edge sets. The sanity
lemmas show that these generated edges are non-diagonal for $2\le N$, giving
\texttt{layerCylinderGraph\_edgeFinset\_eq}: the project-level graph
\texttt{edgeFinset} is exactly the explicit cylinder edge finset.

The project-level Gibbs API is then expanded over this edge decomposition:
\texttt{boltzmannWeight\_layerCylinderGraph\_eq\_edge\_field\_prod} gives the
Boltzmann weight as an edge-factor product times the site-field product, and
\texttt{partitionFunction\_layerCylinderGraph\_eq\_sum\_edge\_field\_prod}
gives the corresponding partition-function sum. For $3\le N$, the transition
edge parametrisation is injective as an unordered edge family; this excludes the
$N=2$ collapse where opposite periodic transition edges become the same
\texttt{Sym2} edge. The product split lemmas for internal edges, transition
edges, and one-body fields then give
\texttt{layerCylinderEdgeFieldProd\_eq\_layerCylinderStackWeight}.

The resulting finite bridge identifies the project-level graph API with the
concrete cyclic layer stack:
\texttt{boltzmannWeight\_layerCylinderGraph\_eq\_layerCylinderStackWeight} and
\texttt{partitionFunction\_layerCylinderGraph\_eq\_isingLayerCylinderPartition}.
For two insertions at the same transverse site, it also gives
\texttt{correlation\_layerCylinderGraph\_same\_transverse\_eq\_layerCylinderSpinTwoPoint}
and the trace-ratio corollary
\texttt{correlation\_layerCylinderGraph\_same\_transverse\_eq\_trace\_ratio}.
Open slab/box geometry, Perron--Frobenius theory, thermodynamic limits, and
exponential decay remain later Issue~\#3511 steps. Reference: Glimm--Jaffe,
2nd ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306.

\paragraph{Cubic transverse boxes as layer cylinders (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
\texttt{TransferMatrix/CubicLayerCylinder.lean} specialises the abstract
finite periodic layer-cylinder bridge to a concrete transverse cubic box in the
integer lattice. The transverse site type is
\[
  \texttt{CubicLayerSite}\;d\;R =
  \uparrow(\texttt{Ambient.cubicBox}\;d\;R),
\]
and the transverse graph is
\[
  \texttt{cubicLayerGraph}\;d\;R =
  \texttt{Ambient.inducedGraph}\;(\texttt{latticeGraph}\;d)\;
    (\texttt{Ambient.cubicBox}\;d\;R).
\]
Adjacent periodic layers are coupled by the identity transition pairs
\texttt{cubicLayerTransitionPairs}, so \texttt{cubicLayerCylinderGraph} is
exactly \texttt{layerCylinderGraph} for this concrete transverse graph and
transition set. The project-level bridges are the corresponding specialisations
of the general graph-stack theorems:
\texttt{boltzmannWeight\_cubicLayerCylinderGraph\_eq\_layerCylinderStackWeight},
\texttt{partitionFunction\_cubicLayerCylinderGraph\_eq\_isingLayerCylinderPartition},
and
\texttt{correlation\_cubicLayerCylinderGraph\_same\_transverse\_eq\_trace\_ratio}.
The result is still a finite periodic cylinder over a finite transverse box;
open longitudinal slabs/boxes, Perron--Frobenius theory, thermodynamic limits,
and exponential decay remain later Issue~\#3511 steps.

\paragraph{Finite positive layer spectral scaffold (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The layer spectral file records the finite algebra needed before the
higher-dimensional Perron--Frobenius step.  Four predicates give the basic
entrywise-matrix and vector positivity vocabulary.  Positive one-layer and
transition weights make the layer transfer matrix entrywise positive; products
and positive powers of entrywise positive finite matrices stay positive, so
positive powers have positive trace.  A strictly positive right eigenpair has
positive eigenvalue, but no existence or uniqueness theorem is asserted here.

For a positive layer weight \(u\), the generally non-symmetric transfer matrix
\(T_{ab}=u_b k_{ab}\) is diagonally similar to the balanced matrix
\[
  S_{ab}=\sqrt{u_a}\,k_{ab}\,\sqrt{u_b}.
\]
Writing \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt u)\), the formal identity is
\[
  T = D^{-1} S D
\]
as recorded by the diagonal-similarity theorem in the Lean file.  Consequently
the partition trace and the two-insertion marked trace are unchanged by
replacing \(T\) by \(S\).  If the transition weight \(k\) is symmetric, then
\(S\) is symmetric, giving the future spectral route a symmetric finite matrix
without changing the cyclic layer observables.

Finally, \texttt{LayerSpectralGapCertificate} packages later spectral input as
a positive scale, a subdominant ratio \(\theta<1\), a lower bound on
\(\operatorname{Tr}(T^N)\), and an upper bound on the marked trace.  The
consumer theorems turn such a certificate into an exponential bound for the
finite cyclic layer two-point trace ratio.  This is a certificate scaffold only:
Perron--Frobenius existence, spectral radius, open-slab geometry, thermodynamic
limits, and final
hyperplane exponential decay remain later Issue~\#3511 steps.

\paragraph{Balanced spectral certificates (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The same finite certificate language is also available directly on the
balanced matrix \(S\).  A balanced certificate records the scale, ratio, and
prefactors together with a lower bound on \(\operatorname{Tr}(S^N)\) and an
upper bound on the balanced marked trace.  Positivity of \(u\) transports this
data back to the ordinary transfer matrix \(T\), because the diagonal
similarity preserves both traces used in the cyclic two-point ratio.  Thus the
future symmetric spectral argument can work on \(S\), while the consumer
theorems still apply to the original finite layer observable.  The constructors
only package explicit trace-bound hypotheses; they do not prove
Perron--Frobenius existence, a spectral-radius theorem, open-slab geometry,
thermodynamic limits, or final hyperplane decay.

\paragraph{Finite orthogonal layer spectral input (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The next finite spectral bridge connects the balanced matrix \(S\) to the
ordinary real Hermitian spectral theorem.  When \(k\) is symmetric, the balanced
matrix is Hermitian.  The Lean file therefore exposes the spectral-theorem
eigenvalues and eigenbasis for \(S\), proves that the eigenbasis diagonalizes
the balanced transfer matrix, and records the finite trace identity
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}(S^N)=\sum_i \lambda_i^N .
\]
For arguments that prefer explicit algebraic data rather than a direct
dependency on the Hermitian spectral theorem, the structure
\texttt{RealOrthogonalSpectralData} packages an orthogonal diagonalization
\[
  M=P\,\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)\,P^T .
\]
It gives the corresponding formula for powers, the partition trace, and the
two-insertion marked trace after transporting the marking matrix to the
spectral basis:
\[
  \operatorname{Tr}(D_f M^a D_f M^b)
  = \sum_{i,j} G_{ij}G_{ji}\lambda_j^a\lambda_i^b,
  \qquad G=P^T D_f P .
\]
The constructor
\texttt{layerBalancedSpectralGapCertificate\_of\_orthogonalSpectralData}
uses these finite spectral-basis formulas together with explicit partition and
one-sided marked-trace bounds to produce a balanced certificate.  The one-sided
cyclic marked-trace estimate is an assumption of the constructor, not a
consequence proved from positivity in this PR.  Thus the development supplies
finite spectral input behind the certificate while still leaving
Perron--Frobenius existence, spectral-radius maximality, open-slab geometry,
thermodynamic limits, and final hyperplane exponential decay for later
Issue~\#3511 work.

\paragraph{Dominant finite spectral-basis bounds (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The next finite step remains inside the same orthogonal spectral-basis setting.
It proves that concrete dominance and cancellation hypotheses imply the
trace-bound inputs required by the balanced certificate.  Suppose a dominant
index \(\ast\) is chosen with \(\lambda_\ast=s>0\), \(0\le \theta<1\), and
\[
  i\ne \ast \quad\Longrightarrow\quad |\lambda_i|\le \theta s .
\]
Then the remaining eigenvalues give the finite lower bound
\[
  \sum_i \lambda_i^N
    \ge s^N-(|\Omega|-1)(\theta s)^N
    \ge \bigl(1-(|\Omega|-1)\theta\bigr)s^N ,
  \qquad N>0,
\]
where the last inequality uses \(0\le\theta\le1\).  The Lean theorem
\texttt{partition\_lower\_of\_dominant\_bounds} records this estimate with
\texttt{finiteSpectralPartitionPrefactor}.  For the marked trace, let
\(G=P^T D_f P\) and assume the one-sided dominant-channel cancellation
\[
  G_{i\ast}G_{\ast i}=0 \qquad\text{for all } i.
\]
Then the terms with \(j=\ast\) vanish in the marked-trace formula, while all
remaining terms satisfy
\[
  |G_{ij}G_{ji}\lambda_j^a\lambda_i^b|
  \le |G_{ij}G_{ji}|\,s^{a+b}\theta^a .
\]
Thus
\[
  \left|\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}G_{ji}\lambda_j^a\lambda_i^b\right|
  \le
  \left(\sum_{i,j}|G_{ij}G_{ji}|\right)s^{a+b}\theta^a .
\]
This is formalised by the marked-trace spectral-prefactor theorem.  The
balanced certificate constructor with suffix
\texttt{orthogonalDominantBounds} combines the partition and marked estimates
into a balanced certificate.
The positivity bridge to mathlib's graph-theoretic matrix vocabulary records
that entrywise positive balanced layer matrices are primitive and irreducible.
These statements are still conditional finite spectral estimates: they do not
prove a Perron--Frobenius eigenvector, spectral-radius maximality, the
dominant-channel cancellation for spin observables, open-slab geometry,
thermodynamic limits, or final hyperplane exponential decay.  Reference:
Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306.

\paragraph{Hermitian spectral data and min-separation marked bounds (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The finite spectral route now also records the cyclic estimate that is natural
before passing to an infinite-volume or long-cylinder limit.  The constructor
\texttt{RealOrthogonalSpectralData.ofHermitian} turns mathlib's Hermitian
spectral theorem into explicit real orthogonal spectral data, and
\texttt{layerSymmetricTransferOrthogonalSpectralData} applies this to the
balanced layer matrix when the transition weight is symmetric.  In these real
orthogonal coordinates the transported marking matrix
\[
  G = P^T D_f P
\]
is symmetric (\texttt{markedMatrix\_transpose},
\texttt{markedMatrix\_comm}).

The one-sided cancellation used by the previous finite certificate,
\(G_{i\ast}G_{\ast i}=0\) for every \(i\), is intentionally left as a strong
conditional hypothesis.  For a finite periodic cylinder, the more natural
dominant-channel condition is only the removal of the non-decaying
dominant-dominant term:
\[
  G_{\ast\ast}=0.
\]
Under the same dominant spectral data
\(\lambda_\ast=s>0\) and
\(|\lambda_i|\le \theta s\) for \(i\ne\ast\), every remaining summand in
\[
  \sum_{i,j}G_{ij}G_{ji}\lambda_j^a\lambda_i^b
\]
has a subdominant eigenvalue on at least one of the two cyclic arcs.  Hence
\[
  \left|\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}G_{ji}\lambda_j^a\lambda_i^b\right|
  \le
  \left(\sum_{i,j}|G_{ij}G_{ji}|\right)s^{a+b}\theta^{\min(a,b)} .
\]
This is the theorem
\texttt{marked\_sum\_abs\_le\_spectralPrefactor\_min}.  The structure
\texttt{LayerBalancedMinSpectralGapCertificate} packages the corresponding
balanced finite certificate, with constructors from explicit spectral data and
from the Hermitian spectral-theorem data.  Its consumers give the cyclic
two-arc bound for \texttt{layerTwoPoint}; if \(a\le b\), the theorem
\texttt{layerTwoPoint\_abs\_le\_left\_of\_balancedMinSpectralGapCertificate}
rewrites the result as the familiar one-sided factor \(\theta^a\).

This is still a conditional finite spectral estimate.  It does not prove
Perron--Frobenius existence, spectral-radius maximality, the condition
\(G_{\ast\ast}=0\) for spin observables, open-slab geometry, thermodynamic
limits, or final hyperplane exponential decay.  Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd
ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306 and \S17.5, pp.~311--312.

\paragraph{Spin-flip symmetry and dominant-channel cancellation (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The finite layer route now records the zero-field symmetry which supplies the
dominant-dominant marked-channel cancellation for spin observables, provided
the chosen dominant spectral column is even under global layer flip.  The
equivalence \texttt{layerStateFlipEquiv} is the global flip on
\texttt{LayerState}; the fixed-site spin observable is odd under it by
\texttt{layerSpinAt\_flip}.  On the Ising-facing layer weights,
\texttt{layerInternalWeight\_flip\_of\_h\_zero} proves one-layer invariance at
\(h=0\), and \texttt{layerTransitionWeight\_flip\_flip} proves adjacent-layer
transition invariance under simultaneous flip of the two layers.

The balanced transfer matrix respects any weight-preserving relabelling
({\scriptsize\texttt{layerSymmetricTransferMatrix\_equiv\_equiv}}); its spin-flip
specialisation is \texttt{layerSymmetricTransferMatrix\_flip\_flip}.  The
matrix-vector form
{\scriptsize\texttt{layerSymmetricTransferMatrix\_mulVec\_comp\_equiv}}
is the corresponding commutation statement for later spectral-column
arguments.  For explicit orthogonal spectral data, the entry expansion
\texttt{RealOrthogonalSpectralData.markedMatrix\_apply} gives
\[
  G_{ij}=\sum_x Q_{xi} f(x) Q_{xj}.
\]
If \(f\) is odd under an involutive equivalence \(\tau\) and the dominant
column \(Q_{\cdot\ast}\) is even under \(\tau\), reindexing this finite sum by
\(\tau\) changes its sign and therefore
\[
  G_{\ast\ast}=0.
\]
This is formalised by
{\scriptsize\texttt{RealOrthogonalSpectralData.markedMatrix\_diagonal\_zero\_of\_equiv\_odd\_even}};
the layer-spin specialisation is
{\scriptsize\texttt{RealOrthogonalSpectralData.markedMatrix\_layerSpinAt\_diagonal\_zero\_of\_flip\_even}}.
The constructors
{\scriptsize\texttt{layerBalancedMinSpectralGapCertificate\_of\_orthogonalDominantBounds\_flipEvenSpin}}
and
{\scriptsize\texttt{layerBalancedMinSpectralGapCertificate\_of\_layerHermitianDominantBounds\_flipEvenSpin}}
therefore replace the explicit \(G_{\ast\ast}=0\) hypothesis of the finite
min-separation certificate by the flip-even dominant-column hypothesis for
spin observables.

This is still a conditional finite bridge.  It does not prove that the
dominant Perron--Frobenius column exists, is spectrally maximal, or is
flip-even; it also does not prove open-slab geometry, thermodynamic limits, or
final hyperplane exponential decay.  Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed.,
\S17.1, pp.~304--306 and \S17.5, pp.~311--312.

\paragraph{Positive/simple dominant-column flip-even bridge (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The new \texttt{LayerPerron} module adds the finite linear-algebra bridge used
after a Perron--Frobenius argument has supplied a positive dominant eigenvector
and a one-dimensional dominant eigenspace.  The spectral-data column lemma first
records that each column of explicit orthogonal spectral data is a right
eigenvector with the corresponding spectral-data eigenvalue.  The scalar
normalisation lemma then shows that if a strictly positive vector \(v\)
satisfies \(v\circ\tau=c\,v\) for an involutive equivalence \(\tau\), then
applying the identity twice gives \(c^2=1\), and positivity forces \(c=1\).
Hence \(v\circ\tau=v\).

The main flip-even lemma applies this to a finite matrix \(M\) commuting with
\(\tau\).  If \(Mv=\lambda v\), \(v>0\), and every \(\lambda\)-eigenvector is a
scalar multiple of \(v\), then \(v\circ\tau\) is again a \(\lambda\)-eigenvector,
so simplicity gives \(v\circ\tau=c\,v\), and the positivity lemma gives
\(v\circ\tau=v\).  The layer wrapper uses the already proved balanced-transfer
commutation under global layer flip.

The new spin-observable constructors therefore replace the direct
dominant-column flip-even hypothesis in the min-separation route by
positive-column and simple-eigenspace inputs.  This is still finite and
conditional: it does not prove
Perron--Frobenius existence, spectral-radius maximality, strict spectral gap,
open-slab geometry, thermodynamic limits, or final hyperplane exponential
decay.  Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306 and \S17.5,
pp.~311--312.

\paragraph{Positive-column eigenvalue-radius bound (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The next finite Perron-facing step is a weak Collatz--Wielandt comparison.
The lemma {\scriptsize\texttt{exists\_positive\_vector\_abs\_bound\_attained}}
chooses the least coordinatewise scale \(C\) against a strictly positive
vector \(v\), so that \(|w_i|\le C v_i\), and records a coordinate where
equality holds.  If \(M\) is entrywise positive, \(Mv=\lambda v\) with
\(v>0\), and \(Mw=\mu w\), the attaining coordinate gives
\[
  |\mu|\,C v_i
    = |(Mw)_i|
    \le \sum_j M_{ij}|w_j|
    \le \sum_j M_{ij}C v_j
    = \lambda\,C v_i .
\]
Since \(C v_i>0\), this proves \(|\mu|\le\lambda\).  This is formalised as
{\scriptsize\texttt{abs\_eigenvalue\_le\_of\_entrywisePositive\_positive\_eigenpair}}.

For explicit orthogonal spectral data, columns are nonzero right eigenvectors,
and a positive top column has a positive eigenvalue.  The wrappers
{\scriptsize\texttt{RealOrthogonalSpectralData.eigenvalue\_abs\_le\_of\_positive\_column}}
and
{\scriptsize\texttt{layerSymmetricTransfer\_eigenvalue\_abs\_le\_of\_positive\_column}}
therefore show that such a top column bounds every spectral-data eigenvalue in
absolute value.  The scale-fixed finite-certificate constructors then take the
transfer scale to be this top eigenvalue, leaving the strict subdominant
\(\theta\)-bound and the marked-channel cancellation as explicit hypotheses.
This still does not prove Perron--Frobenius existence, uniqueness of the
positive column, a strict subdominant gap, open-slab geometry, thermodynamic
limits, or final hyperplane exponential decay.  Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd
ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306 and \S17.5, pp.~311--312.

\paragraph{Positive-column eigenspace simplicity and strict subdominant ratio (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511).}
The next finite positive-matrix step derives the simple-eigenspace input from
the positive column itself.  Given an entrywise positive matrix \(M\), a
strictly positive eigenpair \(Mv=\lambda v\), and another vector
\(Mw=\lambda w\), choose
\[
  C=\max_i \frac{w_i}{v_i},\qquad z=Cv-w .
\]
Then \(z_i\ge 0\) for all \(i\), and \(z_{i_0}=0\) at an attaining coordinate.
Since \(Mz=\lambda z\),
\[
  0=(Mz)_{i_0}=\sum_j M_{i_0j}z_j .
\]
Each summand is nonnegative and every \(M_{i_0j}\) is strictly positive, so
all \(z_j\) vanish.  Thus \(w=Cv\).  This is formalised as
{\scriptsize\texttt{eigenvector\_smul\_of\_entrywisePositive\_positive\_eigenpair}}.

The strict comparison uses this one-dimensionality argument for \(M^2\).  If
\(Mw=\mu w\), \(w\ne0\), and equality held in the weak bound
\(|\mu|\le\lambda\), then \(w\) would be an eigenvector of \(M^2\) with
eigenvalue \(\lambda^2\).  Since \(v\) is a positive eigenvector of \(M^2\),
the preceding argument forces \(w\) to be a scalar multiple of \(v\), hence
\(\mu=\lambda\).  Therefore every different real eigenvalue satisfies
\(|\mu|<\lambda\).

For explicit orthogonal spectral data, distinct columns are not scalar
multiples.  A positive top column therefore spans its eigenspace, every
non-top column has strictly smaller absolute eigenvalue, and finiteness gives
some \(\theta<1\) with
\[
  |\lambda_i|\le \theta\,\lambda_\ast \qquad (i\ne\ast).
\]
The layer wrappers expose these facts for the balanced Hermitian transfer
matrix, and the new positive-column spin-observable certificate constructors
derive the simple-eigenspace input from positivity.  The quantitative
certificate condition \(((|\Omega|-1)\theta)<1\) remains an explicit input, and
this still does not prove Perron--Frobenius existence of the positive column,
open-slab geometry, thermodynamic limits, or final hyperplane exponential
decay.  Reference: Glimm--Jaffe, 2nd ed., \S17.1, pp.~304--306 and \S17.5,
pp.~311--312.

\paragraph{Diagonalization and matrix powers (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511 PR~2).}
The Hadamard matrix $H = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$
(\texttt{hadamardMatrix}) satisfies $H^2 = 2\,\mathbb 1$
(\texttt{hadamardMatrix\_mul\_self}), $\det H = -2$
(\texttt{hadamardMatrix\_det}), $H^{-1} = \tfrac12 H$
(\texttt{hadamardMatrix\_inv}). With $D(a) = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_+, \lambda_-)$
(\texttt{transferDiagonal}), the inverse-free Hadamard intertwining
$T(a)\,H = H\,D(a)$ (\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1D\_mul\_hadamard}) powers by
induction to $T(a)^N H = H\,D(a)^N$
(\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1D\_pow\_mul\_hadamard}), i.e.\ the diagonalization
$T(a)^N = H\,D(a)^N H^{-1}$ (\texttt{isingTransferMatrix1D\_pow\_eq\_conj}) with
$D(a)^N = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_+^N, \lambda_-^N)$
(\texttt{transferDiagonal\_pow}). The trace is the cyclic-chain partition
function (for physical $N \ge 1$) $Z_N = \operatorname{Tr}(T(a)^N) = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N$
(\texttt{trace\_isingTransferMatrix1D\_pow}, a pure algebraic identity for all $N$, via \texttt{trace\_mul\_comm} and
$H^{-1}H = \mathbb 1$), and $\det(T(a)^N) = (\lambda_+\lambda_-)^N$
(\texttt{det\_isingTransferMatrix1D\_pow}) -- the transfer-matrix solution of the
one-dimensional Ising chain (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{1D free-energy density (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511 PR~3).}
Building on $\operatorname{Tr}(T(a)^N) = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N$, the per-site
log-partition (dimensionless free-energy) density of the one-dimensional chain
($a = \beta J > 0$) is
$\lim_{N\to\infty} \tfrac1N \log \operatorname{Tr}(T(a)^N) = \log \lambda_+ = \log(2\cosh a)$
(\texttt{tendsto\_log\_trace\_pow\_div\_nat}, \texttt{log\_transferEigenvalueTop\_eq}).
The mechanism is the spectral gap $\lambda_- < \lambda_+$
(\texttt{transferEigenvalueBot\_lt\_top}) with ratio
$\lambda_-/\lambda_+ = \tanh a \in (0,1)$
(\texttt{transferEigenvalue\_ratio\_pos}, \texttt{transferEigenvalue\_ratio\_lt\_one}):
writing $\lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N = \lambda_+^N (1 + \tanh^N a)$, the subdominant
eigenvalue contributes the vanishing correction
$\tfrac1N \log(1 + \tanh^N a) \to 0$ (since $\tanh^N a \to 0$,
\texttt{tendsto\_transferEigenvalue\_ratio\_pow}), leaving the dominant
$\log\lambda_+$ (\texttt{tendsto\_log\_eigenvalueSum\_div\_nat}).  Since
$Z_N = \operatorname{Tr}(T(a)^N)$ for the cyclic chain, this is the transfer-matrix
solution of the 1D Ising free energy $f = -\beta^{-1}\log(2\cosh\beta J)$
(Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Closed-walk trace identity (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511 PR~4).}
The combinatorial core of $Z_N = \operatorname{Tr}(T^N)$, for an arbitrary finite
matrix $M : \mathrm{Matrix}\,\iota\,\iota\,R$ over a commutative semiring (Mathlib
has no such lemma, only the $0/1$ adjacency case). With the open-path weight
$\texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\sigma = \prod_{i : \mathrm{Fin}\,n} M(\sigma\,i_{\mathrm{cast}})(\sigma\,i_{\mathrm{succ}})$
and the append rule
$\texttt{pathWeight}(M, \mathrm{snoc}\,\sigma\,x) = \texttt{pathWeight}(M,\sigma)\cdot M(\sigma(\mathrm{last}\,n))\,x$
(\texttt{pathWeight\_snoc}), the entry formula
$(M^n)_{ab} = \sum_{\sigma : \mathrm{Fin}(n{+}1)\to\iota} [\sigma_0 = a \wedge \sigma_{\mathrm{last}} = b]\,\texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\sigma$
(\texttt{pow\_apply\_eq\_sum}) is proved by induction, peeling the last edge via
$\texttt{Fin.snocEquiv}$. Specialising to the diagonal and summing gives the
\emph{closed-walk trace identity}
$\operatorname{Tr}(M^n) = \sum_{\sigma : \mathrm{Fin}(n{+}1)\to\iota} [\sigma_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{last}}]\,\texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\sigma$
(\texttt{trace\_pow\_eq\_sum}), a weighted sum over vertex sequences returning to
their start. The cyclic form
$\texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,M\,\sigma = \prod_{i} M(\sigma\,i)(\sigma(i{+}1))$
(cyclic in $\mathrm{Fin}\,n$) factors as
$\texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,\tau = \texttt{pathWeight}\,\tau \cdot M(\tau(\mathrm{last}))(\tau\,0)$
(\texttt{closedWalkWeight\_succ}), underlying the cyclic 1D Ising
$Z_N = \operatorname{Tr}(T^N)$ (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Cyclic trace identity and 1D evaluation (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511 PR~5).}
Reindexing the open-return form by the \texttt{init}/\texttt{snoc} bijection
($\texttt{Finset.sum\_bij'}$) between vertex sequences with $\sigma_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{last}}$
and closed walks (using $\texttt{pathWeight\_eq\_closedWalkWeight\_init}$,
$\texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\sigma = \texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,M\,(\mathrm{init}\,\sigma)$
when $\sigma_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{last}}$) yields the purely cyclic identity
$\operatorname{Tr}(M^{m+1}) = \sum_{\tau : \mathrm{Fin}(m{+}1)\to\iota} \texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,M\,\tau$
(\texttt{trace\_pow\_eq\_sum\_cycle}). Specialising to the 1D Ising transfer
matrix $T(a)$ over the spin space $\mathrm{Fin}\,2$ and combining with the
spectral trace $\operatorname{Tr}(T(a)^{m+1}) = \lambda_+^{m+1} + \lambda_-^{m+1}$
gives the cyclic partition function as eigenvalue powers,
$\sum_{\sigma : \mathrm{Fin}(m{+}1)\to\mathrm{Fin}\,2} \texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,T(a)\,\sigma = \lambda_+^{m+1} + \lambda_-^{m+1}$
(\texttt{sum\_closedWalkWeight\_isingTransferMatrix1D}), i.e.\ the transfer-matrix
evaluation $Z_N = \operatorname{Tr}(T^N) = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N$ of the cyclic
$N$-site zero-field Ising chain (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Two-point function via the transfer matrix (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511 PR~6).}
The transfer-matrix expression for the two-point function is
$\operatorname{Tr}(S\,T^n S\,T^{N-n})/\operatorname{Tr}(T^N)$ (its identification with the
Gibbs $\langle\sigma_0\sigma_n\rangle$ via the cyclic config sum is a later step)
with the spin operator $S = \mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$ (\texttt{spinOperator}). The spin
operator swaps the Hadamard eigenvectors, $S\,H = H\,P$ with $P$ the $2\times2$
swap (\texttt{spinOperator\_mul\_hadamard}), hence $H^{-1}SH = P$ and
$P\,D(a)^k P = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_-^k, \lambda_+^k)$. This gives the two-point
trace $\operatorname{Tr}(S\,T^n S\,T^m) = \lambda_-^n\lambda_+^m + \lambda_+^n\lambda_-^m$
(\texttt{twoPointTrace}), so
$\langle\sigma_0\sigma_n\rangle_N = (r^n + r^{N-n})/(1 + r^N)$ with $r = \lambda_-/\lambda_+ = \tanh a$
(\texttt{twoPointCorrelation\_eq\_ratio}). For $a = \beta J > 0$ the subdominant
ratio $r \in (0,1)$ makes the boundary terms vanish, giving the exact exponential
decay $\langle\sigma_0\sigma_n\rangle_N \to (\tanh\beta J)^n$ as $N\to\infty$
(\texttt{tendsto\_twoPointCorrelation}), with correlation length
$\xi = -1/\log\tanh\beta J$ (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Cycle-graph edge enumeration and partition function (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511 PR~7).}
To bridge the project's graph-based Ising partition function on the cyclic chain
to the transfer-matrix's linear site product, the edges of the cycle graph are
enumerated (Mathlib provides only the adjacency):
$(\texttt{cycleGraph}(n{+}2)).\texttt{edgeFinset} = \{\,s(i, i{+}1) : i \in \mathrm{Fin}(n{+}2)\,\}$
(\texttt{cycleGraph\_edgeFinset\_eq\_image}, via $\texttt{Sym2.ind}$ and
$\texttt{cycleGraph\_adj}$). With the injectivity of $i \mapsto s(i, i{+}1)$ on
$\mathrm{Fin}(n{+}3)$ (\texttt{cyclePair\_injective}) this gives the product
reindexing $\prod_{e} f(e) = \prod_{i} f(s(i,i{+}1))$
(\texttt{prod\_cycleGraph\_edgeFinset}) and the edge count $n{+}3$
(\texttt{card\_cycleGraph\_edgeFinset}). Combined with the $h=0$ Boltzmann edge
product (\texttt{boltzmannWeight\_eq\_prod\_exp\_of\_h\_zero}), the partition
function of the cyclic $N$-site chain ($N = n{+}3$) becomes a linear site product
$Z_N = \sum_\sigma \prod_{i} e^{\beta J\,\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}}$
(\texttt{partitionFunction\_cycleGraph\_eq\_sum\_prod}) -- the transfer-matrix
shape (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Gibbs partition function $Z_N = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N$ (\S17.1, Issue~\#3511 PR~8, capstone).}
Via the spin$\leftrightarrow\mathrm{Fin}\,2$ encoding $\texttt{spinEquivFin2}$
($\mathrm{up}\mapsto 0$, $\mathrm{down}\mapsto 1$), under which
$\texttt{spin1D}(\mathrm{encode}\,s) = \mathrm{sign}(s)$ and the Boltzmann edge
factor becomes a transfer-matrix entry
$T(\beta J)(\mathrm{encode}\,s)(\mathrm{encode}\,t) = e^{\beta J\,\mathrm{sign}(s)\mathrm{sign}(t)}$,
the per-configuration site product is a closed-walk weight of the encoded
configuration (\texttt{prod\_exp\_edgeSpin\_eq\_closedWalkWeight}). Reindexing the
configuration sum along $(\mathrm{Fin}\,N \to \mathrm{Spin}) \simeq (\mathrm{Fin}\,N \to \mathrm{Fin}\,2)$
and applying $\texttt{sum\_closedWalkWeight\_isingTransferMatrix1D}$ gives the
classic transfer-matrix evaluation of the Gibbs partition function,
$\texttt{partitionFunction}(\texttt{cycleGraph}\,N)\,\langle J,0,\beta\rangle = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N = (2\cosh\beta J)^N + (2\sinh\beta J)^N$
(\texttt{partitionFunction\_cycleGraph\_eq\_eigenvaluePow}), completing the
transfer-matrix evaluation of $Z_N$ (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Correlation length and mass (\S17.1, \S17.5).}
Writing the two-point decay $\langle\sigma_0\sigma_n\rangle_N \to (\tanh\beta J)^n$
as a pure exponential identifies the mass $m = -\log\tanh\beta J$
(\texttt{correlationMass}, the inverse correlation length, the \S17.5 mass) and
correlation length $\xi = 1/m$ (\texttt{correlationLength}), with $m, \xi > 0$ for
$a = \beta J > 0$ (\texttt{correlationMass\_pos}, \texttt{correlationLength\_pos}).
Then $(\tanh\beta J)^n = e^{-m n}$ (\texttt{tanh\_pow\_eq\_exp\_neg\_mass}) gives
$\langle\sigma_0\sigma_n\rangle_N \to e^{-m n}$
(\texttt{tendsto\_twoPointCorrelation\_exp\_neg\_mass}) -- exponential decay at the
inverse correlation length (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1, \S17.5).

\paragraph{Susceptibility (\S17.1).}
Summing the two-point decay rate over separations gives the magnetic
susceptibility. With $r = \tanh\beta J \in [0,1)$ the geometric series
$\sum_n r^n = (1-r)^{-1}$ converges (\texttt{summable\_tanh\_pow},
\texttt{tsum\_tanh\_pow}), and the two-sided lattice sum gives
$\chi = (1+\tanh\beta J)/(1-\tanh\beta J) = 2\sum_n r^n - 1$
(\texttt{isingSusceptibility1D}, \texttt{isingSusceptibility1D\_eq\_two\_tsum\_sub\_one}),
strictly positive and finite for $\beta J > 0$ (\texttt{isingSusceptibility1D\_pos}),
diverging only as $\beta J \to \infty$ -- the 1D Ising chain has no
finite-temperature phase transition (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Gibbs free-energy density (\S17.1).}
Combining the eigenvalue free-energy limit with the Gibbs $Z_N = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N$
identity gives the free-energy density of the project's \emph{Gibbs} partition
function on the cyclic chain:
$\tfrac1N \log \texttt{partitionFunction}(\texttt{cycleGraph}\,N)\langle J,0,\beta\rangle \to \log(2\cosh\beta J)$
(\texttt{tendsto\_log\_partitionFunction\_cycleGraph\_div\_nat}, over $N = n{+}3$),
and the physical Helmholtz density
$-(\beta N)^{-1}\log Z_N \to -\beta^{-1}\log(2\cosh\beta J)$
(\texttt{tendsto\_gibbs\_freeEnergy\_density}) -- the Gibbs (not merely
transfer-trace) 1D Ising free-energy density (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Trace with diagonal insertions (\S17.1).}
Toward the Gibbs two-point function $\langle\sigma_0\sigma_n\rangle = \operatorname{Tr}(S\,T^n S\,T^{N-n})/\operatorname{Tr}(T^N)$,
the trace with two diagonal insertions $D = \mathrm{diagonal}\,d$ expands as
$\operatorname{Tr}(D\,M^a D\,M^b) = \sum_{i,j} d_i\,d_j\,(M^a)_{ij}(M^b)_{ji}$
(\texttt{trace\_diagonal\_pow\_diagonal\_pow\_expand}), with the single-insertion
form $\operatorname{Tr}(D\,M^a) = \sum_i d_i (M^a)_{ii}$
(\texttt{trace\_diagonal\_mul\_pow}) and the cyclic symmetry
$\operatorname{Tr}(D\,M^a D\,M^b) = \operatorname{Tr}(D\,M^b D\,M^a)$
(\texttt{trace\_diagonal\_pow\_diagonal\_pow\_comm}); the marked closed-walk form
$\sum_\tau d(\tau_0)d(\tau_a)\,\texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,M\,\tau$ (gluing two open
paths) is the next step (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Cyclic-to-open closed-walk conversion (\S17.1).}
The technical key for the marked closed-walk identity, avoiding all cyclic
$\mathrm{Fin}$-arithmetic, is
$\texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,M\,\tau = \texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,(\mathrm{snoc}\,\tau\,(\tau\,0))$
(\texttt{closedWalkWeight\_eq\_pathWeight\_snoc\_zero}): appending the first vertex
turns the cyclic closed walk into an open path returning to its start, whose
open-path weight is the cyclic weight. The marked summand
$\texttt{markedClosedWalkWeight}\,M\,d\,\tau = d(\tau_0)d(\tau_a)\,\texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,M\,\tau$
then has the open-path form \texttt{markedClosedWalkWeight\_eq} (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Path gluing (\S17.1).}
Gluing two open paths $\sigma : \mathrm{Fin}(a{+}1)\to\iota$,
$\rho : \mathrm{Fin}(b{+}1)\to\iota$ at a shared vertex ($\rho_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{last}}$)
by appending the interior of $\sigma$ to $\rho$ multiplies their path weights,
$\texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,(\mathrm{append}\,(\mathrm{init}\,\sigma)\,\rho) = \texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\sigma \cdot \texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\rho$
(\texttt{pathWeight\_append}, by induction on $b$ peeling $\rho$ via
$\texttt{Fin.append\_snoc}$). The marked glue
$\texttt{markedGlue}\,\sigma\,\rho = \mathrm{append}\,(\mathrm{init}\,\sigma)\,(\mathrm{init}\,\rho)$
is the closed walk with marks $\texttt{markedGlue}\,\sigma\,\rho\,0 = \sigma_0$ and at
site $a$ equal to $\rho_0$ (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).
Under the gluing conditions $\rho_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{last}}$ and
$\rho_{\mathrm{last}} = \sigma_0$, its cyclic closed-walk weight factors as
$\texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,M\,(\texttt{markedGlue}\,\sigma\,\rho) = \texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\sigma \cdot \texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\rho$
(\texttt{closedWalkWeight\_markedGlue}), via the open-path conversion and
$\texttt{pathWeight\_append}$.

\paragraph{Marked trace as a sum over glued pairs (\S17.1).}
Reordering four nested sums (\texttt{sum\_reorder\_4}, a \texttt{calc} chain of
$\texttt{Finset.sum\_comm}$) and collapsing the endpoint sums, the trace with two
diagonal insertions becomes a sum over glued open-path pairs:
$\operatorname{Tr}(D\,M^a D\,M^b) = \sum_{\sigma,\rho} [\sigma_{\mathrm{last}}=\rho_0 \wedge \rho_{\mathrm{last}}=\sigma_0]\, d(\sigma_0)d(\rho_0)\,\texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\sigma\cdot\texttt{pathWeight}\,M\,\rho$
(\texttt{trace\_diagonal\_pow\_diagonal\_pow\_eq\_sum\_glued}). With
\texttt{closedWalkWeight\_markedGlue} this is the marked closed-walk trace identity
up to the path-pair bijection (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Marked closed-walk trace identity (\S17.1).}
The reconstruction maps $\texttt{σOf}\,\tau = \mathrm{snoc}\,(\tau\circ\mathrm{castAdd}\,b)\,(\tau\,a)$,
$\texttt{ρOf}\,\tau = \mathrm{snoc}\,(\tau\circ\mathrm{natAdd}\,a)\,(\tau\,0)$ satisfy
$\texttt{markedGlue}\,(\texttt{σOf}\,\tau)\,(\texttt{ρOf}\,\tau) = \tau$
(\texttt{markedGlue\_σOf\_ρOf}, via $\texttt{Fin.append\_castAdd\_natAdd}$). The
$\texttt{Finset.sum\_bij'}$ bijection between closed walks and glued path pairs then
yields the marked closed-walk trace identity
$\operatorname{Tr}(D\,M^a D\,M^b) = \sum_{\tau : \mathrm{Fin}(a{+}b)\to\iota} d(\tau_0)\,d(\tau_a)\,\texttt{closedWalkWeight}\,M\,\tau$
(\texttt{trace\_diagonal\_pow\_diagonal\_pow\_eq\_sum\_markedClosedWalk}) -- the
combinatorial core of the Gibbs two-point function (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{1D marked closed-walk sum (\S17.1).}
Specialising to the 1D Ising transfer matrix $T(a)$ with marks
$\texttt{spin1D} = (1,-1)$ (so the marking matrix is $S = \mathrm{diagonal}\,\texttt{spin1D}$,
\texttt{spinOperator\_eq\_diagonal\_spin1D}) and combining with \texttt{twoPointTrace},
the closed-walk form of the two-point numerator is
$\sum_{\tau : \mathrm{Fin}(n{+}m)\to\mathrm{Fin}\,2} \texttt{markedClosedWalkWeight}\,T(a)\,\texttt{spin1D}\,\tau = \lambda_-^n\lambda_+^m + \lambda_+^n\lambda_-^m$
(\texttt{sum\_markedClosedWalkWeight\_isingTransferMatrix1D}, $= \operatorname{Tr}(S\,T^n S\,T^m)$),
the bridge toward the Gibbs two-point function (Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1).

\paragraph{Gibbs two-point function as the transfer-matrix ratio (\S17.1).}
This is the standard cyclic transfer-matrix computation of the 1D Ising
two-point function, providing the Gibbs reading of the mass and exponential-decay
discussion of Glimm--Jaffe~\S17.1.
The previous paragraphs supply the transfer-matrix numerator
$\operatorname{Tr}(S\,T^n S\,T^m)$ in closed-walk form; it remains to identify the
project's \emph{Gibbs} correlation
$\langle\sigma_0\sigma_n\rangle = \texttt{correlation}\,(\texttt{cycleGraph}\,N)\,\langle J,0,\beta\rangle\,\{0,n\}$
